corporate-business.title: Business essentials
corporate-business.description: Finance for non-finance people, Excel and analytics, product management, project management (PMP-style, Agile, Scrum, Kanban), negotiation and sales — explained with Indian and global examples.

courses.title: Finance for non-finance managers
courses.summary: Read a P&L, balance sheet and cash-flow statement, understand margins, unit economics and break-even, and build a simple business case with payback and NPV.
outcomes: Learners can read a P&L and explain gross margin, EBITDA and net profit
Learners can explain the balance sheet equation and why cash differs from profit
Learners can compute break-even and unit economics
Learners can build a simple business case with payback and NPV

scenes.text: Aditya runs operations for a Jaipur D2C clothing brand. Revenue grew 40% this year and the team celebrated.
The CFO says profit fell. Aditya is confused: 'How can we sell more and earn less?'
She walks him down the P&L: discounts and courier costs rose faster than sales, and marketing spend doubled.
Aditya now watches gross margin and contribution per order, not just revenue.

steps.title: The P&L ladder
steps.body:
A **profit and loss statement (P&L)** shows performance over a period (month, quarter, year):
- **Revenue** (sales, net of returns and discounts)
- − **Cost of goods sold (COGS)** — direct costs of what you sold (materials, manufacturing, direct labour)
- = **Gross profit** → *Gross margin % = gross profit ÷ revenue*
- − **Operating expenses (Opex)** — salaries, rent, marketing, software
- = **EBITDA** (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation)
- − **Depreciation & amortisation**
- = **EBIT / operating profit**
- − **Interest** − **Tax**
- = **Net profit (PAT, profit after tax)**

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Revenue ₹10 crore; COGS ₹6 crore → gross profit ₹4 crore (**40% gross margin**).
Opex ₹2.5 crore → EBITDA ₹1.5 crore (15%).
Depreciation ₹0.3 crore → EBIT ₹1.2 crore.
Interest ₹0.2 crore → profit before tax ₹1.0 crore.
Tax (assume 25%) ₹0.25 crore → **net profit ₹0.75 crore (7.5%)**.

If revenue grows 40% but COGS grows 60% (more discounts, costlier shipping), gross margin falls — exactly Aditya's problem.

steps.title: Questions to ask about any P&L
steps.body:
- What's the **gross margin** trend? (Pricing power and cost control.)
- Which **opex lines** are growing faster than revenue?
- Is EBITDA positive? Is the business **operationally profitable**?
- What's **one-off** vs recurring?
- How does this compare to **budget** and **last year**?

steps.title: Common confusions
steps.body:
- **Revenue ≠ profit.** Growth can destroy value if margins are negative.
- **EBITDA ≠ cash.** It ignores capital spending, working capital and interest.
- **Margin vs markup:** a product costing ₹60 sold at ₹100 has a 40% margin (40/100) but a 67% markup (40/60).

activity.prompt: Put the P&L lines in order from top to bottom.
items: Revenue
Cost of goods sold
Gross profit
Operating expenses
EBITDA
Depreciation & amortisation
EBIT (operating profit)
Interest and tax
Net profit (PAT)

quiz.q: Gross margin % equals…
quiz.why: The answer is "Gross profit ÷ revenue". Reason: Revenue minus COGS, as a share of revenue. The other choices, such as "Opex ÷ revenue" and "Revenue ÷ COGS", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: EBITDA excludes…
quiz.why: The answer is "Interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation". Reason: It's earnings before those items. The other choices, such as "COGS" and "Salaries", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A product costs ₹60 and sells for ₹100. Its margin is…
quiz.why: The answer is "40%". Reason: 40/100 = 40%. (Markup is 40/60 ≈ 67%.). The other choices, such as "100%" and "60%", do not fit the question. (Question: A product costs ₹60 and sells for ₹100. Its margin is…)

quiz.q: Why can profit fall while revenue rises?
quiz.why: The answer is "Costs (COGS/opex) grow faster than revenue". Reason: Margins matter. The other choices, such as "It can't" and "Tax is always 100%", do not fit the question.

lessons.title: Balance sheet, cash flow and working capital

scenes.text: Sunita's auto-parts firm in Pune lands a big order from a car maker. The P&L shows a healthy profit.
But the customer pays in 90 days, while Sunita must pay suppliers in 30 and salaries every month.
By month two she can't pay suppliers. Her bank explains: 'Profit is an opinion; cash is a fact.'
She negotiates 60-day supplier terms and arranges a working-capital loan. The order becomes a success.

steps.title: The balance sheet
steps.body:
A **balance sheet** is a snapshot at a point in time:
**Assets = Liabilities + Equity**
- **Assets:** what the business owns or is owed — cash, receivables (money customers owe), inventory, machines, software.
- **Liabilities:** what it owes — payables to suppliers, loans, taxes due.
- **Equity:** owners' stake — capital invested plus retained profits.

It always balances because every rupee of assets is financed either by borrowing or by owners.

steps.title: Cash flow statement
steps.body:
Shows how cash moved in a period, in three parts:
- **Operating:** cash from running the business (profit adjusted for non-cash items and working-capital changes).
- **Investing:** buying/selling assets (machines, acquisitions).
- **Financing:** loans, repayments, equity raised, dividends.

A company can show profit and still run out of cash if customers pay slowly, inventory piles up, or big investments are made.

steps.title: Worked example: the cash conversion cycle
steps.body:
**Cash conversion cycle (CCC) = inventory days + receivable days − payable days.**
Sunita: inventory 30 days + receivables 90 days − payables 30 days = **90 days** her cash is tied up.
After negotiating supplier terms to 60 days: 30 + 90 − 60 = **60 days**.
Shorter CCC = less cash needed to grow. Levers: collect faster, hold less inventory, pay later (fairly — Indian MSME rules require timely payment to registered micro and small suppliers).

steps.title: Manager's takeaway
steps.body: Even if you don't work in finance, your decisions affect cash: payment terms you agree with customers, inventory you order, capital projects you request. Ask: *'When does the cash come in, and when does it go out?'*

activity.prompt: A business has inventory days of 45, receivable days of 60 and payable days of 40. What is its cash conversion cycle in days?

quiz.q: The balance sheet equation is…
quiz.why: The answer is "Assets = Liabilities + Equity". Reason: It always balances. The other choices, such as "Cash = Profit" and "Assets = Revenue", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Receivables are…
quiz.why: The answer is "Money customers owe the company". Reason: An asset. The other choices, such as "Money the company owes suppliers" and "Inventory", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Why can a profitable company run out of cash?
options: Customers pay slowly and inventory/investments tie up cash
quiz.why: The answer is "Customers pay slowly and inventory/investments tie up cash". Reason: Timing of cash flows. The other choices, such as "Profit is always cash" and "Taxes are zero", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Cash conversion cycle = …
options: Inventory days + receivable days − payable days
quiz.why: The answer is "Inventory days + receivable days − payable days". Reason: Days cash is tied up. The other choices, such as "Revenue ÷ cost" and "Payables − receivables", do not fit the question.

scenes.text: Zoya opens a cloud kitchen in Bengaluru. Orders are booming on delivery apps.
Her mentor asks: 'After food cost, packaging, app commission and discounts, what do you earn per order?' Zoya doesn't know.
It's ₹18 per order. Her monthly fixed costs are ₹2.7 lakh. She needs 15,000 orders a month just to break even.
She cuts discounts, raises prices on bestsellers and adds high-margin combos. Contribution rises to ₹45 and break-even drops to 6,000 orders.

steps.title: Fixed vs variable costs; contribution
steps.body:
- **Variable costs** change with each unit sold (ingredients, packaging, commission, delivery).
- **Fixed costs** stay roughly the same regardless of volume within a range (rent, salaries, software).
- **Contribution per unit = price − variable cost per unit.**
- **Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit.**

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Zoya (revised): average order ₹350; variable costs ₹305 (food ₹120, packaging ₹25, app commission ₹90, discount ₹40, other ₹30). Contribution = ₹45.
Fixed costs ₹2,70,000/month → **break-even = 2,70,000 ÷ 45 = 6,000 orders/month** (≈ 200 a day).

steps.title: Unit economics for subscription and tech businesses
steps.body:
- **CAC (customer acquisition cost)** = sales & marketing spend ÷ new customers.
- **LTV (lifetime value)** ≈ average monthly contribution per customer × expected customer lifetime (months).
- A common rule of thumb in SaaS is **LTV : CAC of about 3 : 1 or better**, and **CAC payback** within roughly a year — heuristics, not laws.
- **Churn** (customers leaving) dramatically affects LTV: if monthly churn is 5%, average lifetime ≈ 1 ÷ 0.05 = 20 months.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating discounts as marketing and forgetting they reduce contribution.
- Ignoring returns and cancellations (very significant in Indian e-commerce, including cash-on-delivery refusals).
- 'We'll make it up on volume' — if contribution is negative, more volume means bigger losses.

activity.prompt: A product sells for ₹500, variable cost is ₹300 per unit, and fixed costs are ₹6,00,000 per month. How many units per month to break even?

quiz.q: Contribution per unit is…
quiz.why: The answer is "Price − variable cost". Reason: What each unit contributes to fixed costs and profit. The other choices, such as "Price − fixed cost" and "Revenue × margin", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Break-even units equal…
quiz.why: The answer is "Fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit". Reason: Standard formula. The other choices, such as "Profit ÷ cost" and "Variable ÷ fixed", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: With 5% monthly churn, average customer lifetime is about…
quiz.why: The answer is "20 months". Reason: 1 ÷ 0.05 = 20. The other choices, such as "5 months" and "50 months", do not fit the question. (Question: With 5% monthly churn, average customer lifetime is about…)

quiz.q: If contribution per unit is negative, growing volume…
quiz.why: The answer is "Increases losses". Reason: Each unit loses money. The other choices, such as "Creates profit" and "Has no effect", do not fit the question.

lessons.title: Building a business case: payback and NPV

scenes.text: Manish proposes ₹1.2 crore of sorting robots for a Gurugram warehouse. He says it 'will save a lot'.
The CFO asks: 'How much, when, and compared to what?'
Manish builds a business case: ₹40 lakh savings a year for 5 years, a payback of 3 years, and an NPV at 12%.
Approved — with a pilot milestone at month six.

steps.title: Structure of a business case
steps.body:
- **Problem / opportunity** (with numbers).
- **Options** (including do nothing).
- **Costs:** upfront (capex) and ongoing (opex).
- **Benefits:** savings, revenue, risk reduction — over time.
- **Financial metrics:** payback, NPV, sometimes IRR.
- **Risks and assumptions** — and sensitivity (what if savings are 30% lower?).
- **Recommendation and milestones.**

steps.title: Payback and time value of money
steps.body:
**Payback period** = how long until cumulative benefits equal the investment. Manish: ₹1.2 crore ÷ ₹40 lakh/year = **3 years**. Simple, but it ignores benefits after payback and the time value of money.

**Time value of money:** ₹100 today is worth more than ₹100 in a year (you could invest it). **Discounting** converts future cash to today's value: PV = CF ÷ (1 + r)^t, where r is the discount rate (often the company's cost of capital).

steps.title: Worked example: NPV
steps.body:
Investment ₹120 lakh today; savings ₹40 lakh/year for 5 years; discount rate 12%.
Present values: Year 1: 40/1.12 ≈ 35.7; Y2: 40/1.2544 ≈ 31.9; Y3: ≈ 28.5; Y4: ≈ 25.4; Y5: ≈ 22.7. Sum ≈ **144.2 lakh**.
**NPV = 144.2 − 120 ≈ +₹24 lakh** → positive, so it creates value at a 12% hurdle rate.
In Excel: =NPV(12%, savings range) − investment (note Excel's NPV assumes the first value is one period from now).

steps.title: Sensitivity analysis
steps.body: Test the key assumptions: if savings are only ₹30 lakh/year, PV ≈ 108 lakh → NPV ≈ −₹12 lakh. Now leadership knows **the case depends on achieving savings above roughly ₹33 lakh/year** — which is why a pilot milestone makes sense. Presenting sensitivity shows honesty and builds trust.

activity.label: Annual savings from the robots (₹ lakh), 5 years, 12% discount rate, ₹120 lakh investment

bands.text: NPV clearly negative (about −₹48 lakh at ₹20 lakh/yr; −₹12 lakh at ₹30 lakh/yr). Don't invest unless strategic reasons justify it.
Close to break-even (NPV ≈ 0 near ₹33 lakh/yr). Pilot first and validate savings.
Positive NPV (≈ +₹24 lakh at ₹40 lakh/yr). Good case if assumptions hold.
Strongly positive NPV (≈ +₹96 lakh at ₹60 lakh/yr). Check whether such savings are realistic.

quiz.q: Payback period ignores…
options: Benefits after payback and time value of money
quiz.why: The answer is "Benefits after payback and time value of money". Reason: It's simple but limited. The other choices, such as "The investment" and "Costs", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A positive NPV at the company's discount rate means…
options: The project is expected to create value
quiz.why: The answer is "The project is expected to create value". Reason: PV of benefits exceeds cost. The other choices, such as "Payback is under one year" and "Nothing", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: The present value of ₹40 lakh received in one year at 12% is about…
quiz.why: The answer is "₹35.7 lakh". Reason: 40 ÷ 1.12 ≈ 35.7. The other choices, such as "₹30 lakh" and "₹44.8 lakh", do not fit the question. (Question: The present value of ₹40 lakh received in one year at 12% is about…)

quiz.q: Sensitivity analysis shows…
options: How results change if key assumptions change
quiz.why: The answer is "How results change if key assumptions change". Reason: Tests robustness. The other choices, such as "The font size" and "Market share", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Gross profit = …
questions.why: The answer is "Revenue − COGS". Reason: Definition. The other choices, such as "Net profit + tax" and "Assets − liabilities", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Assets = …
questions.why: The answer is "Liabilities + Equity". Reason: Balance sheet equation. The other choices, such as "Revenue − Cost" and "Profit", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Fixed costs are costs that…
options: Don't change with volume in a range
questions.why: The answer is "Don't change with volume in a range". Reason: Rent, salaries. The other choices, such as "Change per unit" and "Are always zero", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Selling at ₹100 with cost ₹75: margin is…
questions.why: The answer is "25%". Reason: 25/100. The other choices, such as "75%" and "100%", do not fit the question. (Question: Selling at ₹100 with cost ₹75: margin is…)

questions.q: Customers paying in 90 days increases…
questions.why: The answer is "Receivable days and cash needs". Reason: Cash tied up. The other choices, such as "Profit directly" and "Equity", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Break-even: fixed ₹3,00,000; contribution ₹150/unit →
questions.why: The answer is "2,000 units". Reason: 300000/150. The other choices, such as "1,500 units" and "3,000 units", do not fit the question. (Question: Break-even: fixed ₹3,00,000; contribution ₹150/unit →)

questions.q: EBITDA is not the same as cash because it ignores…
questions.why: The answer is "Capex, working capital and interest". Reason: Non-cash and financing items. The other choices, such as "Revenue" and "COGS", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Investing cash flow includes…
questions.why: The answer is "Buying machines". Reason: Asset purchases. The other choices, such as "Paying salaries" and "Taking a loan", do not fit the question. (Question: Investing cash flow includes…)

questions.q: Payback: ₹90 lakh investment, ₹30 lakh/yr savings →
questions.why: The answer is "3 years". Reason: 90/30. The other choices, such as "4 years" and "30 years", do not fit the question. (Question: Payback: ₹90 lakh investment, ₹30 lakh/yr savings →)

questions.q: LTV with ₹500 monthly contribution and 4% monthly churn ≈
questions.why: The answer is "₹12,500". Reason: Lifetime 25 months × ₹500. The other choices, such as "₹5,000" and "₹20,000", do not fit the question. (Question: LTV with ₹500 monthly contribution and 4% monthly churn ≈)

questions.q: CCC with inventory 20, receivables 45, payables 35 days =
questions.why: The answer is "30 days". Reason: 20+45−35. The other choices, such as "65 days" and "100 days", do not fit the question. (Question: CCC with inventory 20, receivables 45, payables 35 days =)

questions.q: A project's NPV is positive at 10% but negative at 15%. This tells you…
options: Its value depends on the hurdle rate; IRR is between 10% and 15%
questions.why: The answer is "Its value depends on the hurdle rate; IRR is between 10% and 15%". Reason: IRR is where NPV = 0. The other choices, such as "It's always bad" and "It's always good", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Revenue +40%, COGS +60%. Gross margin…
questions.why: The answer is "Falls". Reason: Costs outgrow sales. The other choices, such as "Rises" and "Doubles", do not fit the question. (Question: Revenue +40%, COGS +60%. Gross margin…)

courses.title: Excel and analytics for work
courses.summary: From messy data to decisions: essential formulas, lookups, pivot tables, clean data and simple dashboards — the spreadsheet skills every office uses.
outcomes: Learners can use core formulas with correct relative/absolute references
Learners can combine data with XLOOKUP or INDEX/MATCH
Learners can summarise data with pivot tables and SUMIFS
Learners can clean data and build a simple, honest dashboard

scenes.text: Rekha in a Kolkata FMCG firm copies a commission formula down 400 rows. The tax rate cell reference shifts with each row.
Half the commissions are calculated with blank cells as the rate. Payouts are wrong.
A colleague shows her the $ sign: $B$1 stays fixed when copied.
She also adds a check total. Errors like this are now caught before payouts.

steps.title: Core formulas
steps.body:
- **=SUM(B2:B100)**, **=AVERAGE()**, **=MIN()**, **=MAX()**, **=COUNT()** (numbers), **=COUNTA()** (non-empty).
- **=IF(C2>=100000,"Target met","Below")** — logic.
- **=ROUND(C2*0.18,2)** — rounding (e.g., GST at 18%).
- **=IFERROR(formula,0)** — handle errors gracefully (but don't hide real problems).
- **=TEXT(A2,"dd-mmm-yyyy")** — format dates as text.

steps.title: Relative vs absolute references
steps.body:
- **A1** (relative): changes when copied (A1 → A2 when copied down).
- **$A$1** (absolute): never changes.
- **$A1 / A$1** (mixed): locks column or row only.

Press **F4** (on Windows Excel) while editing a reference to cycle through these. Use absolute references for constants like tax rates, exchange rates, targets — and keep constants in clearly labelled cells, never typed inside formulas.

steps.title: Worked example: commission
steps.body:
B1 = commission rate (5%). Sales in C2:C401.
Commission in D2: **=C2*$B$1**, copied down. Check: **=SUM(D2:D401)** should equal **=SUM(C2:C401)*B1**. A quick check formula like this catches many errors.

steps.title: Spreadsheet risk
steps.body: Studies of real-world spreadsheets have repeatedly found errors are common. Protect yourself: label inputs, separate inputs/calculations/outputs, add check totals, avoid hard-coded numbers in formulas, and have someone review important models.

activity.prompt: Complete the formulas.
activity.text: To keep the tax rate in B1 fixed when copying, write =C2*___. To show 'Target met' if C2 is at least 1,00,000, write =___(C2>=100000,"Target met","Below").

quiz.q: Which reference stays fixed when copied?
quiz.why: The answer is "$A$1". Reason: Both row and column locked. The other choices, such as "None" and "A$1 only for columns", do not fit the question. (Question: Which reference stays fixed when copied?)

quiz.q: COUNTA counts…
quiz.why: The answer is "Non-empty cells". Reason: Any non-empty. The other choices, such as "Errors" and "Empty cells", do not fit the question. (Question: COUNTA counts…)

quiz.q: Why avoid typing constants inside formulas?
options: They're hard to find and update
quiz.why: The answer is "They're hard to find and update". Reason: Label inputs in cells. The other choices, such as "It's slower" and "Excel forbids it", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A check total helps…
quiz.why: The answer is "Catch calculation errors". Reason: Simple validation. The other choices, such as "Nothing" and "Print", do not fit the question. (Question: A check total helps…)

scenes.text: Imran in HR must match 8,000 employee IDs from the payroll file with departments from another file.
He starts doing it manually with Ctrl+F. It would take days.
A teammate writes one XLOOKUP formula and copies it down. Done in two minutes.
They also find 37 IDs that don't match — new joiners missing from the department list.

steps.title: XLOOKUP
steps.body:
Available in Microsoft 365 and Excel 2021 and later:
**=XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found])**
Example: **=XLOOKUP(A2, Depts!A:A, Depts!C:C, "Not found")** — finds A2's ID in column A of the Depts sheet and returns column C.

Advantages: looks left or right, exact match by default, built-in 'not found' value.

steps.title: INDEX/MATCH and VLOOKUP
steps.body:
For older versions:
- **=INDEX(Depts!C:C, MATCH(A2, Depts!A:A, 0))** — MATCH finds the row (0 = exact match), INDEX returns the value.
- **=VLOOKUP(A2, Depts!A:C, 3, FALSE)** — works only when the ID is the first column; **always use FALSE** (exact) for IDs, or you may get wrong matches silently.

steps.title: Why lookups fail
steps.body:
- Extra spaces: use **=TRIM()**.
- Numbers stored as text (e.g., '00123' vs 123): convert consistently.
- Duplicates in the lookup list: lookups return the first match only — check uniqueness.
- Approximate match accidentally on (VLOOKUP without FALSE).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Make two small tables: Table 1 with 10 employee IDs; Table 2 with IDs and departments (leave 2 IDs missing). Use XLOOKUP with 'Not found', then count the not-found rows with =COUNTIF(range,"Not found").

statements.s: VLOOKUP can look up a value to the left of the key column.
statements.why: VLOOKUP only returns columns to the right; XLOOKUP or INDEX/MATCH can look left.

statements.s: For IDs, VLOOKUP's last argument should be FALSE.
statements.why: Exact match avoids silent wrong results.

statements.s: Extra spaces can make lookups fail.
statements.why: Use TRIM to clean.

statements.s: MATCH(…,0) means approximate match.
statements.why: 0 means exact match.

quiz.q: XLOOKUP's fourth argument is…
quiz.why: The answer is "Value if not found". Reason: Built-in fallback. The other choices, such as "Column number" and "Sort order", do not fit the question. (Question: XLOOKUP's fourth argument is…)

quiz.q: INDEX/MATCH advantage over VLOOKUP is…
options: Can look left and is robust to column inserts
quiz.why: The answer is "Can look left and is robust to column inserts". Reason: Flexible. The other choices, such as "Faster typing" and "Only works on text", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: '00123' vs 123 mismatch is a problem of…
quiz.why: The answer is "Numbers stored as text". Reason: Make types consistent. The other choices, such as "Colours" and "Formulas", do not fit the question. (Question: '00123' vs 123 mismatch is a problem of…)

quiz.q: Duplicates in a lookup list cause…
options: The first match to be returned
quiz.why: The answer is "The first match to be returned". Reason: Check uniqueness. The other choices, such as "Nothing" and "An error always", do not fit the question.

scenes.text: Naveen has 50,000 rows of sales — date, state, product, amount. His manager asks: 'Sales by state by month, by tomorrow.'
Naveen thinks he'll need to write hundreds of formulas.
He builds a pivot table in three minutes: states as rows, months as columns, sum of amount as values.
He adds a SUMIFS check for one state to confirm the pivot is right.

steps.title: Pivot tables
steps.body:
Steps: select your data (ideally formatted as a Table with Ctrl+T), **Insert → PivotTable**, then drag fields:
- **Rows:** State
- **Columns:** Month (group dates by month)
- **Values:** Sum of Amount
- **Filters:** Product category

Refresh when data changes. Pivot tables summarise thousands of rows in seconds and let you slice data differently by dragging fields.

steps.title: SUMIFS and COUNTIFS
steps.body:
- **=SUMIFS(Amount, State, "Kerala", Month, "Jan")** — sum with multiple conditions.
- **=COUNTIFS(State, "Kerala", Amount, ">10000")** — count with conditions.
- **=AVERAGEIFS()** similarly.

Use them for fixed report layouts and to cross-check pivot results.

steps.title: Worked example: a cross-check
steps.body: Pivot says Kerala January sales = ₹42,31,000. Check with =SUMIFS(D:D, B:B, "Kerala", E:E, "Jan") → same. If different, look for typos (*'kerala '*, *'Kerla'*), missing dates or rows outside the pivot range.

steps.title: Analyst habits
steps.body:
- Keep raw data untouched in one sheet; analyse in another.
- Use Tables so ranges expand automatically.
- Note data source and date on every report.
- Explain the 'so what': *'Kerala sales dropped 18% in January, mostly in the snacks category.'*

activity.prompt: Match the task to the best tool.
pairs: Summarise sales by state and month quickly
Sum sales for one state and one month in a fixed report
Make ranges grow automatically as data is added

quiz.q: In a pivot table, 'Values' usually contain…
quiz.why: The answer is "Aggregations like sum or count". Reason: Summaries. The other choices, such as "Colours" and "Formulas only", do not fit the question. (Question: In a pivot table, 'Values' usually contain…)

quiz.q: SUMIFS allows…
quiz.why: The answer is "Summing with multiple conditions". Reason: Multi-criteria. The other choices, such as "Text only" and "Only one condition", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: After data changes, a pivot table needs…
quiz.why: The answer is "Refresh". Reason: Pivots don't auto-refresh by default. The other choices, such as "Nothing ever" and "Deletion", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Why keep raw data untouched?
options: Traceability and to avoid accidental changes
quiz.why: The answer is "Traceability and to avoid accidental changes". Reason: Audit trail. The other choices, such as "It's prettier" and "No reason", do not fit the question.

scenes.text: Priya's customer list has city names as 'Mumbai', 'Bombay', 'mumbai ', 'MUMBAI' and 'Mum'.
Her dashboard shows Mumbai with far fewer customers than reality.
She cleans the data: trims spaces, standardises case, maps synonyms with a lookup table, and removes duplicates.
Mumbai jumps to #1. The marketing budget is reallocated correctly.

steps.title: Cleaning checklist
steps.body:
- **TRIM** spaces; **PROPER/UPPER** for consistent case.
- **Standardise** synonyms (Bombay → Mumbai, Bengaluru/Bangalore) with a mapping table.
- **Remove duplicates** (Data → Remove Duplicates) — but first define what counts as a duplicate (same email? same phone?).
- **Fix data types:** dates as dates, numbers as numbers.
- **Handle blanks:** decide whether to exclude, fill, or flag.
- **Validate:** totals and counts before vs after cleaning.

steps.title: A simple dashboard
steps.body:
- **3–5 key metrics** at the top (e.g., revenue, orders, average order value, return rate) with comparison to last period.
- **One trend chart** (line).
- **One breakdown** (sorted bar by region or product).
- **Filters/slicers** for period and region.
- **Notes:** data source, refresh date, definitions.

Design for the question the reader asks every week, not for every possible chart.

steps.title: Data privacy
steps.body: Customer data (names, phones, emails, addresses) is personal data. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 sets obligations for handling personal data, with rules being brought into force in phases — follow your company's data policies. Share only what's necessary, mask personal details in dashboards, and never email raw customer lists to personal accounts.

steps.title: Beyond Excel
steps.body: As data grows, teams move to tools like Power BI, Tableau, Looker or SQL databases, and Python for analysis. The thinking is the same: clean data, clear metric definitions, honest charts and a clear 'so what'.

activity.prompt: Put a data-cleaning workflow in order.
items: Copy raw data to a working sheet
Trim spaces and standardise case
Map synonyms using a lookup table
Fix data types (dates, numbers)
Define and remove duplicates
Validate counts and totals
Build pivots and the dashboard

quiz.q: 'Bombay' and 'Mumbai' in the same column should be…
quiz.why: The answer is "Standardised with a mapping table". Reason: Consistent categories. The other choices, such as "Counted twice" and "Left as is", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Before removing duplicates you should…
quiz.why: The answer is "Define what a duplicate is". Reason: Avoid deleting real records. The other choices, such as "Sort by colour" and "Delete random rows", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A good dashboard has…

quiz.why: The answer is "3–5 key metrics, a trend, a breakdown and notes". Reason: Focus. The other choices, such as "No dates" and "Only a table", do not fit the question.

courses.title: Product management essentials
courses.summary: How product managers find the right problems, prioritise, write specs, define metrics and launch — with examples from Indian and global products.
outcomes: Learners can run problem discovery with users
Learners can prioritise with RICE and other frameworks
Learners can write a clear PRD with success metrics
Learners can plan and evaluate a launch

lessons.title: Discovery: falling in love with the problem

scenes.text: A Bengaluru agri-tech startup builds a complex crop-price prediction feature for farmers. Usage after launch: 2%.
PM Kavitha visits farmers in Karnataka villages and listens.
Farmers say their real problem is knowing which nearby mandi pays the best price today — and how to get a truck there.
A simpler 'today's prices near you + transport booking' feature, with voice in Kannada, reaches 40% weekly usage.

steps.title: Problem before solution
steps.body:
A PM's first job is to understand **who** the user is, **what problem** they have, **how painful** it is, and **how they solve it today**. A common framing is **Jobs To Be Done (JTBD)**: *'When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [outcome].'*
Example: *'When my harvest is ready, I want to know which nearby mandi pays the most today, so I can earn more without wasting a trip.'*

steps.title: User interviews that work
steps.body:
- Ask about **past behaviour**, not hypothetical futures: *'Tell me about the last time you sold your crop.'* not *'Would you use an app that…?'*
- Ask **why** and **how** repeatedly; listen more than talk.
- Avoid leading questions (*'Don't you think this would be great?'*).
- Talk to **5–10 users** per segment to see patterns.
- Observe in context if possible — the field, the shop, the office.

steps.title: Worked example: validating cheaply
steps.body: Before building, Kavitha tested demand with a WhatsApp message at 7 am in three villages listing the top 5 mandi prices. In two weeks, 600 farmers had subscribed and asked for transport help. This **'concierge MVP'** (doing it manually first) proved demand before engineering spent months.

steps.title: Discovery traps
steps.body:
- Building what the loudest customer or the CEO asks for without understanding the underlying problem.
- Designing for 'users like me' (urban, English-speaking, high-end phone) when real users differ.
- Confusing **stated** preferences ('I'd pay for that') with **revealed** behaviour (do they actually pay?).

activity.prompt: Good interview question or poor one?

items.text: Tell me about the last time you sold your crop.
Would you use an app that predicts prices?
What did you do when the price was lower than expected?
Don't you think this feature is great?
How did you decide which mandi to go to?
How much would you pay for this, hypothetically?

quiz.q: JTBD focuses on…
options: The job the user is trying to get done in a situation
quiz.why: The answer is "The job the user is trying to get done in a situation". Reason: Situation, motivation, outcome. The other choices, such as "Hiring" and "Job titles", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Good interview questions ask about…
quiz.why: The answer is "Past behaviour". Reason: Behaviour is more reliable. The other choices, such as "Hypothetical futures" and "Pricing only", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A concierge MVP is…
options: Delivering the value manually before building
quiz.why: The answer is "Delivering the value manually before building". Reason: Cheap validation. The other choices, such as "A hotel service" and "A full product", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Revealed preference means…
quiz.why: The answer is "What users actually do". Reason: Behaviour beats statements. The other choices, such as "What users say" and "What competitors build", do not fit the question.

lessons.title: Prioritisation: RICE, MoSCoW and saying no

scenes.text: Rahul, PM at a Pune HR-tech company, has 50 feature requests from sales, support, the CEO and customers.
Everyone says theirs is urgent. Sales threatens a lost deal.
Rahul scores items with RICE and shares the scoring openly.
Stakeholders still argue, but now about numbers and assumptions, not volume. The roadmap gains trust.

steps.title: RICE scoring
steps.body:
**RICE = (Reach × Impact × Confidence) ÷ Effort** (a framework popularised by Intercom):
- **Reach:** users affected per period (e.g., 4,000/quarter).
- **Impact:** effect per user (e.g., 3 = massive, 2 = high, 1 = medium, 0.5 = low, 0.25 = minimal).
- **Confidence:** how sure you are (100%, 80%, 50%).
- **Effort:** person-months.

It forces explicit assumptions and makes comparison fairer.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
- **Bulk payroll upload:** Reach 2,000, Impact 2, Confidence 80%, Effort 2 → (2000×2×0.8)/2 = **1,600**.
- **Dark mode:** Reach 8,000, Impact 0.25, Confidence 100%, Effort 1 → **2,000**.
- **SSO for enterprise:** Reach 500, Impact 3, Confidence 80%, Effort 3 → **400**.

The scores are inputs to judgement, not the final answer — SSO may still be strategic if it unlocks big enterprise deals. Say so explicitly.

steps.title: Other tools
steps.body:
- **MoSCoW:** Must, Should, Could, Won't (this time) — good for release scope.
- **Kano model:** basic expectations vs performance features vs delighters.
- **Cost of delay:** how much value is lost per week of delay.
- **Impact vs effort 2×2:** quick wins, big bets, fill-ins, money pits.

steps.title: Saying no gracefully
steps.body:
*'Thanks — this is a real problem for those customers. It's not in this quarter's plan because we're focused on payroll accuracy, which affects 10× more users. I've logged it with your data; we'll revisit in the next planning cycle. Is there a workaround that would help in the meantime?'*
Acknowledge, explain the trade-off, record it, offer an alternative.

activity.prompt: RICE: Reach 3,000 users/quarter, Impact 1, Confidence 50%, Effort 0.5 person-months. What is the RICE score?

quiz.q: RICE stands for…
quiz.why: The answer is "Reach, Impact, Confidence, Effort". Reason: Prioritisation inputs. The other choices, such as "Rank, Index, Count, Estimate" and "Risk, Issue, Change, Escalation", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: In MoSCoW, 'W' means…
quiz.why: The answer is "Won't (this time)". Reason: Explicitly out of scope. The other choices, such as "Want" and "Wish", do not fit the question. (Question: In MoSCoW, 'W' means…)

quiz.q: RICE scores should be…
options: Inputs to judgement, with strategy considered
quiz.why: The answer is "Inputs to judgement, with strategy considered". Reason: Frameworks support, not replace, judgement. The other choices, such as "Kept secret" and "The final unquestionable answer", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A graceful 'no' includes…
quiz.why: The answer is "Acknowledgement, trade-off, logging, alternative". Reason: Respect and transparency. The other choices, such as "A vague 'maybe later'" and "Silence", do not fit the question.

scenes.text: A PM writes a one-line ticket: 'Add referral programme.' Engineers build a share button.
Marketing expected rewards, tracking, fraud checks and UPI cashback.
The next PM, Sneha, writes a proper PRD with goals, user stories, scope, non-goals and metrics.
The referral launch works first time, with fraud rules preventing fake accounts.

steps.title: What a PRD contains
steps.body:
A **product requirements document** (or one-pager/spec):
- **Problem & why now** (with evidence).
- **Goals and success metrics.**
- **Users & use cases** (user stories: *'As a customer, I want to invite a friend so we both get ₹100 cashback'*).
- **Scope:** what's in; **non-goals:** what's out.
- **Requirements & acceptance criteria.**
- **Edge cases & risks** (fraud, privacy, accessibility, low-end phones, poor networks).
- **Open questions; launch plan.**

steps.title: Choosing metrics
steps.body:
- **North Star metric:** the one metric that best captures value delivered to users (e.g., weekly active merchants who received a payment).
- **AARRR funnel** (Dave McClure's 'pirate metrics'): Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue.
- **Guardrail metrics:** what must not get worse (crash rate, fraud, support tickets, page load time).
- Define metrics precisely: *'Activation = merchant receives first payment within 7 days of signup.'*

steps.title: Worked example: A/B test thinking
steps.body:
Hypothesis: *'Showing ₹100 cashback on the home screen will increase referrals sent by 20%.'*
- Control: current home screen. Variant: cashback banner.
- Primary metric: referrals sent per active user. Guardrail: fraud rate.
- Decide the sample size and run time *before* starting, and don't stop early just because results look good — that inflates false positives.

steps.title: Vanity metrics
steps.body: Downloads, page views or registered users can look impressive while real value is low. Prefer metrics tied to repeated value (active use, retention, completed transactions).

activity.prompt: Match the AARRR stage to an example metric.
pairs: Merchant receives first payment within 7 days

quiz.q: Non-goals in a PRD…
options: List what's explicitly out of scope
quiz.why: The answer is "List what's explicitly out of scope". Reason: Prevents scope creep and misunderstanding. The other choices, such as "Are bugs" and "Are optional jokes", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A guardrail metric is…
options: Something that must not get worse
quiz.why: The answer is "Something that must not get worse". Reason: Protects against harmful wins. The other choices, such as "A deadline" and "The main growth metric", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Why not stop an A/B test early when results look good?
quiz.why: The answer is "It inflates false positives". Reason: Peeking bias. The other choices, such as "It saves money" and "It's illegal", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Which is a vanity metric?
quiz.why: The answer is "Total app downloads". Reason: Doesn't show real value. The other choices, such as "Completed transactions" and "Activation rate", do not fit the question.

scenes.text: A shopping app launches a new checkout to 100% of users on the first day of the Diwali sale.
A bug with one bank's cards causes failed payments for hours, during peak traffic.
Next year, PM Arjun launches in stages: 1% → 10% → 50% → 100% over two weeks before the sale, with a kill switch.
Two bugs are found at 1% and fixed. Diwali checkout runs smoothly.

steps.title: Staged rollouts
steps.body:
- **Feature flags** let you turn features on for a percentage of users and off instantly.
- **Staged rollout:** internal users → 1% → 10% → 50% → 100%, watching metrics and guardrails at each stage.
- **Kill switch & rollback plan** ready before launch.
- **Avoid launching big changes right before peak events** unless they've been tested at scale.

steps.title: Go-to-market checklist
steps.body:
- **Support** trained with FAQs; **sales** briefed.
- **Docs and in-app guidance** ready (in relevant languages).
- **Marketing** messages aligned with what's actually shipping.
- **Legal/compliance** checks (privacy, payments rules, accessibility).
- **Monitoring dashboards** and on-call owners.

steps.title: After launch: learn
steps.body:
- Review metrics vs hypothesis at 1, 2 and 4 weeks.
- Read support tickets and user feedback.
- Decide: **iterate, scale, or roll back.**
- Write a short launch retro: what worked, what didn't, what we'll do differently.

A launch is the start of learning, not the end of the project.

steps.title: India-specific considerations
steps.body: Test on low-end Android phones and poor networks, support regional languages, consider UPI and cash-on-delivery flows, and remember festive peaks (Diwali, regional festivals, salary days around the 1st) bring huge traffic spikes.

activity.prompt: Launch readiness checklist.
items: Feature flag and kill switch in place
Staged rollout plan with metric checkpoints
Guardrail metrics on a live dashboard
Support team trained with FAQs
Docs/in-app help ready in key languages
Legal, privacy and accessibility reviewed
Tested on low-end phones and slow networks
Launch retro scheduled

quiz.why: The answer is "Turning features on/off for subsets of users". Reason: Controlled rollout. The other choices, such as "Changing the logo" and "Free hosting", do not fit the question.

quiz.why: The answer is "Compare metrics to hypothesis and decide iterate/scale/rollback". Reason: Launch = start of learning. The other choices, such as "Delete the dashboard" and "Move on immediately", do not fit the question.

options: 'Tell me about the last time you…'

questions.why: The answer is "1,000". Reason: (1000×2×0.5)/1. The other choices, such as "2,000" and "4,000", do not fit the question. (Question: RICE: Reach 1,000, Impact 2, Confidence 50%, Effort 1 →)

questions.q: Guardrail metrics…
questions.why: The answer is "Must not get worse". Reason: Protect quality. The other choices, such as "Are deadlines" and "Are vanity metrics", do not fit the question.

questions.q: A concierge MVP validates…
questions.why: The answer is "Demand before building". Reason: Cheap learning. The other choices, such as "Code quality" and "Hiring", do not fit the question. (Question: A concierge MVP validates…)

questions.why: The answer is "Increases false positives". Reason: Peeking. The other choices, such as "Has no effect" and "Is best practice", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Activation is best defined as…
options: A precise first-value event within a time window
questions.why: The answer is "A precise first-value event within a time window". Reason: Precise definitions. The other choices, such as "Any page view" and "Any signup", do not fit the question.

questions.q: A low RICE item that unlocks enterprise deals should be…
options: Considered on strategic grounds, explicitly explained
Ignored because the score is low

questions.q: Launching a new checkout to 100% on sale day is risky mainly because…
options: Bugs hit peak traffic with large blast radius
questions.why: The answer is "Bugs hit peak traffic with large blast radius". Reason: Stage before peaks. The other choices, such as "Users dislike change" and "It's illegal", do not fit the question.

courses.title: Project management: PMP-style basics, Agile, Scrum and Kanban
courses.summary: Plan and deliver projects: scope, schedule, critical path, risk and stakeholders; Scrum roles, events and artifacts; Kanban flow; and how to prepare for PMP-style and Scrum certifications. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can build a WBS and find the critical path
Learners can manage risks and stakeholders with simple registers
Learners can explain Scrum accountabilities, events and artifacts accurately
Learners can apply Kanban WIP limits and choose a delivery approach

lessons.title: Scope, WBS and the critical path

scenes.text: Farhan must move a 200-person Hyderabad office to a new building in 8 weeks. His plan is a single line: 'Move office'.
Week 3: nobody ordered network cabling, which takes 4 weeks to deliver.
A PMO colleague helps him break the work into a WBS and map dependencies.
They find the critical path runs through cabling and fit-out. Expedited ordering saves the deadline.

steps.title: The constraints
steps.body:
Every project balances **scope, time and cost** (the classic 'triple constraint'), with **quality**, risk and stakeholder satisfaction close behind. Change one and the others are affected: more scope with the same deadline needs more cost or carries more risk.

Start with a **project charter**: objective, scope, key deliverables, timeline, budget, sponsor, success criteria.

steps.title: Work breakdown structure (WBS)
steps.body:
Break the deliverable into smaller **work packages** until each can be estimated and owned:
- **Office move** → Site readiness (fit-out, cabling, furniture) · IT (network, desks, testing) · People (seating plan, communication) · Logistics (packing, movers) · Closure (old-site handover).

The WBS is about **deliverables**, not a to-do list in random order. Anything not in the WBS is not in scope.

steps.title: Worked example: critical path
steps.body:
Tasks (days): **A** design layout (3) → **B** order furniture (4) → **D** install & test (2); **A** → **C** network cabling (6) → **D**.
- Path A-B-D = 3 + 4 + 2 = **9 days**.
- Path A-C-D = 3 + 6 + 2 = **11 days**.

The **critical path** is the longest path: **A-C-D, 11 days**. Any delay on A, C or D delays the project. B has **float** (slack) of 2 days.

steps.title: Estimating
steps.body:
- Ask the people doing the work.
- Use ranges or three-point estimates: (Optimistic + 4×Most likely + Pessimistic) ÷ 6 (the PERT formula).
- Add contingency based on risk — and make it visible, not hidden padding.
- Track actual vs estimate to improve over time.

activity.prompt: Tasks: A (4 days) then B (5 days) then E (3 days); and A then C (2) then D (4) then E. What is the critical path length in days?

quiz.q: The critical path is…
options: The longest path of dependent tasks determining the minimum duration
quiz.why: The answer is "The longest path of dependent tasks determining the minimum duration". Reason: Delays on it delay the project. The other choices, such as "Optional tasks" and "The shortest path", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Float (slack) is…
options: Time a task can slip without delaying the project
quiz.why: The answer is "Time a task can slip without delaying the project". Reason: Non-critical tasks have float. The other choices, such as "Budget surplus" and "Overtime", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A WBS is organised around…
quiz.why: The answer is "Deliverables". Reason: Decomposition of scope. The other choices, such as "People's names" and "Random tasks", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: PERT estimate with O=2, M=4, P=12 days is…
quiz.why: The answer is "5 days". Reason: (2 + 16 + 12) ÷ 6 = 5. The other choices, such as "12 days" and "6 days", do not fit the question. (Question: PERT estimate with O=2, M=4, P=12 days is…)

scenes.text: A Mumbai bank's CRM project reports 'green' for six months. Inside, it's red: data migration is far behind.
Two weeks before go-live, the truth comes out. Go-live slips four months.
New PM Anita introduces a risk register and honest RAG status with clear criteria.
Problems now surface early, and the sponsor trusts the reports.

steps.title: Risk register
steps.body:
For each risk: **description, probability, impact, owner, response, trigger.** Responses to threats:
- **Avoid** (change plan to remove it)
- **Mitigate** (reduce probability or impact)
- **Transfer** (insurance, contract)
- **Accept** (with contingency)
- **Escalate** (outside your authority)

A **risk** is uncertain and in the future; an **issue** has already happened.

steps.title: Stakeholder management
steps.body: Identify stakeholders, assess their **power and interest**, understand what they need, and plan communication: who gets what, how often, in what format. A **RACI** chart (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) clarifies roles — with exactly **one Accountable** per deliverable.

steps.title: Worked example: honest RAG status
steps.body:
Define criteria in advance:
- **Green:** on track for date, budget and scope.
- **Amber:** at risk; recovery plan within the team's control.
- **Red:** will miss without sponsor decision or help.

*'Status: AMBER. Data migration 2 weeks behind (62% vs 80% planned). Recovery: added 2 data engineers; will recover by 15 May. Decision needed: none yet; will escalate to Red if not recovered by 1 May.'*

steps.title: Watermelon reporting
steps.body: 'Green outside, red inside' happens when people fear bad news. Leaders get honest reports by **thanking people for early amber/red**, not punishing them. As a PM, report reality — your credibility is the project's most important asset.

activity.prompt: Match the risk response to the example.
pairs: Drop a risky new technology from the plan
Run extra testing to reduce defect impact
Buy insurance or shift risk via contract
Raise a regulatory risk to the steering committee

quiz.q: A risk differs from an issue because…
options: A risk is uncertain and future; an issue has happened
quiz.why: The answer is "A risk is uncertain and future; an issue has happened". Reason: Timing and certainty. The other choices, such as "They're the same" and "Risks are always good", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: In RACI, how many 'Accountable' per deliverable?
quiz.why: The answer is "Exactly one". Reason: Clear ownership. The other choices, such as "None" and "As many as possible", do not fit the question. (Question: In RACI, how many 'Accountable' per deliverable?)

quiz.q: 'Watermelon' status means…
quiz.why: The answer is "Green reported, red reality". Reason: Hidden problems. The other choices, such as "A fruit budget" and "Healthy project", do not fit the question.

scenes.text: A Chennai team says they 'do Scrum': 2-hour daily stand-ups, a manager assigning tasks, and sprints with no goal.
Developers hate it; delivery is no faster.
A new Scrum Master, Elena, walks them through the Scrum Guide's actual structure.
With a Sprint Goal, a 15-minute Daily Scrum and a real Product Owner, the team ships a usable increment every sprint.

steps.title: Scrum in one page (Scrum Guide 2020)
steps.body:
**Three accountabilities:** Product Owner (maximises product value; owns the Product Backlog), Scrum Master (establishes Scrum and helps the team improve), Developers (create the usable Increment each Sprint).

**Five events:** the **Sprint** (fixed length, one month or less), **Sprint Planning**, **Daily Scrum** (15 minutes, for the Developers), **Sprint Review**, **Sprint Retrospective**.

**Three artifacts, each with a commitment:** Product Backlog → **Product Goal**; Sprint Backlog → **Sprint Goal**; Increment → **Definition of Done**.

Scrum teams are typically **10 or fewer** people and are self-managing.

steps.title: Agile values
Common Scrum anti-patterns
steps.body:
- Daily Scrum as a long status meeting for a manager.
- No Sprint Goal — just a list of tickets.
- Product Owner is a committee or unavailable.
- 'Done' means 'coded' but not tested or deployable.
- Skipping retrospectives when busy (the time you need them most).
- Changing sprint scope constantly in ways that endanger the Sprint Goal.

steps.title: Certification note
steps.body: Scrum certifications are offered by different bodies (e.g., Scrum.org and Scrum Alliance), with their own formats. PMI's PMP exam covers predictive, agile and hybrid approaches and has eligibility requirements (project-management education hours and experience, depending on your education). *Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.*

lessons.title: Kanban flow and choosing an approach

story.title: The support team drowning in tickets

scenes.text: A Noida IT support team has 300 open tickets and everyone works on 8 at once.
Average resolution takes 9 days; customers are furious.
They adopt a Kanban board with WIP limits: no more than 3 tickets 'In progress' per person.
Within a month, resolution time drops to 4 days — by doing less at once.

steps.title: Kanban basics
steps.body:
- **Visualise** work on a board (To do → In progress → Review → Done).
- **Limit work in progress (WIP)** per column or person.
- **Manage flow:** measure cycle time and throughput; remove bottlenecks.
- **Make policies explicit** (what 'done' means for each column).
- **Improve continuously.**

Kanban suits continuous work (support, operations, maintenance) where fixed sprints feel artificial.

steps.title: Little's Law
steps.body:
For a stable system: **average cycle time = average WIP ÷ average throughput.**
If a team has 60 items in progress and completes 15 per week, average cycle time ≈ 60 ÷ 15 = **4 weeks**. Halve WIP to 30 with the same throughput → about **2 weeks**. This is why WIP limits speed things up.

steps.title: Predictive, agile or hybrid?
steps.body:
- **Predictive (waterfall):** clear, stable requirements; high cost of change (construction, regulatory projects, hardware).
- **Agile (Scrum/Kanban):** uncertain requirements, need for fast feedback (software products, digital services).
- **Hybrid:** common in large enterprises — e.g., fixed milestones and budgets with agile delivery inside.

Choose based on uncertainty and cost of change, not fashion.

steps.title: Stop starting, start finishing
steps.body: The Kanban slogan captures the lesson: finishing work delivers value; starting work only creates inventory. When you're tempted to pick a new ticket, first ask: *'Can I help finish something already in progress?'*

courses.title: Negotiation and B2B sales
courses.summary: Prepare and run negotiations with BATNA, ZOPA and anchoring; discover customer needs; handle objections; and close and grow accounts ethically.
outcomes: Learners can prepare a negotiation using BATNA, reservation point and ZOPA
Learners can use interest-based negotiation and trade concessions wisely
Learners can run discovery conversations with SPIN-style questions
Learners can handle objections and close ethically

story.title: The vendor who knew his walk-away

scenes.text: Procurement manager Deepika negotiates a ₹2 crore annual facilities contract in Mumbai. The vendor asks for ₹2.4 crore.
She has prepared: a second vendor quote at ₹2.1 crore (her BATNA) and market benchmarks.
She anchors at ₹1.9 crore with a clear rationale. The vendor's own walk-away is around ₹2.0 crore.
They settle at ₹2.05 crore with better service levels. Both sides feel it's fair.

steps.title: Key concepts
steps.body:
From *Getting to Yes* (Fisher & Ury) and negotiation research:
- **BATNA:** Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement — what you'll do if there's no deal. A strong BATNA is your biggest source of power.
- **Reservation point (walk-away):** the worst deal you'll accept.
- **ZOPA:** Zone Of Possible Agreement — the overlap between both sides' reservation points.
- **Anchoring:** the first number often strongly influences the outcome.

steps.title: Worked example: finding the ZOPA
steps.body:
Buyer (Deepika): walk-away = ₹2.1 crore (her BATNA quote). Seller: walk-away = ₹2.0 crore (below this he'd lose money).
**ZOPA = ₹2.0 – 2.1 crore.** A deal anywhere in this range beats both sides' alternatives. If the seller's walk-away were ₹2.2 crore, there would be **no ZOPA** — and walking away would be rational.

steps.title: Using anchors well
steps.body:
- If you have good information, **anchor first** — ambitious but justifiable (*'Based on two benchmarks, we're looking at ₹1.9 crore'*).
- If the other side anchors extremely, **don't counter immediately**; re-anchor with your own rationale.
- Always attach a **reason** to numbers.
- Prepare a list of **tradeables**: payment terms, volume, contract length, service levels, delivery dates.

steps.title: Preparation mistakes
steps.body:
- Not knowing your BATNA — you'll accept bad deals or reject good ones.
- Revealing your walk-away.
- Negotiating only on price.
- Bluffing about alternatives you don't have — it can backfire and damages trust.

activity.prompt: Complete the definitions.
activity.text: Your best option if no deal is reached is your ___. The overlap between both sides' walk-away points is the ___.

options: Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement
quiz.why: The answer is "Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement". Reason: From Getting to Yes. The other choices, such as "Buyer's Assured Target Number" and "Best Available Trade Network Agreement", do not fit the question.

quiz.why: The answer is "There's no ZOPA". Reason: No overlap. The other choices, such as "Buyer must pay ₹55 lakh" and "Deal at ₹52 lakh is certain", do not fit the question.

quiz.why: The answer is "Negotiating power". Reason: You can walk away. The other choices, such as "A legal right" and "Weakness", do not fit the question. (Question: A strong BATNA gives you…)

quiz.why: The answer is "Give a rationale". Reason: Justified anchors persuade. The other choices, such as "Reveal your walk-away" and "Start with your walk-away", do not fit the question.

scenes.text: A startup founder, Kiran, and an enterprise client in Dubai are stuck on price: he wants ₹80 lakh, they offer ₹60 lakh.
Kiran asks why ₹60 lakh. The client's budget for this financial year is capped; next year's budget is larger.
He proposes ₹60 lakh this year for phase 1, with phase 2 at ₹35 lakh next year, plus a case-study right.
Both get more than their original positions.

steps.title: Positions vs interests
steps.body:
A **position** is what someone says they want (*'₹60 lakh max'*). An **interest** is why (*budget cap this year, need to show results to leadership*). Solving for interests creates options: phasing, payment terms, scope, guarantees, references.

Ask: *'Help me understand what's driving that number?'* and *'What would make this work for you?'*

steps.title: Trading concessions
steps.body:
- **Never give without getting:** *'If you can commit to a 3-year term, we can reduce the annual fee by 5%.'*
- **Concede in decreasing steps** (e.g., 5%, then 2%, then 1%) — it signals you're nearing your limit.
- **Trade low-cost-to-you, high-value-to-them** items.
- **Package** issues together rather than settling one at a time.

steps.title: Recognising tough tactics
steps.body:
- **Good cop/bad cop** — address the decision-maker's interests directly.
- **Last-minute nibble** ('just add free training') — trade: *'Sure, if we can finalise today.'*
- **Fake deadline / exploding offer** — test it calmly.
- **Silence** — don't rush to fill it with concessions.
- **Personal attacks** — name it calmly and refocus on the issues.

Use ethical tactics yourself: lying about material facts can harm relationships and, in some cases, have legal consequences.

steps.title: Cultural notes
steps.body: In many Indian business settings, negotiation is relationship-based and bargaining is expected — a first offer is rarely final. With some global counterparts (e.g., in parts of Northern Europe), first offers may be closer to final and heavy haggling can seem untrustworthy. Research the counterpart's norms and adapt.

lessons.title: Discovery selling: questions that uncover needs

scenes.text: Sales rep Arnav opens his meeting with a Delhi hospital chain by demoing all 40 features of his software.
The CIO checks her phone. 'Thanks, we'll get back to you.' They never do.
His manager coaches him to ask questions first: what's happening now, what's the problem, what it costs, what a solution would be worth.
At the next hospital, the CIO reveals that billing errors cost them crores a year. Arnav demos only the three features that solve it. Deal won.

steps.title: SPIN questions
steps.body:
From Neil Rackham's research on large sales (*SPIN Selling*):
- **Situation:** facts about the current state (*'How do you handle billing today?'*). Use sparingly.
- **Problem:** difficulties (*'Where do errors happen?'*).
- **Implication:** consequences (*'What does that cost in rework and delayed insurance claims?'*).
- **Need-payoff:** value of solving it (*'If errors fell by half, what would that mean for your team?'*).

Implication and need-payoff questions help the buyer articulate value themselves.

steps.title: Qualification
steps.body:
Not every lead is worth pursuing. Frameworks help:
- **BANT:** Budget, Authority, Need, Timeline.
- **MEDDIC:** Metrics, Economic buyer, Decision criteria, Decision process, Identify pain, Champion.

Ask respectfully: *'Who else is involved in the decision? What does your approval process look like? Is there a budget set aside?'*

steps.title: Worked example: discovery flow
steps.body:
- S: *'How many claims do you submit monthly?'* → 12,000.
- P: *'What share get rejected first time?'* → about 9%.
- I: *'What happens to a rejected claim?'* → 2–3 weeks delay, staff time, cash-flow strain.
- N: *'If first-time rejection fell to 3%, what would that free up?'* → *'Probably two people's time and faster cash.'*
Now the demo focuses on claims validation — and the value is in the client's own words.

steps.title: Listen more than talk
steps.body: Many sales coaches advise letting the customer talk for most of a discovery call. Take notes, summarise back (*'So the biggest issue is first-time claim rejection, costing roughly…'*), and confirm before proposing.

quiz.why: The answer is "Situation, Problem, Implication, Need-payoff". Reason: Rackham's model. The other choices, such as "Sell, Pitch, Insist, Negotiate" and "Start, Present, Inform, Next", do not fit the question.

quiz.why: The answer is "Consequences of the problem". Reason: Builds urgency. The other choices, such as "Your product features" and "Pricing", do not fit the question.

quiz.why: The answer is "Budget, Authority, Need, Timeline". Reason: Qualification. The other choices, such as "Brand, Ads, Network, Trust" and "Buy, Ask, Negotiate, Thank", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Why demo only relevant features?
quiz.why: The answer is "Focuses on the customer's value". Reason: Relevance wins. The other choices, such as "Hides weaknesses" and "Saves electricity", do not fit the question.

scenes.text: A Coimbatore textile firm tells salesperson Meghna, 'Your ERP is too expensive.'
Instead of discounting, she asks, 'Expensive compared to what?'
They're comparing with a cheaper tool that lacks GST e-invoicing integration they need. She shows the cost of manual work.
They sign — and a year later expand to three more plants because the implementation went well.

steps.title: Handling objections
steps.body:
A simple sequence:
- **Listen** fully.
- **Acknowledge** (*'That's a fair concern.'*).
- **Explore** (*'Compared to what? What would make it worth it?'*).
- **Respond** with evidence (ROI, references, trial, guarantees).
- **Confirm** (*'Does that address it?'*).

Common objections: price, timing ('not now'), status quo ('we're fine'), risk ('what if it fails?'), authority ('I need approval').

steps.title: Closing ethically
steps.body:
- **Summarise value and agreed next steps.**
- **Ask directly:** *'Shall we go ahead with the pilot starting 1 March?'*
- Use a **mutual action plan**: dates for legal review, security review, signature, kick-off.
- Avoid pressure tactics and false scarcity. Never promise features that don't exist or misrepresent terms — it damages trust and can create legal exposure.

steps.title: Account management
Ethics and compliance
steps.body: Gifts, hospitality and payments to win business are governed by company policy and anti-bribery laws (including India's Prevention of Corruption Act and, for many multinationals, laws like the US FCPA and UK Bribery Act). Dealing with government buyers has strict rules. When in doubt, ask compliance.

corporate-careers.title: Career toolkit: get hired, get paid, stay well
corporate-careers.description: Resumes, LinkedIn, interviews, comparing offers and negotiating salary in India, switching jobs and exiting cleanly, POSH Act 2013 basics, and recognising and recovering from burnout.

courses.title: Resumes, LinkedIn and interviews
courses.summary: Write a resume that passes screening, use LinkedIn and referrals well, avoid job scams, and answer behavioural, technical, case and HR interview questions with confidence.
outcomes: Learners can write a one-to-two-page, achievement-based resume
Learners can use LinkedIn and referrals effectively and spot job scams
Learners can answer behavioural questions with STAR
Learners can prepare for technical, case and HR rounds and ask good questions

scenes.text: Rohini, with three years in operations in Indore, sends a 4-page resume with her photo, father's name, religion, a 'career objective' and every course since Class 10.
Forty applications, two calls.
A recruiter friend helps her cut it to one page: a summary, quantified achievements, skills matching each job post.
Next twenty applications: seven calls.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body:
- **Header:** name, phone, professional email, city, LinkedIn/portfolio link.
- **Summary (2–3 lines):** who you are and your strongest value. *'Operations analyst with 3 years in e-commerce fulfilment; cut order delays 30% through process redesign.'*
- **Experience:** reverse chronological; for each role, 3–5 achievement bullets.
- **Skills:** relevant tools and methods (Excel, SQL, SAP, Python, Lean).
- **Education & certifications.**

Length: **1 page** for early career; **up to 2 pages** for experienced professionals. Personal details like religion, caste, marital status, father's name or a photo are generally unnecessary unless an employer specifically requires them.

steps.title: Worked example: duties → achievements
steps.body:
Formula: **action verb + what you did + measurable result.**
- *'Responsible for vendor management'* → **'Renegotiated contracts with 12 courier vendors, reducing cost per shipment 11% (₹38 lakh/year).'**
- *'Handled customer complaints'* → **'Resolved ~60 escalations/month; raised CSAT from 78% to 89% in two quarters.'**
- *'Worked on dashboard'* → **'Built a Power BI dashboard used daily by 40 managers to track SLA breaches.'**

steps.title: Applicant tracking systems (ATS)
steps.body:
Many companies screen resumes with software. Help it:
- Use **standard headings** (Experience, Education, Skills).
- Mirror **keywords** from the job description truthfully (if the role says 'stakeholder management' and you've done it, say so in those words).
- Prefer simple layouts; avoid putting key text in images, text boxes or complex tables.
- Save as PDF unless told otherwise; name the file *Rohini_Sharma_Resume.pdf*.

steps.title: Never
steps.body:
- Exaggerate titles, dates, degrees or salaries. Background verification (BGV) checks employers, dates, education and sometimes references; discrepancies can lead to offer withdrawal or termination later.
- Use fake experience certificates — this can have serious consequences, including legal action.
- Send the same resume everywhere without tailoring the summary and top bullets.

items.text: Responsible for team reports
Automated weekly reporting, saving 6 hours/week for 5 managers
Handled client calls
Grew key account revenue 22% YoY by launching a quarterly review
Part of migration project

quiz.q: A strong bullet contains…
options: Action verb, what you did, measurable result
quiz.why: The answer is "Action verb, what you did, measurable result". Reason: Shows impact. The other choices, such as "Adjectives" and "Your hobbies", do not fit the question.

options: Use standard headings and relevant keywords truthfully

options: Can be caught in BGV and lead to withdrawal or termination
quiz.why: The answer is "Can be caught in BGV and lead to withdrawal or termination". Reason: Honesty protects your career. The other choices, such as "Is expected" and "Is harmless", do not fit the question.

lessons.title: LinkedIn, referrals and avoiding job scams

scenes.text: Mohit, a fresh graduate in Patna, gets a WhatsApp message: 'Selected for a work-from-home job at a top company. Pay ₹5,000 for training kit.'
He nearly pays. His cousin, a recruiter, says: 'Genuine employers don't charge you for a job.'
Instead, his cousin helps him fix his LinkedIn profile and ask alumni for referrals.
Two months later, a referral leads to a real interview and offer.

steps.title: A LinkedIn profile that works
steps.body:
- **Photo:** clear, professional, face visible.
- **Headline:** not just your title — *'Data Analyst | SQL, Power BI | Supply-chain analytics'*.
- **About:** 3–5 lines on what you do, your strengths and what you're looking for.
- **Experience:** same achievement bullets as your resume.
- **Skills & recommendations:** ask 2–3 colleagues for specific recommendations.
- **Activity:** occasionally share something useful you learned — consistency beats virality.

steps.title: Worked example: asking for a referral
steps.body:
*'Hi Sana, I'm Mohit, also from NIT Patna (2024 batch). I saw a Data Analyst opening at your company (job ID 4471). I have SQL and Power BI experience from my internship where I built a sales dashboard used by 20 managers. Would you be open to referring me, or sharing a few minutes of advice about the team? I've attached my resume. Thank you!'*

Short, specific, shows fit, easy to say yes to — and respectful if they say no.

steps.title: Job-scam red flags
steps.body:
- Asking for **money** (registration, training, laptop, security deposit).
- Offers **without any interview**.
- Personal email domains or WhatsApp-only contact pretending to be a big company.
- Pressure to act immediately; requests for Aadhaar/PAN/bank details/OTPs early.
- 'Task-based' online jobs that pay small amounts then ask you to 'invest'.

Verify on the company's official careers page. Report cyber fraud at the national helpline **1930** or cybercrime.gov.in.

steps.title: Job-search strategy
steps.body:
- Target 15–30 companies that fit you rather than spraying 300 applications.
- Referrals often get more attention than cold applications.
- Track applications in a simple sheet (company, role, date, contact, status, follow-up).
- Keep learning visibly: projects, certifications, GitHub/portfolio.

statements.s: Genuine employers commonly ask candidates to pay a registration or training fee.
statements.why: Asking for money is a classic scam signal.

statements.s: A specific, short referral request with a job ID is more likely to get a response.
statements.why: It's easy to act on.

statements.s: You should share OTPs with a recruiter to 'verify your bank account'.
statements.why: Never share OTPs; that's fraud.

statements.s: India's cyber-fraud helpline number is 1930.
statements.why: Report online financial fraud quickly at 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in.

statements.s: A LinkedIn headline should only say 'Looking for job'.
statements.why: Show your skills and focus.

quiz.q: A strong LinkedIn headline is…
options: 'Data Analyst | SQL, Power BI | Supply-chain analytics'
quiz.why: The answer is "'Data Analyst | SQL, Power BI | Supply-chain analytics'". Reason: Skills and focus. The other choices, such as "'Student'" and "Blank", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Which is a job-scam red flag?
options: A recruiter with a company email
Interview scheduled via company careers portal
quiz.why: The answer is "Asking for a 'training kit' fee". Reason: Real jobs don't charge you. The other choices, such as "A technical test" and "A recruiter with a company email", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A good referral request includes…
options: Who you are, the job ID, your fit, a clear ask
quiz.why: The answer is "Who you are, the job ID, your fit, a clear ask". Reason: Easy to act on. The other choices, such as "Just 'pls refer'" and "Your full life story", do not fit the question.

quiz.why: The answer is "1930". Reason: National cyber-crime helpline. The other choices, such as "1098" and "14416", do not fit the question. (Question: Report online financial fraud in India at…)

scenes.text: In a Bengaluru product-company interview, Nisha is asked, 'Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager.'
She says, 'I'm very adjustable, I never have conflicts.' The interviewer's face goes blank.
Before her next interview, she prepares eight STAR stories from her work.
She answers the same question with a real story and its outcome — and gets the offer.

steps.title: The STAR method
steps.body:
- **Situation:** brief context (1–2 sentences).
- **Task:** your responsibility or goal.
- **Action:** what *you* did — the longest part; use 'I'.
- **Result:** measurable outcome and what you learned.

Aim for 1.5–2.5 minutes. Interviewers often probe: *'What would you do differently?'*, *'What did your manager say?'* — so use real stories.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
**Q: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager.**
- **S:** *'My manager wanted to launch a new checkout before Diwali.'*
- **T:** *'I owned testing and saw the payment failure rate in staging was 4%.'*
- **A:** *'I shared the data privately, proposed a 10% rollout first, and offered to work extra days to fix the top two bugs.'*
- **R:** *'We launched to 10%, found a bank-specific issue, fixed it, and went to 100% with failures under 1%. My manager later asked me to lead release readiness.'*

steps.title: Build a story bank
steps.body:
Prepare 8–10 stories that can answer many questions:
- a success you're proud of; a failure and lesson; a conflict; influencing without authority; tight deadline; ambiguity; leading/mentoring; a customer problem; an ethical dilemma; learning something fast.

Many big tech firms publish their leadership principles or values — map your stories to them.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'We' throughout — the interviewer can't see your part.
- No result, or no numbers.
- Badmouthing past employers or managers.
- Fake or borrowed stories — follow-up questions expose them.
- Answering 'my weakness is I'm a perfectionist' — choose a real, minor weakness with an improvement plan.

activity.prompt: Arrange this STAR answer in order.
items: Situation: Our biggest client threatened to leave after three missed SLAs.
Task: As team lead, I had to stabilise delivery within a month.
Action: I mapped the root causes, added a daily triage, and personally updated the client twice a week.
Result: SLAs were met for 3 straight months and the client renewed for 2 years.

quiz.q: In STAR, which part should be the longest?
quiz.why: The answer is "Action". Reason: Your actions show your skills. The other choices, such as "Situation" and "Task", do not fit the question. (Question: In STAR, which part should be the longest?)

quiz.q: Saying 'I never have conflicts' is weak because…
options: It avoids the question and lacks evidence
quiz.why: The answer is "It avoids the question and lacks evidence". Reason: Interviewers want real behaviour. The other choices, such as "It's too long" and "It's rude", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A good 'weakness' answer is…
options: A real, minor weakness with an improvement plan
quiz.why: The answer is "A real, minor weakness with an improvement plan". Reason: Self-awareness and growth. The other choices, such as "A major job-critical weakness" and "'None'", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Why use 'I' in the Action part?
quiz.why: The answer is "To show your specific contribution". Reason: Clarity of your role. The other choices, such as "It's grammar" and "No reason", do not fit the question.

scenes.text: Arjun solves a coding problem silently for 30 minutes and gets it mostly right. He's rejected.
His friend Leela, solving a similar problem, talks through her approach, asks clarifying questions and tests edge cases aloud. She gets the offer with a less optimal solution.
Arjun realises interviewers assess thinking and communication, not just the final answer.
He practises 'thinking aloud' and clears his next interview.

steps.title: Technical rounds: think aloud
steps.body:
- **Clarify** inputs, outputs and constraints.
- **State a simple approach first**, then improve it (time/space complexity if relevant).
- **Talk as you work**; if stuck, say what you're considering.
- **Test** with examples and edge cases (empty input, duplicates, very large values).
- For system design: requirements → high-level design → data model → scaling → trade-offs.

steps.title: Case interviews (consulting, product, analytics)
steps.body:
- **Clarify the objective** (*'Is the goal profit, market share or growth?'*).
- **Structure** the problem (e.g., profit = revenue − cost; revenue = price × volume).
- **Estimate** with round numbers, explaining assumptions (*'India's population ~1.4 billion; urban share ~35%…'*).
- **Synthesise:** give a recommendation with reasons and risks, top-down.

Structure and clear reasoning usually matter more than the exact number.

steps.title: HR round: common questions
steps.body:
- **'Tell me about yourself':** present → past → future in 60–90 seconds: *'I'm a data analyst at X, where I… Before that I… I'm now looking for a role where I can…'*
- **'Why are you leaving?':** positive and forward-looking — growth, scope, learning — never badmouth.
- **'Expected CTC?':** see the salary negotiation course; give a researched range or ask for the band.
- **'Notice period?':** be accurate; mention if buyout or early release is possible.
- **Questions to ask them:** *'What does success look like in 6 months? What are the team's biggest challenges? How is performance evaluated?'*

steps.title: Logistics and follow-up
steps.body:
- Test camera, mic and internet; have a backup (phone hotspot).
- Quiet, well-lit space; close notifications.
- Keep a glass of water and your resume nearby.
- Send a short thank-you note within 24 hours referencing something specific discussed.
- If you're rejected, politely ask for feedback; some companies will share.

activity.prompt: Interview-day checklist.
items: Researched the company, product and recent news
Prepared 8–10 STAR stories
Practised 'tell me about yourself' in 90 seconds
Prepared 3 questions to ask

Know my expected range and notice period
Kept resume and water nearby
Planned a thank-you note within 24 hours
