courses.title: Offers, salary negotiation and switching jobs (India)
courses.summary: Compare offers properly (fixed, variable, ESOPs, benefits), negotiate salary confidently and honestly, decide when and how to switch, and understand notice periods, relieving letters, gratuity and non-compete basics.
outcomes: Learners can compare offers using fixed pay, variable, ESOPs and benefits
Learners can negotiate salary with research, ranges and trade-offs
Learners can decide when to switch and handle counter-offers and BGV
Learners can understand exit formalities, gratuity and non-compete basics

scenes.text: Siddharth has two offers in Bengaluru: Company A at ₹24 lakh CTC and Company B at ₹21 lakh CTC.
He asks both for a break-up. A's CTC includes ₹4 lakh variable (paid only on ratings), ₹2 lakh joining bonus and ESOPs counted at a high valuation.
B's ₹21 lakh is almost all fixed, with better health insurance for his parents.
B's guaranteed first-year cash is higher, and its fixed base will drive future hikes. He chooses B.

steps.title: Break the CTC into parts
steps.body:
- **Fixed pay:** basic, HRA, allowances — guaranteed monthly.
- **Variable / performance bonus:** depends on rating and company results; ask what percentage was actually paid in the last 2–3 years.
- **Joining bonus:** one-time; often has a **clawback** if you leave within 12 months or so.
- **Retention bonus:** paid later if you stay.
- **ESOPs / RSUs:** equity; check vesting schedule, valuation, and (for startups) whether they can actually be sold.
- **Employer PF, gratuity, insurance** and other benefits.

Compare **first-year guaranteed cash** and **fixed pay**, because future hikes are usually a percentage of fixed pay.

steps.title: Equity basics
steps.body:
- **RSUs** (common at listed multinationals): shares granted that vest over time; value moves with the share price.
- **ESOPs** (common at startups): options to buy shares at a set price; valuable only if the company's value rises and there's a way to sell (buyback, acquisition, IPO).
- A common vesting pattern is **4 years with a 1-year cliff** (nothing vests until 12 months, then monthly/quarterly) — but check your grant.
- Taxation of equity in India can occur at exercise/vesting and at sale; consult a tax professional.

steps.title: Worked example: first-year guaranteed cash (illustrative)
steps.body:
- **A:** fixed ₹16L + joining ₹2L + variable (historically ~70% paid of ₹4L → ~₹2.8L, not guaranteed) → **guaranteed ₹18L**; expected ~₹20.8L.
- **B:** fixed ₹19.5L + variable ₹1L (usually 100% paid) → **guaranteed ₹19.5L**; expected ₹20.5L.

A's headline is ₹3L higher, but B pays more guaranteed cash, and B's higher fixed base means each future % hike is worth more. Non-money factors — role, manager, learning, stability, commute, WFH policy — matter too.

steps.title: Questions to ask HR
steps.body:
- Can I see the full CTC break-up?
- What % of variable was paid in the last few years?
- Joining-bonus clawback terms?
- ESOP/RSU vesting schedule and valuation basis?
- Health insurance coverage (self, spouse, children, parents?) and sum insured?
- Notice period, probation and leave policy?
- WFH/hybrid policy in writing?

activity.prompt: Guaranteed cash or not guaranteed?

items.text: Monthly basic salary
Performance variable pay
HRA
Startup ESOPs
Joining bonus with 12-month clawback
Special allowance

quiz.q: Why does fixed pay matter more for the future?
options: Future hikes are usually a % of fixed pay
quiz.why: The answer is "Future hikes are usually a % of fixed pay". Reason: Compounding effect. The other choices, such as "It's taxed less" and "It doesn't", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A joining bonus clawback means…
options: You may have to repay if you leave early
quiz.why: The answer is "You may have to repay if you leave early". Reason: Check the terms. The other choices, such as "A retention bonus" and "A free gift", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A '1-year cliff' in vesting means…
quiz.why: The answer is "Nothing vests until 12 months". Reason: Common pattern; check your grant. The other choices, such as "Everything vests on day 1" and "You must climb a cliff", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: To evaluate variable pay, ask…
options: What % was actually paid in recent years
quiz.why: The answer is "What % was actually paid in recent years". Reason: History indicates likelihood. The other choices, such as "Nothing" and "Office location", do not fit the question.

scenes.text: HR asks Pooja, a 5-year product designer in Gurugram, 'Current and expected CTC?' She panics and says 'whatever is standard'.
She gets an offer 10% above her current pay — below the market for her skills.
For her next switch, she researches ranges from peers, recruiters and salary surveys, and prepares her case.
She asks for a range grounded in market data and her portfolio — and negotiates a meaningfully higher fixed pay plus a joining bonus to cover her notice buyout.

steps.title: Research first
steps.body:
Sources: peers in similar roles, recruiters, salary-survey reports and public salary-sharing platforms (treat as rough signals), job posts that state ranges. Know three numbers:
- **Target:** what you'll ask for (ambitious but defensible).
- **Expected:** what you think is fair.
- **Walk-away:** below which you'll stay or keep looking (your BATNA — current job or other offers).

Factors: role level, skills in demand, city, company type (startup, product, services, MNC), and your impact evidence.

steps.title: Handling 'current CTC' and 'expected CTC'
steps.body:
In India, recruiters commonly ask for current CTC and may request payslips. **Never inflate your current salary** — BGV and payslips will reveal it.

You can shift focus to the role's value:
*'My current CTC is ₹18 lakh. Based on the scope of this role and market data for senior product designers in Gurugram, I'm looking for ₹26–28 lakh fixed. I'm flexible on the structure.'*

Or ask first: *'Could you share the budgeted band for this role?'*

steps.title: Worked example: negotiating the offer
steps.body:
Offer: ₹23L fixed. Pooja:
*'Thank you — I'm excited about the role. Based on the scope we discussed (leading design for two product lines) and offers in the market, I was hoping for ₹27L fixed. Is there flexibility on the base?'*
HR: *'Max ₹25L fixed.'*
Pooja: *'I understand. Could we bridge the gap with a joining bonus of ₹2L to cover my notice-period buyout, and a review after six months?'*

She's polite, specific, ties the ask to value, and trades across components.

steps.title: Things to avoid
steps.body:
- Fake competing offers — recruiters talk and may ask for proof.
- Ultimatums you won't follow through.
- Negotiating only by email when a call would build rapport (but always get the final offer in writing).
- Accepting verbally and then renegotiating repeatedly.
- Using pressure on someone else's behalf: negotiate for yourself, respectfully.

It's normal and professional to negotiate once or twice; most HR teams expect it.

a.text: HR: 'What's your expected CTC?' You currently earn ₹12 lakh and market data suggests ₹16–18 lakh for this role. What do you say?

choices.label: 'Based on the role and market data, I'm looking for ₹17–18 lakh. Could you share the band?'
choices.feedback: Researched range plus a question.

choices.label: 'Whatever is standard.'
choices.feedback: You've handed control of the number to them.

choices.label: 'My current CTC is ₹15 lakh' (it's actually ₹12 lakh)
choices.feedback: Inflating current pay is risky and dishonest.

b.text: Offer arrives at ₹15.5 lakh fixed. What next?

choices.label: Thank them, restate value, ask for ₹17.5 lakh, open to structure
choices.feedback: Polite, specific counter.

choices.label: Accept immediately
choices.feedback: Fine if it meets your needs, but a polite counter is normal.

c.text: Offer arrives at ₹13 lakh — only 8% more. What now?

choices.label: Respond with market data and ask for ₹17 lakh
choices.feedback: Recover by anchoring with evidence.

d.text: HR asks for your last three payslips. What do you do?

choices.label: Correct yourself honestly: 'I misspoke — my CTC is ₹12 lakh.'
choices.feedback: Embarrassing but recoverable; lying further is not.

choices.label: Edit the payslips
choices.feedback: Forgery can lead to offer withdrawal and legal consequences.

e.text: HR comes back at ₹17 lakh fixed. You accept in writing. Well negotiated.

e2.text: You have the job. Next time, consider one polite counter backed by data.

e3.text: BGV detects the forgery; the offer is withdrawn and you're flagged. Honesty is non-negotiable.

quiz.q: Before negotiating you should know…
quiz.why: The answer is "Target, expected and walk-away numbers". Reason: Preparation. The other choices, such as "Your manager's salary" and "Nothing", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Inflating your current CTC…
options: Is risky; payslips and BGV can expose it
quiz.why: The answer is "Is risky; payslips and BGV can expose it". Reason: Honesty. The other choices, such as "Helps always" and "Is standard", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: If HR can't raise fixed pay, you might ask for…
options: Joining bonus, early review or other components
quiz.why: The answer is "Joining bonus, early review or other components". Reason: Trade across components. The other choices, such as "Nothing" and "A threat", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A good negotiation tone is…
quiz.why: The answer is "Polite, specific and value-based". Reason: Professional. The other choices, such as "Apologetic and vague" and "Silent", do not fit the question.

lessons.title: When and how to switch jobs

scenes.text: Rahul switched jobs three times in two years for 30–40% hikes each time.
Now senior-role interviewers ask, 'Why so many moves? What did you build?' He has no long project to show.
His friend Ayesha stayed 3 years, led a major launch and got promoted, then switched for a senior role.
Rahul learns: switches are fine — but each one should add a story of impact, not just a number.

steps.title: Good reasons to switch
steps.body:
- Learning has plateaued and there's no path to grow.
- Pay is significantly below market and internal routes have been tried.
- Toxic or unethical environment.
- A role that fits your long-term direction.
- Life needs (city, family, health).

Before switching, consider **internal moves** — new team, new manager, new domain — which can give growth without resetting relationships.

steps.title: Evaluate the new role, not just the hike
steps.body: Ask in interviews: team stability, manager's style, what success looks like, recent attrition, product/business health, on-call or travel expectations. Talk to current or former employees if possible. A 40% hike into a failing team or a bad manager can cost you more than it pays.

steps.title: Counter-offers, BGV and offer etiquette
steps.body:
- **Counter-offers:** decide in advance what would make you stay. If you're leaving for non-money reasons, a raise rarely fixes them.
- **Background verification:** expect checks of employment dates, designation, salary (sometimes), education and references. Keep relieving letters and payslips.
- **Offer etiquette:** don't accept multiple offers and 'ghost' the rest; if you decline, inform promptly and politely. Many recruiters and companies remember.

steps.title: Timing tips
steps.body:
- Consider bonus and appraisal timing — leaving just before a bonus payout or vesting date can cost real money.
- Joining-bonus clawbacks from your current job (if any) may apply if you leave early.
- Start conversations quietly; don't announce on LinkedIn ('open to work' banner visible to all) unless you're comfortable your employer sees it — LinkedIn lets you signal privately to recruiters.

a.text: You've accepted an external offer with a 35% hike. Your manager offers a 30% raise to stay. You left mainly because there's no growth path. What do you do?

choices.label: Ask whether the growth issue would change; if not, thank them and decline
choices.feedback: Decide on your real reasons, not just money.

choices.label: Accept the counter immediately
choices.feedback: Money doesn't fix the original reason.

choices.label: Use the counter to ask the new company for even more
choices.feedback: Possible, but risky after you've accepted.

b.text: Your manager says the growth path won't change soon. How do you exit?

choices.label: Thank them warmly, confirm notice and handover plan

lessons.title: Exits and your entitlements: notice, F&F, gratuity, non-compete

scenes.text: Kavya's new employer wants her to join in 30 days. Her contract says 90 days' notice.
She asks her manager about early release after a full handover; the company agrees to release her in 60 days and adjust some leave.
For the remaining gap, her new employer agrees to reimburse a notice buyout as a joining bonus.
She leaves with her relieving letter, full-and-final settlement and PF transfer done — and a warm farewell.

steps.title: Notice period options
steps.body:
Your notice period is set by your **employment contract and company policy** (and applicable labour law). Options commonly include:
- **Serve full notice.**
- **Early release** by mutual agreement (often after handover).
- **Buyout:** paying (or having salary adjusted) for unserved days, if your policy permits.
- **Leave adjustment** against notice, if policy allows.

Leaving without completing notice or agreement can lead to recovery of dues and a problematic relieving letter. Get any agreement **in writing**.

steps.title: Full and final settlement (F&F)
steps.body: Typically includes: last salary, **leave encashment** (if policy allows), pending reimbursements, bonus dues as per policy, **gratuity** if eligible, minus any recoveries (notice shortfall, clawbacks, company assets). Also collect: **relieving letter, experience letter, Form 16** and payslips, and transfer your **PF** using your UAN.

steps.title: Worked example: gratuity
steps.body:
Gratuity is generally payable after **five years of continuous service** (fixed-term employees may qualify after one year under the Code on Social Security, 2020 — check current rules and your HR). A widely used formula for employees covered by the law:
**Gratuity = 15 × last drawn (basic + DA) × completed years of service ÷ 26**
Example: basic + DA ₹52,000; 6 years → 15 × 52,000 × 6 ÷ 26 = **₹1,80,000**.
There is a statutory maximum limit (currently ₹20 lakh) — check for updates.

steps.title: Non-compete, confidentiality and moonlighting
steps.body:
- **Non-compete after employment:** under Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, agreements in restraint of trade are generally void, and Indian courts have generally not enforced post-employment non-competes. However, **confidentiality** obligations and restrictions **during** employment are enforceable, and non-solicitation clauses may be considered by courts.
- **Never take confidential data**, code or client lists when you leave.
- **Moonlighting:** working another job without permission can breach your contract.

*This is general education, not legal advice. For your situation, consult HR or a qualified lawyer.*

courses.guardianNote: Designed for adult professionals. Covers workplace sexual harassment law (POSH Act 2013) in factual, non-graphic terms, and workplace burnout and mental health with helpline information.

lessons.title: What the POSH Act covers

scenes.text: At a Hyderabad firm, a senior colleague repeatedly sends Swati late-night messages about her looks and 'jokes' about her clothes in team meetings.
Others laugh awkwardly. Swati feels anxious coming to work but wonders if it's 'serious enough'.
In her company's POSH training, she learns that unwelcome sexually coloured remarks are explicitly covered — and that 'just a joke' doesn't change that.
She learns how the Internal Committee works and that she has the right to raise a complaint.

steps.title: The law in brief
steps.body:
The **Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013** — commonly called the **POSH Act** — protects women from sexual harassment at the workplace in India. It applies to public and private sector workplaces, organised and unorganised, including domestic workers.

Key duties on employers include: a written policy, awareness programmes, and an **Internal Committee (IC)** at every office or branch with **10 or more employees**. Where an organisation has fewer than 10 employees (or the complaint is against the employer), complaints can go to the **Local Committee** set up by the District Officer.

steps.title: What counts as sexual harassment
Where is the 'workplace'?
steps.body: The Act defines workplace broadly — not just the office, but places visited during the course of employment, including **transportation provided by the employer**, client sites, offsites and work events. Harassment through **messages, email, chats or video calls** connected to work can also be covered.

steps.title: Beyond the Act
steps.body:
The POSH Act specifically protects women. Many companies have **gender-neutral anti-harassment policies** that also protect men and people of all gender identities — check your company's policy. Some forms of sexual harassment are also offences under India's criminal law (the **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, BNS**, in force from 1 July 2024). In an emergency or if you are in danger, call **112**.

*This is general education, not legal advice.*

statements.s: An Internal Committee is required at offices with 10 or more employees.
statements.why: Each office/branch with 10+ employees must constitute an IC.

statements.s: If the person 'was only joking', it cannot be sexual harassment.
statements.why: The test is whether the conduct is unwelcome; intent doesn't excuse it.

statements.s: Harassment in employer-provided transport can be covered.
statements.why: The Act's definition of workplace includes it.

statements.s: Repeated unwelcome sexual messages on work chat can be covered.
statements.why: Verbal and non-verbal conduct of a sexual nature includes messages.

statements.s: The POSH Act applies only to government offices.
statements.why: It covers public and private workplaces.

lessons.title: How the Internal Committee process works

scenes.text: Swati writes down dates, messages and witnesses, and submits a written complaint to the IC presiding officer.
The IC acknowledges it confidentially and explains the process, including that she may ask for conciliation or a full inquiry.
During the inquiry, she asks for interim relief so she doesn't report to the colleague; the IC recommends it.
The IC completes the inquiry, finds the allegations proved and recommends action; the employer acts on it.

steps.title: Who is on the IC
Key steps and timelines
steps.body:
- **Complaint:** in writing, within **3 months** of the incident (or the last incident in a series). The IC can extend this by up to a further 3 months if there were reasons that prevented filing. If the woman can't write, the IC must give reasonable assistance; in some circumstances others (e.g., a relative or friend) can file on her behalf.
- **Conciliation:** before inquiry, **at the request of the aggrieved woman**; a monetary settlement cannot be the basis of conciliation.
- **Inquiry:** completed within **90 days**; both sides are heard following principles of natural justice.
- **Report:** provided within 10 days of completing the inquiry; the employer must act on recommendations within **60 days**.
- **Interim relief** during inquiry, on written request: e.g., transfer of either party, leave, or restraining the respondent from assessing the complainant's work.
- **Appeal:** available within 90 days of the recommendations.

steps.title: Confidentiality and protection
steps.body:
The Act prohibits publishing or making known the identity and details of the complainant, respondent, witnesses and proceedings. Retaliation against a complainant or witness should be treated as a serious violation under company policy.

On false complaints: the Act allows action for a **malicious** false complaint, but it explicitly states that **mere inability to substantiate a complaint or provide adequate proof** does not attract such action. This protects genuine complainants.

steps.title: If you're considering a complaint
steps.body:
- Write down dates, times, places, what was said/done, and witnesses.
- Save messages, emails and screenshots securely.
- You can speak confidentially to an IC member first to understand options.
- Seek emotional support — a trusted friend, EAP counsellor, or Tele-MANAS (14416).
- If you're in immediate danger, call **112**.

*This is general education, not legal advice.*

scenes.text: At a team offsite in Goa, a manager makes a sexual comment about a new joiner, Fatima. A few people laugh.
Her colleague Vivek feels uncomfortable but doesn't know what to do.
He redirects the conversation, then checks in privately with Fatima: 'That wasn't okay. Are you alright? I'm happy to be a witness if you ever want to raise it.'
Fatima feels less alone. With support, she decides how she wants to proceed.

steps.title: The 5 Ds of bystander action
steps.body:
A widely taught bystander framework:
- **Direct:** speak up if safe — *'That's not okay.'*
- **Distract:** interrupt — change the topic, ask the person to help with something.
- **Delegate:** get help — a manager, HR, IC member, security.
- **Delay:** check in afterwards — *'Are you okay? What would help?'*
- **Document:** note what happened (dates, words, witnesses) and give it to the affected person to use as they choose.

Your safety matters; choose the option that fits the situation.

steps.title: If you're a manager
steps.body:
- **Take every report seriously**; listen without judgement.
- **Don't investigate yourself** or try to 'settle it informally' — point to the IC and policy, and inform HR/IC as your policy requires.
- **Maintain confidentiality.**
- **Prevent retaliation** — watch for changes in work allocation, ratings or exclusion of the complainant.
- **Model behaviour:** shut down inappropriate jokes immediately; ensure safe travel and event arrangements.

Managers who ignore or mishandle reports can face disciplinary action under company policy.

steps.title: What not to say
steps.body:
- *'Are you sure? He's a nice guy.'*
- *'Why didn't you say something then?'*
- *'Just ignore it; it'll blow over.'*
- *'It's a cultural thing / that's how he talks.'*

These discourage reporting. Instead: *'Thank you for telling me. You have options; here's how the process works. What would help you right now?'*

steps.title: Building a respectful culture
steps.body: Everyone can contribute: don't laugh along with sexist or demeaning jokes, include colleagues of all genders in opportunities, respect boundaries (personal space, after-hours messages, social media), and take your organisation's POSH training seriously.

lessons.title: Burnout: recognise, prevent, recover

scenes.text: Prakash, a team lead at a Chennai IT firm, has worked 12-hour days for eight months, including weekends, covering for two vacant roles.
He feels exhausted even after sleep, snaps at his family, and doesn't care about projects he once loved.
His doctor rules out other causes and suggests he may be experiencing burnout; she recommends rest and talking to a counsellor.
He speaks to his manager with a clear plan, takes leave, sets boundaries, and slowly recovers.

steps.title: What burnout is
Common causes
steps.body:
Research on burnout (notably by Christina Maslach and colleagues) points to mismatches in six areas: **workload, control, reward, community, fairness and values**. Examples: chronic understaffing, constant urgency, no say over your work, unrecognised effort, conflict or isolation, unfair treatment, or work that conflicts with your values.

This matters: burnout is often a **workplace problem**, not just an individual weakness — solutions need both personal and organisational change.

steps.title: Worked example: talking to your manager
steps.body:
*'Priya, I want to flag something. For eight months I've been covering two vacant roles, working most weekends. I'm exhausted and I'm worried about quality and my health. Could we (1) prioritise which projects can pause, (2) speed up the two hires or get temporary help, and (3) I'd like to take a week's leave next month. I'll prepare a handover.'*

It's factual, links to business risk, and proposes solutions.

steps.title: Recovery and prevention habits
steps.body:
- Protect **sleep**, movement and meals; small daily breaks.
- Set **boundaries**: notification-free hours, a clear end to the workday, real leave.
- **Reduce load**: prioritise, delegate, say no to low-value work.
- **Reconnect**: friends, family, hobbies, purpose.
- **Talk to someone**: EAP counsellors, a therapist, or **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7 in India).

**See a professional** if symptoms last more than two weeks, affect daily life, or include hopelessness. If you have thoughts of harming yourself, seek help immediately — call **14416** or **112**.

*This is general education, not medical advice.*

activity.label: How many weeks have you felt exhausted, cynical or less effective at work?

bands.text: Short-term stress is normal. Rest, a lighter week and a good night's sleep often help.
Watch the pattern. Protect sleep, set boundaries, and talk to your manager about workload.
This sounds like chronic stress. Talk to your manager with a concrete plan, use leave, and consider speaking to a counsellor (EAP or Tele-MANAS 14416).
Long-lasting symptoms deserve professional support. Please see a doctor or mental-health professional. If you ever feel hopeless or unsafe, call 14416 or 112 now.

scenes.text: Rajiv, a project manager in Bengaluru, writes: 'It is hereby requested that, in view of the aforementioned considerations, necessary action may kindly be initiated at the earliest so as to facilitate the timely completion…'
His US client replies: 'Sorry, what do you need from us?'
His coach rewrites it: 'Please approve the test plan by Friday so we can finish on time.'
Thirteen words instead of ninety. Approved the same day.

steps.title: The plain-language rules
steps.body:
- **Short words:** *use* not *utilise*; *start* not *commence*; *help* not *facilitate*.
- **Short sentences:** aim for an average under ~20 words; one idea per sentence.
- **Active voice:** *'The team fixed the bug'* not *'The bug was fixed by the team'*. Active voice shows who does what.
- **Concrete over abstract:** *'Reduce delivery time from 5 to 3 days'* not *'optimise delivery efficiency'*.
- **Cut filler:** *'at this point in time'* → *now*; *'in order to'* → *to*; *'due to the fact that'* → *because*.

steps.title: Worked example: three rewrites
steps.body:
- *'The meeting has been rescheduled by the management due to unavoidable circumstances.'* → **'Management moved the meeting to Thursday because the client can't attend Wednesday.'**
- *'We would like to inform you that your request is under process.'* → **'We're working on your request and will reply by 5 pm tomorrow.'**
- *'Kindly revert with the needful at the earliest.'* → **'Please send the signed form by Monday.'**

Notice how each rewrite adds a **specific** fact (day, time, reason) — plain language is usually more informative, not less.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using jargon and acronyms for readers outside your team (spell out on first use: *'user acceptance testing (UAT)'*).
- Thinking formal = professional. Clarity is professional.
- Hedging everything: *'It might perhaps be possible that…'* — say what you think and how confident you are.
- Burying numbers in paragraphs; put key numbers where the eye lands.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Take your last long email. Cut it by 40% without losing any fact. Then read it aloud — if you run out of breath in a sentence, split it.

activity.prompt: Match the wordy phrase to its plain version.

quiz.q: Which sentence is in active voice?
options: The report was approved by the director.
quiz.why: The answer is "The director approved the report.". Reason: Active voice names the actor first. The other choices, such as "Approval was given." and "The report was approved by the director.", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A good average sentence length for business writing is…
quiz.why: The answer is "Under about 20 words". Reason: Shorter sentences are easier to read and translate. The other choices, such as "50–60 words" and "Length doesn't matter", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Plain language usually makes writing…
options: More specific and easier to act on
quiz.why: The answer is "More specific and easier to act on". Reason: It replaces vague formulas with concrete facts. The other choices, such as "Less informative" and "Childish", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: When should you spell out an acronym?
options: On first use for readers who may not know it
quiz.why: The answer is "On first use for readers who may not know it". Reason: Then use the short form. The other choices, such as "Only in titles" and "Every time", do not fit the question.

scenes.text: Ishita, a new consultant in Mumbai, presents findings in the order she discovered them: data sources, methods, 14 observations, and finally a recommendation on slide 22.
The client CFO interrupts on slide 4: 'What are you recommending?'
Her manager teaches her the pyramid: answer first, then 3 supporting reasons, then the evidence.
Her next deck opens with 'Close two of the five warehouses to save ₹18 crore a year' — and the CFO engages for an hour.

steps.title: Answer first, then support
steps.body:
The **pyramid principle** (popularised by Barbara Minto) says: start with your **main point**, then group supporting arguments (ideally three), each backed by evidence.

- **Top:** governing thought — *'We should close two of five warehouses.'*
- **Middle:** key reasons — *cost, service levels, risk.*
- **Bottom:** data — *rent, utilisation, delivery times.*

Busy readers can stop at any level and still get the message.

steps.title: SCQA for introductions
steps.body:
To set up the main point, use **Situation – Complication – Question – Answer**:
- **S:** *We run five warehouses in western India.*
- **C:** *Utilisation has dropped to 55% since we moved to direct-to-store shipping.*
- **Q:** *Should we keep all five?*
- **A:** *No — close Nashik and Rajkot and save about ₹18 crore a year with no loss of 2-day delivery.*

SCQA works for emails, memos, presentations and even interview answers.

steps.title: Worked example: a pyramid email
steps.body:
*Subject: Recommendation: move to vendor B for cloud backup (saves ₹14 lakh/yr)*

*Recommendation: switch to vendor B from 1 April.*
*Why:*
- *Cost: ₹14 lakh/year lower for the same storage.*
- *Reliability: 2 outages last year vs 7 for vendor A.*
- *Compliance: data stays in Indian data centres.*
*Risk: migration takes 3 weeks; we'll run both in parallel during that time.*
*Decision needed by 15 Feb.*

steps.title: MECE grouping
steps.body: Group supporting points so they are **MECE — mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive**: no overlaps, no big gaps. *'Cost, reliability, compliance'* is MECE-ish; *'cost, price, money'* overlaps. MECE thinking makes your argument feel complete and easy to follow.

activity.prompt: Arrange this SCQA introduction in order.
items: Situation: Our app has 2 million monthly users in India.
Complication: 40% drop off at the payment step.
Question: How do we reduce payment drop-off?
Answer: Add UPI autopay and one-tap retry — expected to recover a third of drop-offs.

quiz.q: In the pyramid principle, what comes first?
quiz.why: The answer is "The main point or recommendation". Reason: Answer first, then support. The other choices, such as "All data" and "Methodology", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: SCQA stands for…
quiz.why: The answer is "Situation, Complication, Question, Answer". Reason: A storytelling setup for your main point. The other choices, such as "Summary, Conclusion, Question, Appendix" and "Start, Continue, Quit, Again", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: MECE means…
quiz.why: The answer is "Mutually Exclusive, Collectively Exhaustive". Reason: No overlaps, no gaps. The other choices, such as "Mostly Easy, Clearly Explained" and "Measure Every Cost Early", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Why did the CFO interrupt Ishita?
options: The recommendation was buried at the end
quiz.why: The answer is "The recommendation was buried at the end". Reason: Executives want the answer first. The other choices, such as "She spoke too slowly" and "The slides were ugly", do not fit the question.

lessons.title: One-pagers and decision memos for executives

story.title: The VP who reads at 7 am

scenes.text: Kabir needs his VP, Susan in Seattle, to approve hiring three engineers for a Bengaluru team. He has 10 minutes in her packed calendar.
Instead of 20 slides, he writes a one-page memo and sends it the evening before.
Susan reads it with her morning coffee, writes two questions in the margin, and the meeting takes six minutes.
Approved. 'This is how I like to decide,' she says.

steps.title: The one-page decision memo
steps.body:
A reliable structure:
- **Title + ask:** *'Decision: approve 3 backend hires for Payments (Q3)'*
- **Context (2–3 lines):** why now.
- **Recommendation:** what you propose.
- **Options considered:** 2–3 alternatives with pros/cons (including 'do nothing').
- **Impact:** cost, benefit, metrics.
- **Risks & mitigations.**
- **What we need from you:** the decision, by when.

Some companies, famously Amazon, use longer **narrative memos** read silently at the start of meetings instead of slides; the principle is the same: complete sentences force complete thinking.

steps.title: Worked example: options table
steps.body:
| Option | Cost/yr | Impact | Risk |
- **A. Hire 3 engineers (recommended):** ~₹1.2 crore; launch UPI autopay in Q4; hiring takes 8–10 weeks.
- **B. Use a vendor team:** ~₹1.5 crore; faster start; less ownership, knowledge leaves with vendor.
- **C. Do nothing:** ₹0; autopay slips to next year; competitors may win users.

Showing that you considered alternatives builds trust in your recommendation.

steps.title: Write for the executive's questions
steps.body: Executives tend to ask: *What do you need from me? Why now? What does it cost? What's the risk? What are the alternatives? How will we know it worked?* Answer all six on the page and your meeting will be short.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Hiding the ask on page 3.
- Only one option (looks like you didn't think).
- No numbers, or numbers without sources.
- Sending it five minutes before the meeting. Send it early enough to be read.

activity.prompt: Does your executive memo pass the checklist?
items: The ask and deadline are in the title or first line
Context is 2–3 lines
There's a clear recommendation
At least two alternatives, including 'do nothing'
Costs and benefits have numbers and sources
Risks and mitigations are listed
Success metrics are defined
It fits on one page
Sent early enough to be read

quiz.q: What should the first line of a decision memo contain?
quiz.why: The answer is "The ask and deadline". Reason: Readers need to know what's being asked. The other choices, such as "Company history" and "A joke", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Why include 'do nothing' as an option?
options: It clarifies the cost of inaction
quiz.why: The answer is "It clarifies the cost of inaction". Reason: It frames urgency honestly. The other choices, such as "To confuse" and "It's mandatory", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Narrative memos force…
quiz.why: The answer is "Complete thinking in full sentences". Reason: Bullet fragments can hide gaps in logic. The other choices, such as "More slides" and "Shorter meetings always", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Which question do executives commonly ask?
options: What's the risk and what are the alternatives?
quiz.why: The answer is "What's the risk and what are the alternatives?". Reason: Risk and options are core to decisions. The other choices, such as "What's the font?" and "Who designed the logo?", do not fit the question.

scenes.text: Leena, a policy analyst in Delhi, writes fast but her drafts are full of repetition and typos.
A senior editor teaches her a three-pass method: structure, sentences, then proofing.
It adds 15 minutes to each document.
Within a month, her director starts forwarding her drafts unchanged.

steps.title: Pass 1: structure
steps.body: Ask: Is the main point at the top? Does each section support it? Is anything missing or repeated? Would headings or bullets help? **Fix structure before polishing words** — no point perfecting a paragraph you'll delete.

steps.title: Pass 2: sentences
steps.body:
- Cut filler and repeated ideas.
- Change passive to active where it helps.
- Replace vague words (*'significant', 'various', 'some'*) with numbers or specifics.
- Check each paragraph starts with its point (a **topic sentence**).

steps.title: Pass 3: proofing
steps.body:
- Names, titles, dates, numbers, currency (₹ vs $), time zones.
- Spelling and grammar (spell-checkers help, but don't catch wrong-but-real words like *'form/from'*).
- Read aloud or use a read-aloud tool.
- Check attachments and links.

Grammar tools and AI assistants can help with drafts, but **never paste confidential company or client information into tools your company hasn't approved**, and always check AI output for errors.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Take a 300-word document you wrote. Do the three passes separately, with a short break between. Note how many words you cut and how many errors you caught.

statements.s: You should polish sentences before fixing the structure.
statements.why: Structure first; otherwise you polish text you'll cut.

statements.s: Spell-checkers catch every wrong word.
statements.why: They miss real words used wrongly, like 'form' for 'from'.

statements.s: Reading aloud helps catch awkward sentences and errors.
statements.why: Your ear catches what your eye skips.

statements.s: It's fine to paste confidential client data into any free AI tool to improve grammar.
statements.why: Use only company-approved tools for confidential data.

statements.s: Replacing 'significant increase' with 'a 23% increase' improves clarity.
statements.why: Specific numbers beat vague adjectives.

quiz.q: The correct order of the three editing passes is…
quiz.why: The answer is "Structure, sentences, proofing". Reason: Big to small. The other choices, such as "Sentences, proofing, structure" and "Only proofing", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A topic sentence…
options: Ends a paragraph with a joke
States the paragraph's main point at the start
quiz.why: The answer is "States the paragraph's main point at the start". Reason: Readers skim first sentences. The other choices, such as "Lists references" and "Is optional always", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Which detail is most often wrong in business documents and worth checking?
quiz.why: The answer is "Names, dates, numbers and currency". Reason: These errors damage credibility. The other choices, such as "Line spacing" and "The logo", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Using AI writing tools at work requires…
options: Company-approved tools for confidential data and checking output
quiz.why: The answer is "Company-approved tools for confidential data and checking output". Reason: Confidentiality and accuracy. The other choices, such as "Paying personally" and "Avoiding all editing", do not fit the question.

questions.q: 'Utilise' is better written as…
questions.why: The answer is "Use". Reason: Short words. The other choices, such as "Utilize" and "Make utilisation of", do not fit the question. (Question: 'Utilise' is better written as…)

questions.q: The pyramid principle starts with…
questions.why: The answer is "The answer". Reason: Main point first. The other choices, such as "The team" and "The methodology", do not fit the question. (Question: The pyramid principle starts with…)

questions.q: Active voice example:
options: The bug has been fixed by someone.
questions.why: The answer is "Asha fixed the bug.". Reason: Actor + verb. The other choices, such as "The bug was fixed." and "The bug has been fixed by someone.", do not fit the question.

questions.q: SCQA's 'C' is…
questions.why: The answer is "Complication". Reason: What changed or went wrong. The other choices, such as "Context" and "Cost", do not fit the question. (Question: SCQA's 'C' is…)

questions.q: A decision memo should include at least…
options: Two or more options including 'do nothing'
questions.why: The answer is "Two or more options including 'do nothing'". Reason: Shows thinking. The other choices, such as "One option" and "No options", do not fit the question.

questions.q: MECE grouping avoids…
questions.why: The answer is "Overlaps and gaps". Reason: Clean logic. The other choices, such as "Numbers" and "Bullets", do not fit the question. (Question: MECE grouping avoids…)

questions.q: Which edit pass comes first?
questions.why: The answer is "Structure". Reason: Big picture first. The other choices, such as "Proofing" and "Formatting", do not fit the question. (Question: Which edit pass comes first?)

questions.q: Replace 'due to the fact that' with…
questions.why: The answer is "Because". Reason: Shorter. The other choices, such as "Owing to the reality" and "As per", do not fit the question. (Question: Replace 'due to the fact that' with…)

questions.q: Why send a memo before the meeting?
options: So it can be read and the meeting used to decide
questions.why: The answer is "So it can be read and the meeting used to decide". Reason: Preparation shortens decisions. The other choices, such as "To avoid the meeting" and "It doesn't matter", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which group of reasons is closest to MECE?
questions.why: The answer is "Cost, reliability, compliance". Reason: Distinct categories. The other choices, such as "Cheap, inexpensive, low-cost" and "Fast, quick, rapid", do not fit the question.

questions.q: An executive asks 'How will we know it worked?' You need…
questions.why: The answer is "Success metrics". Reason: Define measurable outcomes. The other choices, such as "A new font" and "More slides", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Best rewrite of 'We would like to inform you that your request is under process'?
options: 'We're working on your request and will reply by 5 pm tomorrow.'
questions.why: The answer is "'We're working on your request and will reply by 5 pm tomorrow.'". Reason: Plain and specific. The other choices, such as "'Noted.'" and "'Your request is being processed kindly'", do not fit the question.

questions.q: A director says, 'Your memo is persuasive but I don't trust the numbers.' The most likely fix?
options: Add sources and assumptions for each number
questions.why: The answer is "Add sources and assumptions for each number". Reason: Credible evidence. The other choices, such as "Add adjectives" and "Make it longer", do not fit the question.

courses.title: Presenting and storytelling with data
courses.summary: Structure talks, design clean slides, choose the right chart and tell a story with data, then handle Q&A and nerves with confidence.
outcomes: Learners can structure a presentation around one key message
Learners can design simple, readable slides with action titles
Learners can choose an honest, appropriate chart for data
Learners can handle Q&A and manage presentation anxiety

lessons.title: Structuring a talk around one message

scenes.text: Neel has 10 minutes at the quarterly town hall of his Pune company to present his team's work. He prepares 30 slides covering everything.
At minute 10 he's on slide 12. The host cuts him off.
A mentor asks him: 'If the audience remembers one sentence, what should it be?'
His next talk: one message, three supports, one ask. Seven slides. People quote his line afterwards.

steps.title: Start with the one-sentence message
steps.body:
Before opening PowerPoint, write: **'After this talk, the audience should ___ because ___.'** For example: *'…approve the pilot in Jaipur because it cut delivery time by 30% in Indore.'*

Everything that doesn't support that sentence is cut or moved to the appendix.

steps.title: A simple talk structure
steps.body:
- **Hook (30 sec):** a story, number or question. *'Last Diwali, 1 in 5 orders in Indore arrived late.'*
- **Message:** state it.
- **Three supports:** each a short section with evidence.
- **Ask / next step:** what you want the audience to do.
- **Close:** restate the message.

Rule of thumb: plan roughly **one to two minutes per content slide** and rehearse with a timer.

steps.title: Worked example: 'tell them' structure
steps.body:
Neel's revised outline:
- Hook: *'1 in 5 Diwali orders were late.'*
- Message: *'Micro-warehouses fixed it in Indore; let's do Jaipur next.'*
- Support 1: late deliveries fell from 20% to 6%.
- Support 2: cost per order fell by ₹11.
- Support 3: customer ratings rose from 3.9 to 4.4.
- Ask: approve ₹2 crore for the Jaipur pilot.
- Close: *'Fewer late Diwalis — Jaipur next.'*

steps.title: Know your audience
steps.body: Executives: decision, numbers, risk — fast. Engineers: how it works, trade-offs. Clients: their problem and outcome. Mixed audiences: lead with the outcome, offer detail in Q&A or an appendix.

activity.prompt: Complete the planning sentence and structure.
activity.text: After this talk, the audience should ___ because ___. Structure: hook, message, three supports, ___, close.
answers: it works|of the evidence|the results|the data

quiz.q: The first thing to prepare for a talk is…
quiz.why: The answer is "The one-sentence message". Reason: Content before design. The other choices, such as "The thank-you slide" and "Animations", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A good hook is…
options: A striking story, number or question
quiz.why: The answer is "A striking story, number or question". Reason: It earns attention. The other choices, such as "An agenda slide" and "'Today I will present…'", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: What do you do with content that doesn't support your message?
options: Cut it or move it to an appendix
quiz.why: The answer is "Cut it or move it to an appendix". Reason: Focus. The other choices, such as "Keep everything" and "Speak faster", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: For executives you should emphasise…
quiz.why: The answer is "Decision, numbers and risk". Reason: They decide fast. The other choices, such as "Your journey" and "Methodology details", do not fit the question.

scenes.text: Pallavi's slide has 14 bullet points in 11-point font. She reads them aloud while the audience reads ahead.
Half the room checks phones.
She redesigns: one point per slide, an action title, one chart, big font.
Now people look up at her when she speaks.

steps.title: Action titles
steps.body:
Replace topic titles with **action titles** — a full sentence that states the takeaway:
- Topic: *'Q3 sales'*
- Action: *'Q3 sales grew 18%, driven by Tier-2 cities'*

If someone reads only your titles, they should get the whole story.

steps.title: Clean design rules
steps.body:
- **One idea per slide.**
- Large, readable fonts (as a rough guide, body text around 24 pt or larger for projected slides).
- High contrast; avoid text on busy photos.
- Consistent colours: one highlight colour for 'the point'.
- Fewer words: slides support you; they're not your script.
- Make it **accessible**: don't rely on colour alone (some viewers are colour-blind); add labels.

steps.title: Worked example: before → after
steps.body:
**Before:** title *'Customer feedback'*, 12 bullets of comments.

**After:** title *'Customers love speed but hate our returns process'*; two big quotes; one bar chart showing 'returns' as the top complaint (38%) in your highlight colour, others in grey.

The audience understands in 5 seconds.

steps.title: Pre-read vs presented deck
steps.body: A deck to be **presented** should be sparse. A deck to be **read** (sent by email) needs more text. Don't use one for the other — or make a sparse main deck plus a detailed appendix.

activity.prompt: Topic title or action title?

items.text: Q3 revenue
Q3 revenue grew 18% on Tier-2 demand
Customer feedback
Returns are our #1 complaint (38%)
Next steps
Approve ₹2 crore to pilot Jaipur in Q1

quiz.q: An action title…
options: States the takeaway as a sentence
quiz.why: The answer is "States the takeaway as a sentence". Reason: Titles carry the story. The other choices, such as "Is one word" and "Shows the date", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Why avoid relying only on colour?
quiz.why: The answer is "Colour-blind viewers may miss it". Reason: Accessibility. The other choices, such as "Projectors can't show colour" and "Colour is expensive", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A presented deck should be…
quiz.why: The answer is "Sparse; you do the talking". Reason: Slides support you. The other choices, such as "Dense with text" and "Only images", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A highlight colour helps…
options: Draw attention to the key point
quiz.why: The answer is "Draw attention to the key point". Reason: Grey context, one highlight. The other choices, such as "Confuse" and "Make slides colourful", do not fit the question.

scenes.text: In a review, Arvind shows a bar chart where complaints 'tripled' — the bars look enormous.
The CFO notices the y-axis starts at 950. Complaints went from 980 to 1,010 — a 3% rise.
Arvind's credibility takes a hit. He hadn't meant to mislead; the tool set the axis automatically.
He now checks every chart: right type, honest axis, clear label.

steps.title: Pick the chart for the question
steps.body:
- **Compare categories:** bar chart (horizontal bars for long labels).
- **Change over time:** line chart.
- **Part of a whole:** stacked bar, or a pie only if there are few slices (around 2–4) with clearly different sizes.
- **Relationship between two numbers:** scatter plot.
- **Distribution:** histogram or box plot.
- **A single key number:** just show the number big, with context (*'₹4.2 crore, up 12% vs last year'*).

steps.title: Honesty rules
steps.body:
- **Bar charts must start at zero** — bar length represents the value. (Line charts may use a non-zero axis if clearly labelled.)
- Don't use 3D effects; they distort sizes.
- Label units and sources.
- Don't cherry-pick date ranges to hide bad periods.
- Show percentages *and* base numbers when the base is small (*'50% growth — from 4 to 6 customers'*).

steps.title: Worked example: the right comparison
steps.body:
Question: *'Which region has the highest return rate?'*
- Data: North 4.1%, South 2.9%, East 6.3%, West 3.5%.
- Best chart: **horizontal bar, sorted from highest to lowest**, East highlighted, others grey, action title *'East's return rate (6.3%) is double the South's'*.

Sorting is a small step that makes patterns obvious.

steps.title: Narrate the chart
steps.body: When presenting a chart: say **what it shows** (*'This is monthly churn'*), **where to look** (*'Focus on the red line after June'*), and **what it means** (*'Churn doubled after the price change'*). Audiences need a guide.

activity.prompt: Match the question to the best chart.
pairs: How did monthly sales change over two years?
Is ad spend related to sales across 50 cities?
A big single number with context

quiz.q: Why must bar charts start at zero?
options: Bar length represents value; truncating exaggerates differences
quiz.why: The answer is "Bar length represents value; truncating exaggerates differences". Reason: Otherwise small changes look huge. The other choices, such as "Software requires it" and "It looks nicer", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Best chart for change over time?
quiz.why: The answer is "Line". Reason: Lines show trends. The other choices, such as "Pie" and "Word cloud", do not fit the question. (Question: Best chart for change over time?)

quiz.q: When is a pie chart acceptable?
options: With a few slices of clearly different sizes
quiz.why: The answer is "With a few slices of clearly different sizes". Reason: Pies are hard to compare with many slices. The other choices, such as "With 15 slices" and "Never", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: '50% growth' on a tiny base should be shown with…
quiz.why: The answer is "The base numbers too". Reason: Avoids misleading impressions. The other choices, such as "Bigger font" and "3D effect", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Sorting bars from highest to lowest…
quiz.why: The answer is "Makes patterns obvious". Reason: Faster reading. The other choices, such as "Is dishonest" and "Is required by law", do not fit the question.

scenes.text: Ayesha presents to her company's leadership in Dubai. A director asks a question she can't answer. Her mind goes blank.
She remembers her coach: 'Pause. Repeat the question. If you don't know, say so and commit to follow up.'
'Good question — I don't have the Q2 split with me. I'll send it by 5 pm today.'
She sends it at 3 pm. The director later says her follow-through impressed him more than the presentation.

steps.title: Handling questions
steps.body:
- **Listen fully**; don't interrupt.
- **Pause** a second — it looks thoughtful.
- **Repeat or rephrase** the question (helps the room and buys time).
- **Answer briefly**, then check: *'Does that answer it?'*
- **Don't know?** *'I don't have that number; I'll send it by 5 pm.'* Then do it.
- **Hostile question?** Stay calm, acknowledge the concern, answer the fact: *'I understand the worry about cost. Here's the breakdown…'*

steps.title: Managing nerves
steps.body:
Nervousness is normal — even experienced speakers feel it. Practical tools:
- **Rehearse aloud** 2–3 times, at least once standing, with a timer.
- Know your **first 30 seconds** by heart.
- **Slow breathing** before you start (e.g., inhale 4, hold 4, exhale 4–6).
- Reframe: the audience wants you to succeed.
- Find 2–3 friendly faces and speak to them.

If anxiety is severe or stops you from working, a counsellor or psychologist can help — it's very treatable.

steps.title: Presence basics
steps.body:
- Stand or sit tall; plant your feet.
- Make eye contact (on video: look at the camera when making key points).
- Speak slower than feels natural; pause after key numbers.
- Cut fillers ('um', 'basically', 'actually') — a pause is better.
- On video, good lighting from the front and a clear microphone matter more than a fancy background.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Record yourself giving a 2-minute version of a talk on your phone. Watch it once for content, once for voice (pace, fillers) and once with the sound off (body language).

activity.label: Calm-before-you-present breath: in 4, hold 4, out 6, rest 2

quiz.q: You don't know the answer to a question. Best response?
options: Say you don't have it and commit to a specific follow-up time
quiz.why: The answer is "Say you don't have it and commit to a specific follow-up time". Reason: Honesty plus follow-through builds trust. The other choices, such as "Make something up" and "Change the subject", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Why repeat a question before answering?
options: It helps the room hear it and gives you thinking time

courses.title: Cross-cultural communication for global teams
courses.summary: Work smoothly with colleagues and clients in the US, Europe, Japan, the Middle East and across India: context, directness, feedback, time zones and Indian-English pitfalls.
outcomes: Learners can explain high- vs low-context communication
Learners can adapt directness and feedback style to a culture
Learners can avoid common Indian-English misunderstandings
Learners can run effective meetings across time zones and cultures

scenes.text: Mark, a manager in Chicago, asks his Indian team lead, Srinivas, 'Can we deliver by Friday?' Srinivas says, 'We will try our best.'
Mark hears 'yes'. Srinivas meant 'very unlikely, but I don't want to refuse you directly'.
Friday comes; nothing is delivered. Both feel let down.
After a cross-cultural workshop, Srinivas learns to say: 'Friday is not realistic; Tuesday is. Here's why.' Mark learns to ask, 'How confident are you, 1 to 10?'

steps.title: Two ends of a spectrum
steps.body:
Anthropologist Edward T. Hall described **high-context** and **low-context** communication:
- **Low-context** (often associated with the US, Netherlands, Germany, Scandinavia, Australia): meaning is in the explicit words. 'Yes' means yes. Directness is valued.
- **High-context** (often associated with Japan, China, Korea, much of India, the Middle East): meaning is also in tone, relationship, what is *not* said. Refusals may be indirect to preserve harmony.

These are **tendencies, not rules** — individuals vary a lot, and many Indians in global firms are quite direct.

steps.title: Worked example: translating 'we'll try'
steps.body:
Phrases that can mean 'probably not' in high-context speech:
- *'We will try our best.'* · *'It will be difficult.'* · *'Let me check and revert.'* · *'Should be possible, sir.'*

For low-context colleagues, be explicit: *'Friday isn't realistic because testing needs 3 days. We can deliver Tuesday, or deliver a partial version Friday without the reports module. Which do you prefer?'*

steps.title: Confidence scales
steps.body: A simple tool that works across cultures: state or ask for **confidence levels**. *'I'm 60% confident on Friday, 95% on Tuesday.'* It replaces vague 'we'll try' with something everyone can plan around, without anyone having to say a blunt 'no'.

steps.title: Reading the room elsewhere
steps.body: With Japanese colleagues, silence may mean thinking, not agreement; decisions may be built through informal consultation before meetings. With many Middle Eastern partners, relationship-building and hospitality come before business. With German or Dutch colleagues, blunt critique of an idea is often not personal. Ask colleagues from that culture what's normal — people appreciate the effort.

activity.prompt: Which phrasing is clear for a low-context reader?

items.text: We will try our best.
Friday isn't realistic; Tuesday is, because testing needs 3 days.
Let me check and revert.
I'm 60% confident on Friday and 95% on Tuesday.
It should be possible, sir.
I'll confirm by 4 pm IST whether Friday works.

quiz.why: The answer is "The explicit words". Reason: Say what you mean. The other choices, such as "Tone and silence" and "Body language only", do not fit the question.

quiz.why: The answer is "Tendencies; individuals vary". Reason: Avoid stereotyping. The other choices, such as "Laws" and "Strict rules for every person", do not fit the question.

lessons.title: Indian English that confuses global colleagues

scenes.text: Pradeep writes to his UK client: 'I have a doubt about the requirement.' The client worries he doubts the project.
He adds, 'Let's prepone the meeting.' The client searches for 'prepone'.
In a friendly call, the client asks about these phrases. They laugh and Pradeep learns which words travel.
He keeps his Indian English at home and with Indian teams — and switches to global English with clients.

steps.title: Indian English is a real variety
steps.body: Indian English is a legitimate variety of English with its own vocabulary — just like British, American or Australian English. Words like *prepone* are understood in India. The issue is only **mutual understanding**: some words confuse readers elsewhere.

steps.title: Common phrases and global alternatives
steps.body:
- *'I have a doubt'* → **'I have a question'** (elsewhere 'doubt' suggests distrust).
- *'Prepone'* → **'bring forward / move earlier'**.
- *'Revert'* → **'reply / get back to you'**.
- *'Do the needful'* → state the specific action.
- *'Out of station'* → **'travelling / away'**.
- *'Passed out of college in 2022'* → **'graduated in 2022'** (elsewhere 'passed out' means fainted!).
- *'Kindly adjust'* → explain what you're asking them to accept.
- *'Same to same'* → **'identical'**.

steps.title: Dates, numbers and time zones
steps.body:
- **Lakh and crore** are not understood globally: ₹1 lakh = 100,000; ₹1 crore = 10 million. For global readers write *'₹10 million (₹1 crore)'* or convert to USD with a date.
- Dates: 04/05 means 4 May in India and the UK but April 5 in the US. Write **'4 May 2026'**.
- Always add time zones: *'3 pm IST / 10:30 am BST'* (IST is UTC+5:30).

steps.title: Don't over-correct
steps.body: You don't need to hide your accent or identity. Clarity is the goal, not imitation. Global colleagues should also learn some context about India — good teams adapt both ways.

scenes.text: Sanne from Amsterdam reviews Rohit's design: 'This is not good. The flow is confusing. Redo section 2.'
Rohit, used to gentler feedback, feels crushed and thinks Sanne dislikes him.
Over a call, Sanne is warm and says she really likes his work. She just gives feedback directly.
Meanwhile Rohit's feedback to her ('maybe we could consider looking at…') was so soft she ignored it. They agree on a shared style.

steps.title: Direct vs indirect negative feedback
steps.body:
Researcher Erin Meyer (*The Culture Map*) notes that cultures differ in how directly they give negative feedback — and this doesn't always match how direct they are in general. Some cultures use **upgraders** ('absolutely wrong', 'totally inappropriate'); others use **downgraders** ('a bit', 'maybe', 'kind of').

When working across cultures, recalibrate: a 'maybe consider' from a Japanese colleague may be serious; a blunt line from a Dutch colleague may be routine.

steps.title: Worked example: one message, two styles
steps.body:
**For a direct-feedback culture:** *'Section 2 doesn't work: users can't find the pay button. Please move it above the fold.'*

**For an indirect-feedback culture:** *'Overall the design is strong. One area we might improve is section 2 — in testing, users struggled to find the pay button. What if it were higher on the page?'*

**Universal safe middle:** be specific about the problem, kind about the person, clear about the request.

steps.title: Agree on norms explicitly
steps.body: In global teams, discuss in a kick-off: *'How do we like to give feedback? How do we disagree in meetings? What does silence mean?'* Writing down a team charter saves months of misunderstanding.

steps.title: Disagreeing in meetings
steps.body: Some cultures (e.g., France, Israel, Netherlands) often see open debate as healthy; others prefer to avoid open confrontation, especially with seniors. If you're from a less confrontational culture, practise phrases: *'Let me offer a different view…'*, *'I see it differently because…'*. If you're from a debate culture, invite quieter colleagues: *'Priya, what's your view?'* and use written input before meetings.

a.text: Your German manager says in front of the team, 'Your estimate is wrong. It's too optimistic.' You feel embarrassed. What do you do?

choices.label: Ask what's driving their view and share your assumptions
choices.feedback: Treat it as a debate about the estimate, not a personal attack.

choices.label: Stay silent and assume they dislike you
choices.feedback: Likely misreading a direct style.

b.text: They explain testing usually takes twice as long. You disagree on one part. How do you say it?

choices.label: 'I agree on testing; I see the API work differently because we're reusing an existing module.'
choices.feedback: Clear, specific disagreement — exactly what a direct culture expects.

choices.label: 'Maybe… perhaps… whatever you think.'
choices.feedback: Your valid point gets lost.

c.text: You avoid them for a week. What would help?

choices.label: Ask in a 1:1 how they prefer to give and receive feedback
choices.feedback: Making norms explicit clears the air.

e1.text: You agree on a revised estimate together. Your manager respects your clear reasoning.

e2.text: The estimate stays unrealistic. Practise stating disagreement directly with reasons.

quiz.why: The answer is "A bit, maybe, kind of". Reason: They soften criticism. The other choices, such as "Absolutely, totally" and "Excellent, perfect", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A blunt comment from a Dutch colleague is most likely…
quiz.why: The answer is "Routine direct feedback". Reason: Recalibrate across cultures. The other choices, such as "A personal attack" and "A joke", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: The universal safe feedback style is…
options: Specific about the problem, kind about the person, clear about the request
quiz.why: The answer is "Specific about the problem, kind about the person, clear about the request". Reason: Works in most cultures. The other choices, such as "Silent" and "Harsh always", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A team charter on communication norms helps…
quiz.why: The answer is "Prevent misunderstandings". Reason: Explicit norms reduce friction. The other choices, such as "Avoid feedback" and "Replace work", do not fit the question.

scenes.text: Deepa in Bengaluru joins an 11 pm IST call every day with San Francisco. She's exhausted; the US team never notices.
She proposes rotating slots and moving updates to written async summaries.
The team agrees: two live calls a week at alternating times, a shared doc for daily updates, and decisions posted in the channel.
Deepa sleeps again, and the US team says decisions are clearer.

steps.title: Find and protect the overlap
steps.body: India (UTC+5:30) overlaps easily with Europe's morning, while the US West Coast has very little overlap with Indian working hours. Map everyone's working hours, find the overlap, and **reserve it for things that truly need live discussion** — decisions, conflicts, brainstorming. Everything else can be **asynchronous** (written).

steps.title: Async-first habits
steps.body:
- Daily written updates in a shared doc or channel.
- Recorded demos instead of live ones.
- Decisions documented with context and owners.
- Clear 'reply-by' times with time zones (*'by 10 am PT / 10:30 pm IST'*).
- Handover notes at the end of each day ('follow-the-sun' teams).

steps.title: Share the pain fairly
steps.body: If late calls are unavoidable, **rotate** times so one region doesn't always sacrifice. Leaders should notice who is always on at midnight. Raising this is legitimate: *'Could we rotate the weekly sync? India has had the late slot for six months.'*

steps.title: Holidays and calendars
steps.body: Check holidays in all regions (Thanksgiving in the US, Golden Week in Japan, Ramadan schedules in the Gulf, Diwali/Pongal/Onam in India). Note that many Gulf countries have a Friday–Saturday or Saturday–Sunday weekend depending on the country — check rather than assume. Put a shared holiday calendar in your team space.

corporate-fresher.title: Fresher survival kit
corporate-fresher.description: Your first job, decoded: the first 90 days, emails, meetings, Teams/Slack etiquette, asking for help and how appraisals really work — with Indian and global office stories.

courses.title: Your first 90 days at work
courses.summary: A practical playbook for the jump from campus to company: onboarding, reading your team, your first deliverable and recovering from early mistakes.
outcomes: Learners can run a structured first week and build a 30-60-90 day plan
Learners can map who matters in their team and what each person needs
Learners can deliver a first task with clear check-ins
Learners can own and recover from a mistake professionally

lessons.title: Day 1 to week 1: onboarding without panic

scenes.text: Ananya, a B.Tech graduate from Nagpur, joins a Pune IT services company. Her laptop arrives at 3 pm, her ID card says 'pending', and nobody has told her which project she is on.
She sits quietly for two days, afraid to 'disturb' anyone. Her batch-mate Rohit, on the other hand, asks HR for the onboarding checklist and messages his manager to set up a 15-minute intro call.
By Friday Rohit has access to the code repository, has met four teammates and has a written list of what is expected of him. Ananya has watched compliance videos and feels invisible.
Same company, same week. The difference was not talent — it was knowing that onboarding is something you actively drive, not something that happens to you.

steps.title: Onboarding is your first project
steps.body:
Most companies have an onboarding process, but it is rarely perfect. Laptops arrive late, access requests get stuck, managers are busy. Treat your first week as your first project with a simple goal: **by Friday, know what you will be working on, who you work with, and how to get access to the tools.**

In the first week, aim to:
- Complete mandatory HR and compliance training (code of conduct, information security, POSH awareness) — these are often tracked and overdue items get flagged.
- Get all access: email, chat (Teams/Slack), VPN, ticketing tool, code or document repositories, timesheet tool.
- Have a 1:1 with your manager and at least an introductory chat with your buddy or a senior teammate.
- Write down the names and roles of everyone you meet the same day.

steps.title: Worked example: the first message to your manager
steps.body:
If your manager has not reached out by Day 2, it is completely normal and professional to message first:

*'Hi Priya, I've joined the team today and completed my HR induction. Could we set up a 15–20 minute call this week so I can understand the project, your expectations for my first month, and who I should connect with? I'm free any time after 2 pm. Thanks! — Ananya'*

Why it works: it is short, it shows initiative, it proposes a time and it asks three specific things. It does not complain ('nobody told me anything') even if that is true.

steps.title: Keep a 'first-week notebook'
steps.body:
Create one document (OneNote, Notion, a plain notebook) with four headings:
- **People** — name, role, what they own, how they prefer to be contacted.
- **Tools & access** — what you have, what is pending, the ticket number for each request.
- **Jargon** — every acronym you hear (SOW, SLA, UAT, P1, RCA, BAU). Look it up or ask once, then note it.
- **Questions** — collect non-urgent questions and ask them together in your 1:1 instead of interrupting someone ten times.

In three months this notebook becomes your personal wiki, and it is gold when the next fresher joins.

steps.title: Common mistakes in week one
steps.body:
- **Sitting silently and waiting.** Silence reads as 'not interested', even when you are just shy.
- **Over-promising.** Saying 'I'll finish this by tomorrow' before you understand the task.
- **Ignoring security rules** — copying company code to a personal drive, sharing screenshots of client data in personal WhatsApp groups, or using unapproved AI tools on confidential data. These can lead to serious disciplinary action even for freshers.
- **Comparing packages and projects loudly with batch-mates.** It creates bad feelings and the information is often wrong anyway.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Before your next working day, write the three questions you would ask your manager in your first 1:1. Good first-week questions:
- What does success look like for me in the first 30 and 90 days?
- How do you prefer updates — chat, email, or in our 1:1?
- Who are the two or three people I should learn from first?

lessons.title: Reading your team: people, power and needs

scenes.text: Karthik joins a Bengaluru product startup. On paper, his manager is Neha, the engineering manager. He sends all his questions to her.
In meetings, though, everyone looks at Suresh, a quiet senior engineer, before any technical decision is made. Karthik's pull requests keep waiting for Suresh's review.
His buddy explains over chai: 'Neha decides priorities and your rating. Suresh decides what good code looks like. Fatima in QA decides whether your feature ships. You need all three.'
Karthik draws a simple map of his team: who decides what, who knows what, and who needs what from him. His reviews start moving faster within two weeks.

steps.title: The org chart is only half the story
steps.body:
Every team has a **formal structure** (who reports to whom) and an **informal structure** (who people actually trust, ask and follow). As a fresher you need to understand both.

For each important person, find out:
- **What do they own?** Priorities, technical decisions, quality, the client relationship, budgets.
- **What do they need from you?** Updates, clean work, timely responses, no surprises.
- **How do they like to communicate?** Some want a quick chat message, some want a short email, some want you to just walk over (or call).

This is not 'politics' in a bad sense. It is simply understanding how work flows.

steps.title: Worked example: a simple team map
steps.body:
Karthik's map looked like this:
- **Neha (Engineering Manager)** — owns priorities, my rating, leave approval. Needs: weekly status, early warning on delays. Prefers: Slack + Friday 1:1.
- **Suresh (Senior Engineer)** — owns code quality and architecture. Needs: small pull requests with clear descriptions. Prefers: comments on the PR, not DMs at night.
- **Fatima (QA Lead)** — owns release sign-off. Needs: test notes and how to reproduce. Prefers: a ticket comment.
- **Arjun (Product Manager)** — owns *what* we build and why. Needs: honest effort estimates.

One page, ten minutes to write, and it changed how he worked.

steps.title: Indian and global team patterns
steps.body:
In many Indian service companies you will meet layers: associate → senior associate → tech lead → project manager → delivery manager, plus a client-side manager abroad. In product companies and global teams the structure is often flatter, but informal influence is just as real.

If your team works with a client in the US or UK, notice who talks to the client. That person often shapes how your work is perceived. A short, clear update you write may be forwarded directly to the client — so write every update as if it could be.

steps.title: Build relationships before you need them
steps.body:
- Have a 15-minute virtual coffee with each teammate in your first month. Ask: *'What do you work on? What do you wish new joiners knew?'*
- Thank people specifically: *'Thanks for the review, Suresh — the comment on error handling taught me something.'*
- Help where you can: freshers are often great at documentation, testing, scripts and fresh questions.

Trust is built in small deposits long before you need a big withdrawal (like a favour on a tight deadline).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Draw your own team map with at least four people. For each: what they own, what they need from you, and how they prefer to communicate. If you do not know an answer, that is your next question for your buddy.

activity.prompt: Match each person to what they usually own in a software team.
pairs: Priorities, performance ratings and team health
Acceptance of deliverables for the client
Policies, leave, grievances and appraisal process

quiz.q: What is the 'informal structure' of a team?
options: Who people actually trust, consult and follow, beyond the org chart
quiz.why: Informal influence often decides how quickly work moves; understanding it is a core workplace skill.

quiz.q: Your reviews keep getting stuck with a senior engineer. What helps most?
options: Send smaller pull requests with clear descriptions and learn their standards
Message them repeatedly late at night
quiz.why: Making the reviewer's job easy and meeting their quality bar is the fastest route.

quiz.q: Why write every client-facing update carefully?
options: Because grammar is graded in appraisals
Because your update may be forwarded directly to the client
quiz.why: The answer is "Because your update may be forwarded directly to the client". Reason: In service and global teams, updates often travel further than you expect. The other choices, such as "Because long emails look impressive" and "Because grammar is graded in appraisals", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Which is a healthy way to build relationships in month one?
options: Gossiping about the manager to bond
Short virtual coffees asking what people work on and what new joiners should know
Avoiding everyone until you have proven yourself
quiz.why: The answer is "Short virtual coffees asking what people work on and what new joiners should know". Reason: Curious, respectful conversations build trust and teach you how the team works. The other choices, such as "Only talking to your batch-mates" and "Gossiping about the manager to bond", do not fit the question.

lessons.title: Your first deliverable and the 30-60-90 plan

scenes.text: Meera, a fresher analyst at a Gurugram consulting firm, is asked by her manager Vikram to 'pull together the sales numbers for the west region'.
She works till midnight for three days, builds a 40-slide deck with every chart she can imagine, and proudly presents it on Thursday.
Vikram sighs: 'I needed one table of quarterly sales by state for a client call on Tuesday. I already had the call without it.'
Next time, Meera confirms the output, the deadline and the purpose in one message before starting — and shares a rough draft on Day 1. Her second task lands perfectly.

steps.title: Clarify before you start: the 4 questions
steps.body:
Most fresher 'failures' are actually **misunderstood tasks**. Before you start any task, confirm:
- **What** exactly is the output? (A table? A slide? Working code? A one-line answer?)
- **Why** is it needed? (Who will use it and for what decision?)
- **When** is it needed, and is there an earlier checkpoint?
- **How good** does it need to be? (Quick rough estimate vs polished client deliverable.)

Then **play it back** in writing: *'Just to confirm: you need a table of Q1–Q4 sales by state for the west region, for Tuesday's client call, rough is fine. I'll share a draft by Monday noon.'*

steps.title: Worked example: the early draft rule
steps.body:
Show a rough version when you are about **20–30% done**, not 100%.

Meera's second task: 'Compare our pricing with three competitors.' On Day 1 she sent a skeleton: a table with the three competitor names, the columns she planned (plan name, price per user, features) and two cells filled in. Vikram replied in five minutes: 'Add a column for annual discount; skip the features.'

That five-minute correction saved her a day of work. Early drafts feel uncomfortable because they are incomplete — that is exactly why they are valuable.

steps.title: Build a 30-60-90 day plan
steps.body:
A 30-60-90 plan is a one-page document you agree with your manager:
- **First 30 days — Learn:** understand the product/domain, tools, team and processes; complete training; deliver a small task.
- **Days 31–60 — Contribute:** own small features or analyses end-to-end; start reviewing others' simple work; fix your knowledge gaps.
- **Days 61–90 — Own:** be the go-to person for one small area; suggest one improvement; work with less supervision.

Share it in your 1:1 and ask, *'Does this match what you expect from me?'* This turns vague expectations into a shared written agreement, which protects you at appraisal time.

steps.title: Hidden traps
steps.body:
- **Gold-plating:** spending days perfecting what was needed roughly.
- **Silent struggle:** being stuck for two days without telling anyone. A useful rule for freshers: if stuck for more than 30–60 minutes on the same problem after genuinely trying, ask.
- **Status surprises:** saying 'on track' every day and 'delayed' on the deadline day. Bad news early is a gift; bad news late is a problem.
