steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Take any task you have been given recently. Write a three-line playback message: what, why, when (with an early checkpoint). Then draft your own 30-60-90 plan in nine bullet points — three for each phase.

activity.prompt: Put the steps for handling a new task in the best order.
items: Listen to the request and note it down
Ask what, why, when and how good
Play back your understanding in writing
Share a rough draft at about 25% done
Incorporate feedback and finish
Deliver with a short summary and next steps

quiz.q: Meera built 40 slides when her manager needed one table. What was the root cause?
options: She did not clarify the output, purpose and deadline before starting
quiz.why: Unclear expectations, not ability, caused the waste. Clarifying and playing back prevents it.

quiz.q: When should you show a first draft?
options: At roughly 20–30% done, as a skeleton
Never — just deliver the final version
quiz.why: The answer is "At roughly 20–30% done, as a skeleton". Reason: Early drafts catch misunderstandings cheaply. The other choices, such as "After the deadline" and "Never — just deliver the final version", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of the 'Learn' phase in a 30-60-90 plan?
options: Understanding domain, tools, team and processes while delivering small tasks
Delivering the biggest project of the year
quiz.why: The answer is "Understanding domain, tools, team and processes while delivering small tasks". Reason: The first 30 days are mostly about orientation and small wins. The other choices, such as "Asking for a promotion" and "Changing team processes", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: You have been stuck on a bug for two days. What should you have done?
options: Asked for help after a reasonable time of genuine effort, explaining what you tried
Kept quiet to avoid looking weak
quiz.why: Silent struggle wastes time; a focused help request with what you tried is respected.

quiz.q: Why get your 30-60-90 plan agreed in writing?
options: To avoid ever talking to your manager
It creates shared expectations you can refer to at appraisal time
quiz.why: The answer is "It creates shared expectations you can refer to at appraisal time". Reason: Written, agreed expectations reduce surprises in reviews. The other choices, such as "HR requires 90 pages" and "To avoid ever talking to your manager", do not fit the question.

lessons.title: When you mess up: owning and recovering

scenes.text: Sam Fernandes, three weeks into a Goa-based fintech, runs a clean-up script on what he thinks is his local database. It is the shared staging database. The QA team's test data disappears.
His first instinct is to hide it and hope someone else gets blamed. His hands are shaking.
Instead, within ten minutes he messages his lead: 'I made a mistake — I ran the clean-up script against staging. QA test data is gone. I've stopped the script. How can I help restore it?'
The lead restores a backup in an hour. In the review, the team adds a confirmation prompt to the script. Sam's honesty is mentioned positively in his first feedback.

steps.title: Mistakes are expected; hiding them is not
steps.body:
Every professional makes mistakes. Managers mostly judge you on **what happens next**. A simple recovery formula:
- **1. Stop the bleeding** — if something is still breaking, stop it (stop the script, pause the email campaign).
- **2. Tell the right person quickly** — usually your lead or manager, within minutes for anything affecting others.
- **3. State facts, not excuses** — what happened, impact, what you've done so far.
- **4. Offer help with the fix.**
- **5. Learn and prevent** — suggest a process fix (a checklist, a confirmation prompt, a review step).

steps.title: Worked example: a good 'I made a mistake' message
steps.body:
*'Hi Rakesh — I made an error. I sent the draft invoice to the client instead of the final one at 3:10 pm. The difference is the tax line (₹18,400). I haven't contacted the client yet. Could you advise whether you or I should send a correction? I've prepared the correct version and a short note.'*

It has: what happened, when, the impact, what has not yet been done, a question about next steps, and a prepared solution.

steps.title: Blameless reviews (RCAs)
steps.body:
Many tech companies do **blameless post-mortems** or **RCAs (root cause analyses)** after incidents. The idea: people rarely fail on purpose; systems allow mistakes. A good RCA asks *'Why was it possible to run that script on staging?'* rather than *'Who is the idiot?'*

A common technique is the **5 Whys**: keep asking 'why' until you reach a process cause you can fix. As a fresher, contributing honestly to an RCA is a chance to show maturity.

steps.title: What makes it worse
steps.body:
- Hiding or deleting evidence (logs, emails).
- Blaming tools, teammates or 'unclear instructions' as your first sentence.
- Over-apologising for days — one sincere apology plus action is enough.
- Repeating the same mistake: that is when trust really drops. Write down your lesson.

steps.title: Look after yourself too
steps.body: The first big mistake can feel crushing, especially if you are the first in your family in a corporate job and carry everyone's expectations. Talk to a trusted senior or friend, sleep, and remember: one mistake handled well usually *increases* trust. If you feel persistently anxious or low, talk to someone — your company may offer a confidential Employee Assistance Programme (EAP), and India's Tele-MANAS helpline is 14416.

a.text: You realise you emailed a client the wrong pricing file 20 minutes ago. Your manager is in a meeting. What do you do first?

choices.label: Message your manager immediately with the facts and ask how to correct it
choices.feedback: Fast, factual escalation is exactly right.

choices.label: Wait and hope the client doesn't open it
choices.feedback: Hoping rarely works; the client may act on wrong prices.

choices.label: Email the client yourself saying 'please ignore' without telling anyone
choices.feedback: Well-meant, but the client relationship belongs to your manager; uncoordinated messages can confuse.

b.text: Your manager replies: 'Thanks for flagging. Send a short correction from your account, cc me.' What do you write?

choices.label: A brief note: 'Please disregard the earlier file; the correct version is attached. Apologies for the confusion.'
choices.feedback: Short, clear and professional.

choices.label: A long emotional apology explaining your whole week
choices.feedback: Too much. Clients want clarity, not drama.

c.text: Next morning the client calls your manager asking why prices went up 15%. Your manager asks you if you know anything.

choices.label: Admit it honestly now and offer to help fix it
choices.feedback: Late, but honesty now still limits damage.

choices.label: Say you have no idea
choices.feedback: Lying turns a small mistake into a trust problem.

d.text: The client replies to everyone asking which prices are final; your manager is surprised. What now?

choices.label: Explain to your manager immediately and apologise for not looping them in
choices.feedback: Good recovery — always loop in the owner.

e1.text: Mistake fixed in under an hour. Your manager trusts you more because you flagged it fast.

e2.text: It's fixed, but next time keep corrections short and factual.

e3.text: The damage is contained. Lesson: escalate early and let the relationship owner decide the client message.

e4.text: Email logs show it was you. Now the issue is honesty, not a file — a much harder thing to repair. Always own it.

quiz.q: What is the first step if your mistake is still causing damage?
options: Stop the damage (e.g., stop the script)
quiz.why: The answer is "Stop the damage (e.g., stop the script)". Reason: Containment comes first; explanations come after. The other choices, such as "Write the RCA" and "Update your resume", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: What is a 'blameless post-mortem'?
options: A review focusing on how the system allowed the mistake, to prevent repeats
A review that ignores the problem
A meeting to decide who gets fired
quiz.why: The answer is "A review focusing on how the system allowed the mistake, to prevent repeats". Reason: Blameless reviews look for process fixes and encourage honest reporting. The other choices, such as "A review that ignores the problem" and "A party after a release", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Which opening line is best when reporting your mistake?
options: 'I made an error: here is what happened and the impact…'
quiz.why: The answer is "'I made an error: here is what happened and the impact…'". Reason: Owning it and stating facts builds trust. The other choices, such as "'This tool is terrible…'" and "'Nobody told me…'", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: The '5 Whys' technique is used to…
options: Find a root cause by repeatedly asking why
quiz.why: The answer is "Find a root cause by repeatedly asking why". Reason: Asking 'why' repeatedly moves from the symptom to a fixable process cause. The other choices, such as "Rank employees" and "Count mistakes", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Onboarding is best treated as…
options: Your first project that you actively drive
questions.why: The answer is "Your first project that you actively drive". Reason: Driving your own onboarding gets you productive faster. The other choices, such as "Optional" and "A holiday week", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which is a good first-1:1 question?
options: Who is the laziest person here?
What does success look like for me in 30 and 90 days?
questions.why: The answer is "What does success look like for me in 30 and 90 days?". Reason: It sets clear expectations early. The other choices, such as "Who is the laziest person here?" and "When is my promotion?", do not fit the question.

questions.q: A 'first-week notebook' should include…
questions.why: The answer is "People, tools/access, jargon and questions". Reason: These four headings become your personal team wiki. The other choices, such as "Salaries of colleagues" and "Only lunch menus", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Before starting a task, you should confirm…
options: Who else got a similar task
What, why, when and how good
questions.why: The answer is "What, why, when and how good". Reason: These four questions prevent most misunderstandings. The other choices, such as "Only the deadline" and "Who else got a similar task", do not fit the question.

questions.q: 'Playing back' a task means…
options: Asking someone else to do it
Repeating your understanding in writing so the requester can correct it
questions.why: The answer is "Repeating your understanding in writing so the requester can correct it". Reason: A written playback catches misunderstandings early. The other choices, such as "Asking someone else to do it" and "Recording the meeting secretly", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Who typically owns release sign-off in a software team?
options: The QA lead or release owner
questions.why: The answer is "The QA lead or release owner". Reason: Quality/release owners decide whether work ships. The other choices, such as "The HR partner" and "The newest fresher", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Gold-plating means…
options: Polishing work far beyond what was needed
questions.why: The answer is "Polishing work far beyond what was needed". Reason: Over-polishing wastes time when 'rough' was requested. The other choices, such as "Asking for feedback early" and "Using gold-coloured slides", do not fit the question.

questions.q: You reported 'on track' daily, then 'delayed' on the deadline day. The core problem is…
options: Late bad news — risks should be flagged early
questions.why: The answer is "Late bad news — risks should be flagged early". Reason: Early warnings let managers re-plan; surprises damage trust. The other choices, such as "Your typing speed" and "The tool", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which is the BEST mistake-reporting message?
options: 'I sent the draft invoice instead of the final at 3:10 pm; the tax line differs by ₹18,400; I have the correct version ready — should you or I send the correction?'
questions.why: The answer is "'I sent the draft invoice instead of the final at 3:10 pm; the tax line differs by ₹18,400; I have the correct version ready — should you or I send the correction?'". Reason: It states facts, impact, status and a prepared fix.

questions.q: Why does a 30-60-90 plan protect you at appraisal time?
options: It records agreed expectations you can show you met
questions.why: The answer is "It records agreed expectations you can show you met". Reason: Agreed written goals make your review fairer and evidence-based. The other choices, such as "It is legally binding" and "It replaces the appraisal", do not fit the question.

questions.q: In an RCA, the best question after 'the script deleted staging data' is…
options: Why was it possible to run it on staging without a safeguard?
questions.why: The answer is "Why was it possible to run it on staging without a safeguard?". Reason: Blameless RCAs target fixable system causes. The other choices, such as "Who ran it?" and "Why are freshers careless?", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Your manager is unavailable, and your mistake affects a client right now. The best approach is usually…
options: Contact the manager or their designated backup quickly with facts and let the relationship owner decide the client message
questions.why: The answer is "Contact the manager or their designated backup quickly with facts and let the relationship owner decide the client message". Reason: Escalate fast through the right channel; coordinate client communication.

questions.q: Which combination builds trust fastest in the first 90 days?
options: Early drafts, clear updates, early risk flags and honest ownership of mistakes
questions.why: The answer is "Early drafts, clear updates, early risk flags and honest ownership of mistakes". Reason: Visible reliability and honesty matter more than heroics. The other choices, such as "Avoiding mistakes by avoiding work" and "Agreeing to every request", do not fit the question.

courses.title: Emails, meetings and Teams/Slack etiquette
courses.summary: How to write emails people read, behave well in meetings, use chat tools without annoying anyone, and ask for help the smart way.
outcomes: Learners can write clear professional emails with good subject lines and asks
Learners can prepare for, contribute to and document meetings
Learners can use Teams/Slack with good etiquette across time zones
Learners can ask for help in a way that gets quick, good answers

scenes.text: Divya, a fresher in a Chennai bank's operations team, emails five people with the subject 'Query'. The email is three paragraphs long and the actual question is in the last line.
Two days pass. No reply. She feels ignored.
Her senior, Lakshmi, rewrites it: subject 'Action needed by Thu: approval for KYC exception (Account 4471)', the ask in the first line, one person in 'To', others in 'Cc'.
Reply in 40 minutes. Divya learns that busy people scan emails in seconds — the structure does the work.

steps.title: Subject line = the headline
steps.body:
A good subject line tells the reader **what it is about and what you need**, so they can prioritise without opening it.
- Weak: *'Query'*, *'Hi'*, *'Urgent!!!'*
- Strong: *'Approval needed by Thu: KYC exception for account 4471'*
- Strong: *'FYI: Release 2.3 moved to 14 March'*
- Strong: *'Decision needed: vendor A vs B for printing (2-min read)'*

Prefixes like **Action needed**, **FYI**, **Decision needed** are widely understood.

steps.title: Bottom line up front (BLUF)
steps.body:
Put your **ask or conclusion in the first one or two lines**, then context. Structure:
- **Line 1:** what you need and by when.
- **Context:** 2–4 short lines or bullets.
- **Details/attachments:** for those who want them.
- **Close:** a clear next step.

Use short paragraphs and bullets. If an email needs scrolling on a phone, consider a call or a document instead.

steps.title: Worked example: before and after
steps.body:
**Before:** *'Dear Sir, Greetings of the day. Hope you are doing well. As discussed I was checking the account and there seems to be some issue with the KYC because the documents are old and the customer says… Kindly do the needful.'*

**After:** *'Hi Rajesh, Could you approve a 15-day KYC exception for account 4471 by Thursday? Context: the customer's address proof expired last month; renewed proof is submitted to the passport office (receipt attached). Without approval, the account freezes on Friday. Thanks, Divya'*

The second version is shorter, clearer and answerable in one click.

steps.title: To, Cc, Bcc and Reply-all
steps.body:
- **To:** people who must act or reply.
- **Cc:** people who need to know but not act. Don't Cc a manager just to 'pressure' someone — it is usually noticed.
- **Bcc:** rarely; e.g., large external lists to protect addresses. Avoid secretly Bcc'ing people on sensitive discussions.
- **Reply-all:** only when everyone on the thread needs your reply. 'Thanks!' to 200 people is not needed.
- Before sending: check attachments, names, tone, and that client data goes only to authorised people.

steps.title: Phrases to retire
steps.body:
Some phrases common in Indian offices can confuse global readers or sound dated:
- *'Kindly do the needful'* → say exactly what you need.
- *'Please revert'* → *'Please reply'* (globally, 'revert' means 'go back to a previous state').
- *'PFA'* → *'Attached is…'*
- *'Greetings of the day'* → a simple *'Hi Rajesh,'* is fine in most modern workplaces.

None of these are 'wrong', but clarity wins, especially with international colleagues.

activity.prompt: Sort each subject line: does it help the reader prioritise?

items.text: Action needed by Fri: sign-off on Q3 test plan
Query
FYI: Office closed on 2 Oct (Gandhi Jayanti)
URGENT!!!!
Decision needed: choose venue A or B for offsite
Hi
Re: Re: Re: Fwd: update

quiz.q: What does BLUF mean in an email?
options: Bottom Line Up Front — the ask or conclusion first
quiz.why: The answer is "Bottom Line Up Front — the ask or conclusion first". Reason: Leading with the ask helps busy readers act quickly. The other choices, such as "Blind Lists Under Footer" and "Bold Letters Use Frequently", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Who belongs in the 'To' field?
options: People who must act or reply
quiz.why: The answer is "People who must act or reply". Reason: 'To' signals responsibility to act; 'Cc' is for information. The other choices, such as "Nobody; use Bcc" and "Only your manager", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: For global colleagues, 'please revert' is better written as…
quiz.why: The answer is "Please reply". Reason: Outside South Asia 'revert' usually means 'go back', so 'reply' is clearer. The other choices, such as "Please do the needful" and "PFA", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: When should you avoid email and switch to a call or document?
options: When the email needs lots of scrolling or back-and-forth
quiz.why: Complex or emotional topics are often better handled live or in a structured doc.

scenes.text: Imran joins a daily stand-up with a London client team. He keeps his camera off, mumbles 'same as yesterday', and leaves.
In a month, the client lead asks Imran's manager, 'What exactly is Imran working on?'
His manager coaches him: prepare three lines before every stand-up, speak first sometimes, and send short notes after important calls.
Six weeks later, the client lead praises 'Imran's crisp updates'. Same work — better meeting habits.

steps.title: Before: prepare in five minutes
steps.body:
- Read the agenda and any pre-read. If there is no agenda, it is fine to ask the organiser politely: *'Is there anything I should prepare?'*
- Write your **update in three lines**: done, doing next, blockers.
- Note **one question or point** you want to raise.
- Join 1–2 minutes early, test audio, and close noisy tabs and notifications.

steps.title: Worked example: a crisp stand-up update
steps.body:
*'Yesterday I finished the payment-retry API and raised the PR. Today I'm writing tests and fixing two review comments. One blocker: I need test card numbers from the payments team — Sana, could you point me to the right person after the call?'*

About 20 seconds. Specific. A clear blocker with a named ask. Compare with *'Working on the API, same as yesterday.'*

steps.title: During: contribute even as a junior
steps.body:
- Speak at least once in meetings where your work is discussed — a question counts.
- Use the raise-hand feature or chat if it's hard to get a word in.
- Keep camera on when the team norm is camera-on, especially for client calls and 1:1s (unless bandwidth or privacy prevents it — just say so).
- Don't multitask visibly; people can hear typing.
- If you don't understand something, ask: *'Sorry, could you clarify what UAT sign-off involves here?'* — usually someone else had the same question.

steps.title: After: minutes of meeting (MoM)
steps.body:
For important meetings, someone should send **minutes** within a few hours: decisions, action items (owner + date), and open questions. Freshers who volunteer to take notes become visible and learn fast.

Template:
- **Decisions:** Go-live moved to 14 March.
- **Actions:** Imran — share test report by Wed; Sana — confirm test cards by Tue.
- **Open:** Need client approval on new error messages.

steps.title: Time zones and meeting manners
steps.body: With US/UK/Australia teams, meetings often land early morning or late evening in India. Agree working-hour overlaps, use calendar time-zone features, and say early if a slot clashes with something important. Decline politely with a reason when you truly cannot add value — *'I don't think I'm needed for this one; could you share the notes?'*

activity.prompt: Complete the stand-up formula and the minutes template.
activity.text: A good stand-up covers what I ___, what I'm doing next, and any ___. Minutes list decisions, action items with an ___ and a date, and open questions.

quiz.q: A strong stand-up update includes…
options: What you finished, what's next and specific blockers
quiz.why: The answer is "What you finished, what's next and specific blockers". Reason: Short, specific updates with blockers make you visible and get help fast. The other choices, such as "Only 'same as yesterday'" and "Complaints about the client", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Minutes of meeting should contain…
options: Decisions, action items with owners and dates, and open questions
quiz.why: The answer is "Decisions, action items with owners and dates, and open questions". Reason: Minutes turn talk into accountable action. The other choices, such as "Jokes from the meeting" and "Who spoke the most", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: You don't understand a term used in a meeting. Best response?
options: Google it during the meeting while ignoring everyone
quiz.why: The answer is "Ask a short clarifying question". Reason: Clarifying questions are normal and often help others too. The other choices, such as "Leave the meeting" and "Stay silent forever", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Why volunteer to take notes as a fresher?
options: It makes you visible and helps you learn the work
quiz.why: The answer is "It makes you visible and helps you learn the work". Reason: Note-takers understand decisions deeply and are noticed. The other choices, such as "It's required by law" and "It avoids speaking", do not fit the question.

scenes.text: Pooja, a fresher in Hyderabad, sends 'hi' to her US-based tech lead, Jason, at 7 pm IST. Then she waits for him to reply before asking her question.
Jason sees 'hi' at 9 am Pacific, replies 'hi?', and goes into meetings. Pooja is asleep. A whole day is lost.
Her teammate shows her the 'no hello' habit: greeting plus full question in one message, with context and links.
Next time, Jason answers in one go, from his phone, between meetings.

steps.title: Greeting + question in one message
steps.body:
Don't send just 'hi' and wait. Write the full message at once:

*'Hi Jason — quick question on the login bug (JIRA-482): should the retry limit be 3 or 5? The spec says 3, but the old code uses 5. Not urgent; today or tomorrow is fine.'*

This respects time zones, lets the person answer asynchronously and tells them the urgency.

steps.title: Channels, threads and DMs
steps.body:
- **Use threads** to reply to a specific message, so channels stay readable.
- **Public channel over DM** for project questions — others learn from the answer, and the knowledge isn't lost. DMs are for personal or sensitive topics.
- **@mentions:** mention a person only when you need them; avoid @channel/@everyone unless it truly concerns everyone now.
- **Status:** keep your status accurate (in a meeting, on leave, focusing). Set an out-of-office when you are away.

steps.title: After-hours and tone
steps.body:
- Messages sent late at night can feel like pressure. Many tools let you **schedule send** for the recipient's working hours.
- Text loses tone. 'Ok.' can sound cold; 'Why did you do this?' can sound like an attack. Prefer *'Could you help me understand the reason for this change?'*
- Avoid all-caps, too many exclamation marks, and sarcasm in writing.
- Never criticise colleagues in chat — screenshots travel, and company chats are company records.

steps.title: Emojis and reactions
steps.body: Emoji reactions (👍 ✅ 👀) are a great way to acknowledge without cluttering a thread — e.g., 👀 = 'I'm looking at it', ✅ = 'done'. Follow team norms: some teams are casual, client channels usually more formal. When unsure, mirror how your seniors write.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Rewrite this message: *'hi'*, *'r u there'*, *'need help'*. Make it one complete message with a greeting, the question, the context (a link or ticket number) and the urgency.

statements.s: Sending just 'hi' and waiting for a reply is efficient across time zones.
statements.why: It forces two round-trips; send the full question at once.

statements.s: Project questions are often better in a public team channel than in a DM.
statements.why: Others benefit and knowledge stays searchable.

statements.s: Using @everyone for a small question is good practice.
statements.why: It interrupts many people; use it only for truly urgent, all-hands information.

statements.s: Scheduling a message for the recipient's working hours is considerate.
statements.why: It avoids after-hours pressure.

statements.s: Company chat messages are private and can never be reviewed.
statements.why: Workplace chats are company records and can be reviewed under policy.

quiz.q: What is the 'no hello' habit?
options: Putting the greeting and the full question in one message
quiz.why: The answer is "Putting the greeting and the full question in one message". Reason: It allows asynchronous answers and saves time. The other choices, such as "Never greeting anyone" and "Only using emojis", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Why use threads?
options: To keep replies attached to the original topic so channels stay readable
quiz.why: The answer is "To keep replies attached to the original topic so channels stay readable". Reason: Threads keep conversations organised. The other choices, such as "Because DMs are banned" and "To hide messages", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A colleague's change broke your code. Best chat message?
options: 'Could you help me understand the reason for this change? It's affecting the login flow.'
Say nothing and revert it secretly
Post a screenshot in the team channel mocking it
quiz.why: The answer is "'Could you help me understand the reason for this change? It's affecting the login flow.'". Reason: Neutral, curious wording keeps it professional. The other choices, such as "'WHY DID YOU DO THIS?'" and "Say nothing and revert it secretly", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: What does a 👀 reaction commonly signal?
quiz.why: The answer is "I'm looking at it". Reason: Many teams use 👀 as 'seen, looking into it'. The other choices, such as "I'm angry" and "Nothing at all", do not fit the question.

lessons.title: Asking for help the smart way

scenes.text: Nikhil messages a senior: 'My code is not working. Please help.' The senior asks five follow-up questions over an hour.
Aisha, stuck on the same kind of issue, writes: what she's trying to do, the exact error, what she already tried, and a link to the branch.
The senior spots Aisha's problem in two minutes. 'Great question,' he replies.
Aisha's reputation grows as 'someone who thinks before asking'. Asking well is a skill, not a weakness.

steps.title: The 4-part help request
steps.body:
- **Goal:** what you are trying to achieve.
- **Problem:** what's happening instead (exact error message, screenshot, data).
- **Tried:** what you already tried and what you found.
- **Ask:** the specific help you want (a pointer, a 10-minute call, a review).

This shows effort, saves the helper's time, and often you solve the problem yourself while writing it (sometimes called 'rubber-duck debugging').

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: *'Hi Rahul — I'm trying to generate the monthly GST report from the new dashboard (goal). The export fails with 'Error 403: insufficient permissions' (problem). I checked my role — it says Analyst — and tried a different browser (tried). Do I need a different role, or is there a request form? A pointer is enough (ask). Thanks!'*

steps.title: When to ask
steps.body:
A balanced rule: try genuinely for a reasonable time (often 30–60 minutes for a technical block; less if a deadline or client is affected), then ask. Ask sooner if:
- you lack access or information only someone else has,
- the issue blocks others,
- you're unsure about something risky (production systems, money, legal or client data).

Never 'try things' on production systems or customer data to avoid asking.

steps.title: Getting past hesitation
steps.body: Many Indian freshers hesitate to ask seniors because of hierarchy or fear of looking weak. In most good teams, **not asking** is seen as the bigger problem. Respect seniors' time by asking well, closing the loop (*'That worked, thank you!'*) and documenting the answer for the next person. Thanking publicly in the team channel is a nice touch.

activity.prompt: Arrange the parts of a strong help request in a sensible order.
items: Greet and state your goal
Describe the exact problem or error
Explain what you already tried
Make a specific ask
Close the loop and thank them once solved

quiz.q: Which help request is strongest?
options: Goal, exact error, what you tried, and a specific ask
Asking five people the same question privately
quiz.why: The answer is "Goal, exact error, what you tried, and a specific ask". Reason: Structured requests are fast to answer and show effort. The other choices, such as "'Call me urgently' with no details" and "'Not working. Help.'", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: When should you ask sooner rather than later?
options: When you're blocked by access only someone else has, or it's risky
quiz.why: The answer is "When you're blocked by access only someone else has, or it's risky". Reason: Access, blocking others and risk all justify asking quickly. The other choices, such as "Never" and "Only on Fridays", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: What is 'closing the loop'?
options: Telling the helper it worked and thanking them
quiz.why: The answer is "Telling the helper it worked and thanking them". Reason: It respects the helper and builds goodwill. The other choices, such as "Logging off early" and "Closing the ticket without fixing", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Why might writing a clear request solve the problem itself?
options: Explaining step by step often reveals your own mistake
quiz.why: The answer is "Explaining step by step often reveals your own mistake". Reason: Articulating the problem clarifies thinking — 'rubber-duck debugging'. The other choices, such as "Magic" and "It doesn't", do not fit the question.

questions.q: The best email subject line is…
options: Action needed by Thu: approve KYC exception for account 4471
questions.why: The answer is "Action needed by Thu: approve KYC exception for account 4471". Reason: It states topic, action and deadline. The other choices, such as "Query" and "URGENT", do not fit the question.

questions.q: 'Cc' is for people who…
options: Need to know but not act
questions.why: The answer is "Need to know but not act". Reason: Cc means 'for information'. The other choices, such as "Must reply within an hour" and "Are your enemies", do not fit the question.

questions.q: In Teams/Slack, the most efficient first message is…
questions.why: The answer is "Greeting + full question + context + urgency". Reason: Supports asynchronous replies. The other choices, such as "'r u there?'" and "An all-caps 'URGENT'", do not fit the question.

questions.q: A good stand-up update is about…
questions.why: The answer is "20–30 seconds: done, next, blockers". Reason: Brief and specific respects everyone's time. The other choices, such as "Silence" and "Only blockers of others", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which is NOT a good use of @everyone?
options: Production outage affecting the whole team
questions.why: The answer is "Asking where the stapler is". Reason: Small questions don't justify interrupting everyone. The other choices, such as "Office closure announcement" and "Production outage affecting the whole team", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Minutes of meeting should be sent…
options: Within a few hours, with decisions and owned actions
questions.why: The answer is "Within a few hours, with decisions and owned actions". Reason: Fresh minutes ensure follow-through. The other choices, such as "Only verbally" and "Never", do not fit the question.

questions.q: 'Kindly do the needful' is problematic mainly because…
options: It doesn't say what you actually need
questions.why: The answer is "It doesn't say what you actually need". Reason: Clarity beats formula phrases. The other choices, such as "It is rude" and "It is too short", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Project questions are often best asked in…
options: A public team channel or thread
questions.why: The answer is "A public team channel or thread". Reason: Shared answers help everyone and stay searchable. The other choices, such as "A printed letter" and "A DM to the CEO", do not fit the question.

questions.q: A 4-part help request contains…
questions.why: The answer is "Goal, problem, tried, ask". Reason: This structure gets fast, accurate help. The other choices, such as "Greeting, joke, emoji, sign-off" and "Only a screenshot", do not fit the question.

questions.q: You must email 300 external partners. To protect their addresses you'd use…
questions.why: The answer is "Bcc". Reason: Bcc hides addresses in large external mailings. The other choices, such as "Reply-all" and "To", do not fit the question.

questions.q: A text message 'Why did you change this?' may be read as…
options: An accusation; reword with curiosity and context
questions.why: The answer is "An accusation; reword with curiosity and context". Reason: Text loses tone; soften with context and curiosity. The other choices, such as "Neutral always" and "A compliment", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which statement about workplace chat is accurate?
options: It is deleted every night by law
It's private property of the employee
It's a company record that may be reviewed under policy
questions.why: The answer is "It's a company record that may be reviewed under policy". Reason: Treat workplace chats as official records. The other choices, such as "It is deleted every night by law" and "It's private property of the employee", do not fit the question.

questions.q: You're unsure whether a fix is safe to run on production. Best action?
options: Ask a batch-mate to run it
Ask before acting, explaining risk and your plan
questions.why: The answer is "Ask before acting, explaining risk and your plan". Reason: Risky actions on production/customer data require asking first. The other choices, such as "Run it at midnight" and "Ask a batch-mate to run it", do not fit the question.

courses.title: Appraisals, feedback and your first payslip
courses.summary: How performance cycles work, how to write a self-assessment, how to take feedback, and how to read your offer letter, CTC and payslip in India.
outcomes: Learners can explain how a typical appraisal cycle and rating work
Learners can write an evidence-based self-assessment
Learners can receive and act on feedback, including tough feedback
Learners can read CTC, in-hand pay, PF and payslip components

scenes.text: Rahul worked late all year at a Noida IT firm. In April, he receives 'Meets Expectations' and a 6% hike. His friend in the same team gets 'Exceeds' and 12%.
Rahul is furious: 'I worked harder!' His manager explains that his goals were never updated after he moved projects, and he never shared his wins.
Rahul learns the cycle: goals are set, mid-year check-ins happen, managers rate, and ratings are calibrated across teams.
This year he keeps a 'wins log' and updates goals within a week of any project change.

steps.title: The typical cycle
steps.body:
Details differ, but most companies follow something like:
- **Goal setting** (start of year): what you'll deliver and how you'll be measured.
- **Check-ins** (mid-year and/or quarterly): progress, feedback, adjustments.
- **Self-assessment:** you describe your results and evidence.
- **Manager assessment & rating:** e.g., a 3- or 5-point scale.
- **Calibration:** managers compare ratings across teams so standards are consistent; your manager may need to defend your rating with evidence.
- **Outcome:** rating, increment, bonus, sometimes promotion.

Many companies in India run the cycle around April (aligned with the financial year, April–March), but others use January or other cycles.

steps.title: Ratings and distributions
steps.body:
Some companies use a **forced or guided distribution** (for example, only a limited share of people can get the top rating). Others have moved away from it. If your company uses one, a good rating depends partly on how your contribution compares with peers — which is why **visible, documented impact** matters.

Ask HR or your manager: *What is our rating scale? Is there a guided distribution? When is calibration?*

steps.title: What managers actually evaluate
steps.body:
Usually two things:
- **What** you delivered (results against goals: features shipped, tickets resolved, accuracy, client feedback).
- **How** you delivered (collaboration, ownership, learning, values).

Hours worked are rarely a direct metric. Working late on the wrong things doesn't raise your rating; delivering important things reliably does.

steps.title: Keep a wins log
steps.body:
Every Friday, take five minutes to note:
- What I delivered (with numbers: '*reduced report time from 3 hours to 20 minutes*').
- Appreciation received (save the email or message link).
- Things I learned or certifications completed.
- Help I gave others.

At appraisal time you'll have a year of evidence instead of trying to remember.

steps.title: Common fresher mistakes
steps.body:
- Not updating goals after a project change.
- Assuming the manager knows everything you did.
- Discussing ratings angrily in public channels.
- Comparing increments with friends without knowing their goals, band or market adjustments.

activity.prompt: Put a typical appraisal cycle in order.

quiz.q: What is 'calibration' in appraisals?
options: Managers comparing ratings across teams for consistent standards
quiz.why: The answer is "Managers comparing ratings across teams for consistent standards". Reason: Calibration aligns ratings, so evidence of impact matters. The other choices, such as "Your salary negotiation" and "Choosing your goals", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: What did Rahul do wrong?
options: He didn't update goals after a project change or share his wins
quiz.why: The answer is "He didn't update goals after a project change or share his wins". Reason: Outdated goals and invisible wins made his impact hard to rate. The other choices, such as "He used a wins log" and "He worked too little", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Managers usually evaluate…
options: What you delivered and how you delivered it
quiz.why: The answer is "What you delivered and how you delivered it". Reason: Results plus behaviours are the common pair. The other choices, such as "Your typing speed" and "Only hours online", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A good wins-log entry is…
options: 'Automated the weekly report; time cut from 3 hours to 20 minutes'
quiz.why: The answer is "'Automated the weekly report; time cut from 3 hours to 20 minutes'". Reason: Specific, measurable impact is persuasive evidence. The other choices, such as "'Did stuff'" and "'Was nice'", do not fit the question.

scenes.text: Sneha, a support engineer in Kochi, writes her first self-assessment: 'I am hard working, sincere and a team player. I always do my best.'
Her mentor asks, 'What did you actually achieve? How would someone who doesn't know you believe it?'
She rewrites: 'Resolved 410 tickets with 96% customer satisfaction (team average 91%); wrote 12 knowledge articles that cut repeat tickets on password resets by about a third.'
Her manager copies two lines straight into the calibration sheet. Sneha learns that evidence speaks louder than adjectives.

steps.title: Use the STAR or CAR structure
steps.body:
For each major goal, describe one or two achievements with:
- **Context/Situation:** what the problem was.
- **Action:** what *you* did (use 'I' for your part, 'we' for team work — be honest).
- **Result:** measurable outcome — time saved, errors reduced, revenue, customer feedback, quality.

Tie each achievement to a goal or company priority.

steps.title: Worked example: adjectives vs evidence
steps.body:
**Weak:** *'I am a quick learner and very dedicated.'*

**Strong:** *'Goal: support the new billing module. Context: I had no prior SQL experience. Action: completed an internal SQL course in 3 weeks and built 5 validation queries. Result: QA found 40% fewer data defects in the billing release compared with the previous release.'*

The strong version proves 'quick learner' without saying it.

steps.title: Be honest about gaps
steps.body: Include one or two areas to grow, with a plan: *'I'd like to improve my estimation; I'll break tasks into sub-tasks under 1 day and compare estimates with actuals monthly.'* Managers trust self-assessments that are balanced; one that claims perfection is often discounted.

steps.title: Avoid these
steps.body:
- Copy-pasting your job description.
- Claiming team results as only yours.
- Criticising colleagues in the form.
- Writing two pages — be concise: 3–5 strong achievements beat 20 weak ones.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Pick one thing you did this month. Write it in one sentence with Context, Action and Result, including at least one number.

activity.prompt: Sort each line: evidence or adjective?

items.text: Resolved 410 tickets at 96% CSAT
I am very sincere and hard working
Wrote 12 help articles; repeat tickets dropped about a third
I am a team player
Automated invoice checks, saving ~6 hours a week
I always give 100%

quiz.q: What makes a self-assessment persuasive?
options: Specific actions and measurable results linked to goals
quiz.why: The answer is "Specific actions and measurable results linked to goals". Reason: Evidence can be used directly in calibration. The other choices, such as "Long adjectives" and "Criticising peers", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: In CAR, the 'R' stands for…
quiz.why: The answer is "Result". Reason: Context, Action, Result. The other choices, such as "Reason" and "Rating", do not fit the question. (Question: In CAR, the 'R' stands for…)

quiz.q: Why include a growth area?
quiz.why: The answer is "Balanced self-assessments are more credible". Reason: Honesty about gaps, with a plan, builds trust. The other choices, such as "It isn't needed" and "HR forces you to lie", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: How should you describe team achievements?
options: Say what the team did and what your part was
quiz.why: The answer is "Say what the team did and what your part was". Reason: Accurate attribution protects your credibility. The other choices, such as "Claim them all as yours" and "Credit only your manager", do not fit the question.

scenes.text: In his mid-year review, Arjun's manager in Mumbai says, 'Your reports have too many small errors. Clients notice.'
Arjun's face burns. He wants to argue that the deadlines were impossible.
He takes a breath and asks, 'Could you show me two examples so I understand the pattern?'
He builds a three-point checklist before sending any report. Three months later his manager says the improvement is obvious.

steps.title: Listen first, respond later
steps.body:
When you get critical feedback:
- **Pause.** Breathe. You don't have to respond immediately.
- **Thank** them — giving feedback is uncomfortable too.
- **Clarify** with examples: *'Could you share a specific instance?'*
- **Summarise:** *'So the issue is small errors in client reports, especially numbers and names.'*
- **Agree a next step** and follow up later. You can disagree, but do it calmly, with facts, after you've understood.

steps.title: Turning feedback into action
steps.body:
Arjun's checklist before sending any report:
- Numbers totalled and cross-checked with source.
- Client name, dates and currency verified.
- Read once aloud (or use read-aloud) for typos.

He then told his manager: *'I've started using this checklist; could you tell me in a month if you see a difference?'* Asking for follow-up feedback shows you took it seriously.

steps.title: Ask for feedback before appraisal time
steps.body:
Don't wait for the annual review. Ask small, specific questions regularly:
- *'What's one thing I could have done better in that client call?'*
- *'On a scale of 1–10, how ready is this document? What would make it a 9?'*

Specific questions get useful answers; 'Any feedback?' usually gets 'All good'.

steps.title: Feedback vs mistreatment
steps.body: Feedback is about your work and behaviour, given respectfully. Insults, public humiliation, comments about your caste, religion, gender, region, body or family, or threats are **not feedback**. Note dates and details and seek help from HR or another trusted senior; harassment of a sexual nature can be raised under the company's POSH policy.

a.text: Your manager says in your 1:1: 'Your presentation yesterday was hard to follow.' You feel defensive. What do you say?

choices.label: 'Thanks for telling me. Which part was hardest to follow?'
choices.feedback: Curiosity turns criticism into useful detail.

choices.label: 'Everyone else's slides were worse.'
choices.feedback: Comparison sounds defensive and ends the learning.

choices.label: Say nothing and look upset
choices.feedback: Your manager can't help if you shut down.

b.text: Manager: 'You started with methodology; the client wanted the recommendation first.' What next?

choices.label: Summarise and propose: 'Next time I'll lead with the recommendation. Could you review my next draft?'
choices.feedback: Clear action plus follow-up request.

choices.label: Argue that methodology is important
choices.feedback: It may be, but first agree on what the audience needs.

c.text: The conversation becomes awkward. Your manager says, 'Let's move on.' What can you still do?

choices.label: Later, message: 'I reacted defensively earlier — could you share more about the presentation?'
choices.feedback: Repairing quickly shows maturity.

choices.label: Avoid the topic forever
choices.feedback: The issue will likely appear in your appraisal.

e1.text: You turned feedback into a plan. Managers remember people who improve after feedback.

e2.text: The feedback stays unresolved. Try again: thank, clarify, summarise, act.

quiz.q: Best first response to critical feedback?
options: Pause, thank, and ask for specific examples
quiz.why: The answer is "Pause, thank, and ask for specific examples". Reason: Understanding comes before responding. The other choices, such as "Cry and leave" and "Argue immediately", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Which question gets more useful feedback?
options: 'What would make this document a 9 out of 10?'
quiz.why: The answer is "'What would make this document a 9 out of 10?'". Reason: Specific questions invite specific answers. The other choices, such as "'Can I go?'" and "'I did fine, right?'", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Which is NOT legitimate feedback?
options: Mocking your accent or region in front of the team
quiz.why: The answer is "Mocking your accent or region in front of the team". Reason: Humiliation and identity-based comments are mistreatment, not feedback. The other choices, such as "'Please update the client earlier'" and "'Your reports have number errors'", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: After acting on feedback, a smart move is to…
options: Ask for a follow-up check in a few weeks
quiz.why: The answer is "Ask for a follow-up check in a few weeks". Reason: Follow-up shows ownership and confirms improvement. The other choices, such as "Never mention it again" and "Ask for a hike immediately", do not fit the question.

lessons.title: Your offer letter, CTC and payslip (India)

story.title: Why is my salary less than I expected?

scenes.text: Fatima's offer letter from a Bengaluru firm says CTC ₹6,00,000. She divides by 12 and expects ₹50,000 a month.
Her first credit is much lower. She panics that there's a mistake.
Her friend in finance walks her through the payslip: employer PF, gratuity, variable pay, insurance, professional tax, income tax (TDS).
Nothing was wrong — CTC is 'cost to company', not 'cash in hand'. Next time she compares offers on take-home and benefits, not just CTC.

steps.title: CTC is not take-home
steps.body:
**CTC (Cost to Company)** is everything the employer spends on you in a year. It can include:
- **Fixed pay:** basic salary, HRA (house rent allowance), special allowance and others.
- **Employer's PF contribution.**
- **Gratuity** provision (paid only if you become eligible, usually after years of continuous service).
- **Variable pay / performance bonus** (often paid annually and depends on ratings and company results).
- **Insurance** premiums, meal cards, and other benefits.

Your **in-hand (net) monthly pay** = monthly gross pay minus deductions such as **employee PF**, **professional tax** (in states that levy it), and **income tax deducted at source (TDS)**.

steps.title: PF in one minute
steps.body: Under the EPF scheme, you and your employer each typically contribute **12% of your basic wages** (plus DA, if any). Part of the employer share goes to the pension scheme (EPS). Your **UAN (Universal Account Number)** stays the same across jobs — use it to transfer your PF when you switch rather than withdrawing it. Details and limits can change; check the EPFO portal or your HR for current rules.

steps.title: Worked example (illustrative numbers only)
steps.body:
Suppose CTC ₹6,00,000 includes ₹60,000 variable pay, ₹21,600 employer PF, ₹14,400 gratuity provision and ₹8,000 insurance.
- Fixed gross = 6,00,000 − 60,000 − 21,600 − 14,400 − 8,000 = **₹4,96,000 a year ≈ ₹41,333 a month**.
- Deductions per month: employee PF ₹1,800, professional tax ~₹200, TDS depends on your regime and declarations.
- In-hand ≈ ₹39,000 before tax.

The exact split varies by company — always ask HR for a **salary break-up** before accepting an offer.

steps.title: Documents to keep forever
steps.body:
- Offer letter, appointment letter and any revision letters.
- Payslips (at least the last few years) and **Form 16** (annual TDS certificate) for filing your income tax return.
- Relieving and experience letters from every employer (needed for background verification at the next job).
- PF passbook / UAN details.

Also choose your tax regime and submit investment declarations when HR asks — slabs and rules change in Union Budgets, so check the current ones on the Income Tax Department's site.

steps.title: Read before you sign
steps.body: Check: joining date, location and transfer clause, notice period, bond or training-cost recovery clauses, probation period, and variable-pay conditions. If a clause is unclear, ask HR in writing. *This is general education, not legal or tax advice.*

activity.prompt: An offer has CTC ₹8,40,000, which includes ₹84,000 variable pay, ₹28,800 employer PF, ₹19,200 gratuity provision and ₹12,000 insurance. What is the fixed gross pay per MONTH (before employee deductions)?

quiz.q: CTC stands for…
quiz.why: The answer is "Cost to Company". Reason: It's the total annual cost to the employer, not take-home. The other choices, such as "Current Tax Charge" and "Cash To Credit", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Why is in-hand pay lower than CTC/12?
options: CTC includes employer PF, gratuity, variable pay and benefits; plus deductions like employee PF and TDS
quiz.why: The answer is "CTC includes employer PF, gratuity, variable pay and benefits; plus deductions like employee PF and TDS". Reason: Several CTC components aren't monthly cash. The other choices, such as "Payroll error always" and "Interns pay a fee", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: What should you do with your UAN when switching jobs?
options: Use the same UAN and transfer PF
quiz.why: The answer is "Use the same UAN and transfer PF". Reason: UAN is portable; transferring preserves savings and service continuity. The other choices, such as "Ignore it" and "Withdraw everything immediately", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Form 16 is…
options: The employer's annual TDS certificate used for filing tax returns
quiz.why: The answer is "The employer's annual TDS certificate used for filing tax returns". Reason: It summarises salary and tax deducted. The other choices, such as "A resignation letter" and "A POSH complaint form", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Many Indian companies align appraisal cycles with…
questions.why: The answer is "The financial year (April–March)". Reason: Common, though not universal. The other choices, such as "The cricket season" and "Your birthday", do not fit the question.

questions.q: A 'wins log' is…
options: A weekly record of achievements with evidence
questions.why: The answer is "A weekly record of achievements with evidence". Reason: It supplies evidence for appraisals. The other choices, such as "An HR form" and "A game", do not fit the question.

questions.q: CTC means…
options: Total annual cost to the employer
questions.why: The answer is "Total annual cost to the employer". Reason: Cost to Company. The other choices, such as "Tax only" and "Bonus only", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which line belongs in a strong self-assessment?
options: 'Cut report time from 3 hours to 20 minutes by automating it'
questions.why: The answer is "'Cut report time from 3 hours to 20 minutes by automating it'". Reason: Measurable results persuade. The other choices, such as "'My teammates are slow'" and "'I am the best'", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Calibration exists to…
questions.why: The answer is "Make ratings consistent across teams". Reason: It aligns standards. The other choices, such as "Punish freshers" and "Replace managers", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Under EPF, employee and employer each typically contribute…
questions.why: The answer is "12% of basic wages (plus DA)". Reason: 12% each is the standard rate; check current rules. The other choices, such as "Nothing" and "2% of CTC", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Best response when feedback stings?
questions.why: The answer is "Pause, thank, ask for examples". Reason: Understanding first. The other choices, such as "Post online" and "Walk out", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which is mistreatment rather than feedback?
options: Comments mocking your caste or region
questions.why: The answer is "Comments mocking your caste or region". Reason: Identity-based humiliation is not feedback. The other choices, such as "'Please double-check totals'" and "'Lead with the conclusion'", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Variable pay usually depends on…
questions.why: The answer is "Ratings and company/business results". Reason: It's performance-linked and may not be paid in full. The other choices, such as "Nothing" and "Your age", do not fit the question.

questions.q: CTC ₹6,00,000 including ₹60,000 variable, ₹21,600 employer PF, ₹14,400 gratuity, ₹8,000 insurance. Fixed gross per year is…
questions.why: The answer is "₹4,96,000". Reason: 6,00,000 − 1,04,000 = 4,96,000. The other choices, such as "₹5,40,000" and "₹4,50,000", do not fit the question. (Question: CTC ₹6,00,000 including ₹60,000 variable, ₹21,600 employer PF, ₹14,400 gratuity, ₹8,000 insurance. Fixed gross)

questions.q: Under a guided distribution, why is documented impact especially important?
options: Because ratings are partly comparative across peers
questions.why: The answer is "Because ratings are partly comparative across peers". Reason: Managers must defend ratings with evidence in calibration. The other choices, such as "Because hours are counted" and "It isn't important", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which offer-letter clause most needs checking before signing?
questions.why: The answer is "Bond/training-cost recovery and notice period". Reason: These have financial and career consequences. The other choices, such as "Font size" and "Company logo colour", do not fit the question.

questions.q: A balanced self-assessment includes…
options: 3–5 evidence-backed achievements plus 1–2 growth areas with a plan
questions.why: The answer is "3–5 evidence-backed achievements plus 1–2 growth areas with a plan". Reason: Balance increases credibility. The other choices, such as "Only weaknesses" and "Only strengths", do not fit the question.

corporate-leadership.title: Leadership for senior managers
corporate-leadership.description: For managers of managers at big tech and large enterprises: leading through layers, strategy and OKRs, org design, influence without authority, executive presence, hiring and firing, calibration, decisions under ambiguity and crisis leadership.

courses.title: Managing managers
courses.summary: The jump from leading individual contributors to leading leaders: changing your job, skip-levels, delegation, coaching managers and building a leadership bench.
outcomes: Learners can describe how the job changes from manager to manager-of-managers
Learners can run effective skip-level meetings without undermining managers
Learners can delegate outcomes with appropriate autonomy
Learners can coach first-line managers and build a succession bench

story.title: Anjali's first month as a Director

scenes.text: Anjali, a star engineering manager at a Hyderabad tech campus, is promoted to Director of 4 managers and 38 engineers.
She keeps doing what made her successful: reviewing code, joining every stand-up, solving technical problems herself.
Within six weeks, her managers feel micromanaged, two strategic projects are drifting, and she's working 14-hour days.
Her VP tells her: 'Your product is no longer the software. Your product is the team of teams.'

steps.title: From doing to designing
steps.body:
Leadership roles shift at each level (a well-known framing is the 'leadership pipeline'):
- **Individual contributor:** results through your own work.
- **First-line manager:** results through people — hiring, feedback, prioritising.
- **Manager of managers:** results through **managers** — choosing and developing leaders, setting direction across teams, allocating resources, designing structure and processes.

The skills that got you promoted (deep technical problem-solving, being the hero) can now hurt if overused. Your new leverage comes from **clarity, people decisions and systems**.

steps.title: Where your time should go
steps.body:
A useful self-audit: track your calendar for two weeks and sort time into:
- **Direction:** strategy, priorities, roadmap, cross-team alignment.
- **People:** 1:1s with managers, skip-levels, hiring, talent reviews, coaching.
- **Operations:** reviews, metrics, incidents, budgets.
- **Doing:** your own hands-on work.

Many new directors find 'doing' far too high and 'direction' and 'people' too low. There's no perfect ratio, but if you are the bottleneck for decisions inside a team, that's a signal.

steps.title: Classic traps
steps.body:
- **Skipping the manager:** giving direct instructions to their engineers. It undermines the manager's authority.
- **Being the escalation point for everything.** Push decisions down.
- **Measuring yourself by activity.** Your output = the output of your organisation.
- **Not letting go of your old team.** Treat your former peers and old team fairly and equally.

steps.title: Your first 90 days as a manager of managers
steps.body:
- 1:1 with each manager: their goals, team health, biggest risks, what they need from you.
- Skip-levels with a sample of engineers.
- Meet key peers and stakeholders (product, design, operations).
- Write a short **'state of the org'**: strengths, risks, 3 priorities — share it and invite corrections.
- Make one or two visible improvements; avoid large reorganisations before you understand the system.

activity.prompt: For a manager of managers, is this high-leverage or a trap?

items.text: Coaching a manager on running better 1:1s
Rewriting an engineer's code yourself at midnight
Clarifying priorities across four teams
Telling a manager's engineer to change tasks without informing the manager
Running a quarterly talent review
Approving every small design decision personally

quiz.q: For a manager of managers, 'your product' is best described as…
options: The organisation: teams, leaders and systems
quiz.why: The answer is "The organisation: teams, leaders and systems". Reason: Leverage comes through leaders and systems. The other choices, such as "The code" and "The slides", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Giving direct instructions to a manager's report without telling the manager…
quiz.why: The answer is "Undermines the manager". Reason: Work through your managers. The other choices, such as "Shows leadership" and "Is required", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A good early artefact for a new director is…
options: A short 'state of the org' with strengths, risks and priorities
A list of who to fire
quiz.why: The answer is "A short 'state of the org' with strengths, risks and priorities". Reason: Shows understanding and invites correction. The other choices, such as "A new logo" and "A reorg in week one", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A sign you're too involved in 'doing' is…
options: Teams wait on you for decisions
quiz.why: The answer is "Teams wait on you for decisions". Reason: You've become a bottleneck. The other choices, such as "You have time for strategy" and "You coach regularly", do not fit the question.

scenes.text: Paul, a director in Bengaluru, hears from his managers that 'everything's fine'. Attrition, however, is 25% in one team.
He starts monthly skip-level conversations with small groups of engineers.
He learns that one manager cancels 1:1s, overloads on-call duty onto two people and takes credit in reviews.
Instead of overruling the manager publicly, Paul coaches him with specific feedback — and checks progress through the next skip-levels.

steps.title: Purpose of a skip-level
Worked example: good questions
steps.body:
- *'What's one thing slowing you down that leadership could fix?'*
- *'Do you understand why we're prioritising X over Y this quarter?'*
- *'What should I start, stop or continue?'*
- *'Who on the team has helped you most recently?'* (surfaces quiet heroes)
- *'How sustainable is your workload, 1–10?'*

In hierarchical cultures, people may hold back with a director. Use small groups, anonymous pre-surveys, and act visibly on what you hear so trust grows.

steps.title: Rules that protect your managers
steps.body:
- Tell managers you run skip-levels and why; share themes (not who said what).
- Don't make decisions in the skip-level that belong to the manager — take issues back to them.
- If you hear about a serious problem (harassment, ethics, safety), follow policy immediately — those don't wait.
- Close the loop: *'Last month you raised on-call load; here's what changed.'*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using skip-levels to collect gossip.
- Breaking confidentiality ('Ravi said you're disorganised').
- Promising things the manager hasn't agreed to.
- Doing them once and never again — trust needs consistency.

a.text: In a skip-level, three engineers say their manager often cancels 1:1s and gives all weekend on-call to the same two people. What do you do?

choices.label: Thank them, promise to look into themes, and take it to the manager as coaching with specifics but without names
choices.feedback: Protects confidentiality and the manager's role.

choices.label: Immediately email the manager: 'Your team says you're bad at 1:1s.'
choices.feedback: Breaks trust on both sides.

choices.label: Reassign on-call yourself the same day
choices.feedback: Bypassing the manager undermines them.

b.text: The manager is defensive: 'They're exaggerating.' How do you respond?

choices.label: Share the observable data (1:1 cancellations, on-call rota) and agree a plan with a check-in date
choices.feedback: Data depersonalises and enables change.

choices.label: Drop it to avoid conflict
choices.feedback: The problem and attrition continue.

c.text: The manager is furious and starts asking who complained. What now?

choices.label: Apologise for the approach, make clear retaliation is unacceptable, reset with data-based coaching
choices.feedback: Recover, and protect the team.

d.text: The manager feels humiliated and the team is confused about who's in charge. What now?

choices.label: Talk with the manager, explain the concern, and let them own the fix
choices.feedback: Return authority to the manager.

e1.text: The manager fixes the rota and protects 1:1s. Next quarter's skip-level shows better morale and the attrition trend eases.

e2.text: Two more engineers resign. Avoiding hard coaching conversations is costly.

quiz.q: The main purpose of skip-levels is…
options: Hearing ground truth and spotting talent and problems
quiz.why: The answer is "Hearing ground truth and spotting talent and problems". Reason: Insight, not bypass. The other choices, such as "Assigning tasks" and "Bypassing managers", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: What should you share with managers from skip-levels?
quiz.why: The answer is "Themes without attributing individuals". Reason: Confidentiality builds trust. The other choices, such as "Exact quotes and names" and "Nothing ever", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: If a skip-level reveals possible harassment, you should…
quiz.why: The answer is "Follow policy immediately". Reason: Serious issues require prompt action. The other choices, such as "Ignore it" and "Tell the team", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: In hierarchical cultures, honest skip-levels are helped by…
options: Small groups, anonymous pre-surveys and visible follow-through
quiz.why: The answer is "Small groups, anonymous pre-surveys and visible follow-through". Reason: Safety and trust. The other choices, such as "Large formal meetings" and "Recording everyone", do not fit the question.

story.title: The migration Vikram couldn't let go

scenes.text: Senior Director Vikram 'delegates' a cloud migration to his manager Farah — then reviews every ticket and changes her plans.
Farah feels she has responsibility without authority. Her team waits for Vikram's approval on everything.
A coach introduces delegation levels and asks Vikram to define the outcome, constraints and check-ins — then step back.
The migration finishes early. Farah is promoted the following year.

steps.title: Levels of delegation
steps.body:
Make the level explicit:
- **1. Do as I say.**
- **2. Research and report; I decide.**
- **3. Recommend; I decide.**
- **4. Decide, then tell me.**
- **5. Decide; tell me only if there's a problem.**

For experienced managers on familiar work, aim for 4–5. For new or high-risk work, start at 3 and move up as trust grows. Many delegation failures come from the leader assuming level 5 and acting like level 1.

steps.title: Worked example: a delegation brief
steps.body:
*'Farah, I'd like you to own the migration to the new cloud region.*
- *Outcome: all payment services migrated by 30 Sept with no customer-visible downtime above 5 minutes.*
- *Constraints: budget ₹2.4 crore; no changes to the card-processing vendor.*
- *Authority: you decide sequencing, staffing within your teams and vendors under ₹25 lakh (level 4).*
- *Check-ins: fortnightly 30-minute review; escalate immediately if downtime risk exceeds the target.*
- *Support from me: unblocking with security and finance.'*

steps.title: Inspect, don't interfere
steps.body: Agree on **leading indicators** (milestones, risk register, test coverage) and review them at check-ins. Ask questions (*'What could stop us hitting 30 Sept?'*) instead of issuing instructions. Intervene only when risk crosses the agreed threshold — and say why.

steps.title: Reverse delegation
steps.body: Watch for 'monkeys on your back': a manager brings you a problem and leaves with you owning it. Reply with: *'What do you recommend?'* and *'What do you need from me to do it?'* — so ownership stays with them.

activity.prompt: Match the situation to the best delegation level.
pairs: New manager, first vendor negotiation, high stakes
Experienced manager, routine hiring in budget
Level 5: decide; tell me if there's a problem
A regulatory filing with exact legal wording

quiz.q: A good delegation brief includes…
options: Outcome, constraints, authority level, check-ins and support
quiz.why: The answer is "Outcome, constraints, authority level, check-ins and support". Reason: Clarity enables autonomy. The other choices, such as "Every step in detail" and "Only the task name", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: 'Reverse delegation' means…
options: A report handing a problem back so you end up owning it
quiz.why: The answer is "A report handing a problem back so you end up owning it". Reason: Keep ownership with the delegate. The other choices, such as "Firing" and "Your manager delegating to you", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: 'Inspect, don't interfere' means…
options: Review agreed indicators and ask questions; intervene only past thresholds
quiz.why: The answer is "Review agreed indicators and ask questions; intervene only past thresholds". Reason: Trust plus verification. The other choices, such as "Micromanage" and "Ignore the project", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: For a new, high-risk task with a new manager, start at…
quiz.why: The answer is "Level 3". Reason: Build trust step by step. The other choices, such as "Level 4 always" and "Level 5", do not fit the question. (Question: For a new, high-risk task with a new manager, start at…)

lessons.title: Coaching managers and building the bench

scenes.text: Meenakshi, a VP in Chennai, is offered a two-year global assignment. Her boss asks: 'Who can step into your role?'
She realises nobody is ready — she has always solved the hardest problems herself.
She spends six months coaching two directors: giving them her steering meetings, stretch projects and honest feedback.
One of them succeeds her. Meenakshi takes the assignment without the organisation wobbling.

steps.title: Coach with questions
steps.body:
A simple coaching structure is **GROW**:
- **Goal:** *What do you want to achieve?*
- **Reality:** *What's happening now? What have you tried?*
- **Options:** *What could you do? What else?*
- **Will / Way forward:** *What will you do, by when? What support do you need?*

Coaching builds judgement; telling builds dependence. Tell when it's urgent or the person truly lacks information; coach when they can find the answer.

steps.title: Succession and the bench
steps.body:
For each critical role (including yours), identify:
- **Ready now** successors,
- **Ready in 1–2 years,**
- the **gaps** for each (e.g., executive communication, P&L ownership, cross-functional influence),
- a **development plan**: stretch assignments, rotations, mentoring, exposure to senior forums.

Around 70% of development is often attributed to on-the-job experience (the '70-20-10' heuristic: experience, relationships, formal learning) — treat it as a rough guide, not a law.

steps.title: Worked example: a stretch assignment
steps.body: Meenakshi gave Director Arun her monthly business review with the CFO for three months. Before each, they rehearsed for 20 minutes; after each, she gave two points of feedback. By month three Arun ran it alone. Cost to her: about 2 hours a month. Benefit: a successor and a freed-up VP.

steps.title: Make the bench diverse and fair
steps.body: Bias easily creeps into who gets 'potential' labels — people who resemble current leaders, speak loudly, or are most visible. Use clear criteria, look at under-represented groups (including women returning from maternity or caregiving breaks), and ask: *who hasn't been given a stretch chance yet?*

activity.prompt: Put the GROW coaching conversation in order.
items: Goal: What do you want to achieve?
Reality: What's happening now, and what have you tried?
Options: What could you do?
Will: What will you do, by when, with what support?

quiz.q: GROW stands for…
quiz.why: The answer is "Goal, Reality, Options, Will". Reason: A classic coaching model. The other choices, such as "Guide, Review, Order, Wait" and "Grow, Run, Observe, Win", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: When should you tell rather than coach?
options: When it's urgent or the person lacks key information
quiz.why: The answer is "When it's urgent or the person lacks key information". Reason: Coach to build judgement otherwise. The other choices, such as "Always" and "Never", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: The 70-20-10 idea suggests development comes mostly from…
quiz.why: The answer is "On-the-job experience". Reason: Treat as a heuristic. The other choices, such as "Nothing" and "Books", do not fit the question. (Question: The 70-20-10 idea suggests development comes mostly from…)

quiz.q: A fair bench process should…
options: Use clear criteria and actively consider overlooked talent
Pick people who resemble current leaders
quiz.why: The answer is "Use clear criteria and actively consider overlooked talent". Reason: Reduces bias. The other choices, such as "Pick people who resemble current leaders" and "Only include the loudest", do not fit the question.

questions.q: For a manager of managers, leverage comes mainly from…
questions.why: The answer is "Leaders, clarity and systems". Reason: Team of teams. The other choices, such as "Approving everything" and "Long hours", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Skip-levels are for…
questions.why: The answer is "Ground truth and talent spotting". Reason: Insight. The other choices, such as "Gossip" and "Firing", do not fit the question. (Question: Skip-levels are for…)

questions.q: GROW's 'R' is…
questions.why: The answer is "Reality". Reason: Current situation. The other choices, such as "Review" and "Risk", do not fit the question. (Question: GROW's 'R' is…)

questions.q: Delegation level 4 means…
questions.why: The answer is "Decide, then tell me". Reason: Autonomy with information. The other choices, such as "Recommend only" and "Research only", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Reverse delegation is countered with…
questions.why: The answer is "'What do you recommend?'". Reason: Keep ownership with them. The other choices, such as "A reorg" and "Silence", do not fit the question.

questions.q: A 'state of the org' memo helps a new leader…
questions.why: The answer is "Show understanding and invite correction". Reason: Shared picture. The other choices, such as "Skip strategy" and "Avoid meetings", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Skip-level feedback should be shared with managers as…
questions.why: The answer is "Themes, not names". Reason: Confidentiality. The other choices, such as "Public posts" and "Nothing", do not fit the question. (Question: Skip-level feedback should be shared with managers as…)

questions.q: A delegation brief's 'constraints' might include…
questions.why: The answer is "Budget and non-negotiables". Reason: Boundaries enable autonomy. The other choices, such as "Nothing" and "Lunch menu", do not fit the question.

questions.q: A big risk in early months as a director is…
options: A large reorg before understanding the system
Writing a state of the org
questions.why: The answer is "A large reorg before understanding the system". Reason: Understand first. The other choices, such as "Running 1:1s" and "Meeting stakeholders", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which signals you're a bottleneck?
options: Teams wait for you on routine decisions
questions.why: The answer is "Teams wait for you on routine decisions". Reason: Push decisions down. The other choices, such as "Managers decide confidently" and "Projects move without you", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Bias in potential assessments often favours…
options: People who resemble current leaders or are most visible
questions.why: The answer is "People who resemble current leaders or are most visible". Reason: Use criteria. The other choices, such as "Returners" and "Quiet high performers", do not fit the question.

questions.q: A skip-level reveals a manager overloads two people with weekend on-call. Best first move?
options: Coach the manager with data and agree a plan, protecting sources
questions.why: The answer is "Coach the manager with data and agree a plan, protecting sources". Reason: Fix through the manager. The other choices, such as "Reassign on-call yourself" and "Announce it publicly", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Leader 'delegates' but reviews every ticket. The effect is usually…
options: Responsibility without authority and slower decisions
questions.why: The answer is "Responsibility without authority and slower decisions". Reason: Mismatch of stated and real delegation. The other choices, such as "Better metrics" and "Faster delivery", do not fit the question.

courses.title: Strategy, OKRs, org design and influence
courses.summary: Turn ambiguity into a clear strategy, cascade it with OKRs, design organisations that fit the strategy, and influence peers and executives without formal authority.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish real strategy from goals and plans
Learners can write good OKRs and avoid common OKR failures
Learners can evaluate org structures and their trade-offs
Learners can build influence without authority across functions

story.title: 'Be the best' is not a strategy

scenes.text: At an offsite in Goa, a VP presents the 'strategy': 'Be the #1 payments platform in India, delight customers, grow 50%.'
A new director, Omar, asks: 'What will we stop doing? Where will we not compete?' Silence.
Over two days they diagnose: they can't beat incumbents in big-city retail, but small-town merchants are underserved.
New strategy: focus on Tier-2/3 merchants with vernacular onboarding and offline support; pause enterprise sales. Teams finally know what to say no to.
