corporate-politics-india.title: Office politics in Indian workplaces
corporate-politics-india.description: Real Indian office situations — credit stealing, the manager's favourite, 'sir/ma'am' hierarchy, festival vs deadline, WFH visibility, appraisal season, toxic peers, cliques, gossip, escalations and resignations — practised through branching scenarios with ethical, practical guidance.

courses.title: Office politics 101: credit, favourites and gossip
courses.summary: Understand workplace politics as the reality of influence, not dirty tricks — and practise handling credit stealing, the manager's favourite and office gossip ethically.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish healthy influence from manipulation
Learners can protect credit for their work without drama
Learners can respond to perceived favouritism constructively
Learners can stay out of gossip while staying connected

scenes.text: Tanvi, a data analyst in Hyderabad, proudly says, 'I don't do politics. My work speaks for itself.' She avoids lunch groups and never talks to anyone outside her team.
When a reorganisation happens, nobody in leadership knows her name. Her best project is presented by someone else's manager.
Her mentor, Ramesh, explains: 'Politics is just how decisions get made among people. You can do it ethically — by being known, trusted and useful.'
Tanvi starts sharing short monthly updates and helping other teams with data. Within a year, she is the person leaders ask for.

steps.title: Politics = influence + relationships + information
steps.body:
Whenever people with different goals share limited resources (budget, promotions, attention), there is politics. It exists in every country and every company — in a 20-person startup and in a 3-lakh-employee IT services firm.

Think of three kinds of behaviour:
- **Healthy influence:** building relationships, making your work visible, understanding stakeholders, persuading with data.
- **Defensive survival:** documenting agreements, clarifying credit, avoiding traps.
- **Toxic politics:** lying, taking credit, spreading rumours, sabotage, favouritism based on caste, region or personal loyalty.

The goal of this course: **get good at the first two, never do the third, and know how to respond when others do.**

steps.title: Why it can feel stronger in Indian workplaces
steps.body:
Some patterns common in many (not all) Indian organisations:
- **High respect for hierarchy** — seniors' opinions often carry extra weight; juniors may hesitate to disagree openly.
- **Relationship-driven work** — who you know (and who vouches for you) can matter as much as formal process.
- **Large teams and pyramids** — many freshers, fewer senior roles, so promotions are competitive.
- **Collective identity** — college, region, language, or previous-company groups form naturally.

None of these are bad in themselves. They become harmful when they replace fairness.

steps.title: The stakeholder map
steps.body:
Draw a 2×2: **influence over your work** (high/low) vs **interest in your work** (high/low).
- High influence, high interest (your manager, skip manager): **manage closely** — regular updates.
- High influence, low interest (a director in another function): **keep satisfied** — brief, occasional, relevant updates.
- Low influence, high interest (peers who depend on you): **keep informed.**
- Low/low: **monitor.**

This simple tool, borrowed from project management, is the ethical core of 'office politics'.

steps.title: Three ethical habits that beat politics
steps.body:
- **Be reliably useful** — deliver what you promise, when you promise.
- **Be visible** — short written updates; speak in meetings; share learnings.
- **Be fair** — give credit generously, don't gossip, keep confidences. Over years, a reputation for fairness is a strong form of power.

activity.prompt: Sort each behaviour.

items.text: Sending your manager a monthly impact summary
Confirming a verbal agreement by email
Presenting a teammate's analysis as your own
Helping another team with a data problem
Spreading a rumour that a peer is leaving
Keeping notes of who agreed to what in meetings
Favouring people from your home state in task allocation

quiz.q: Which is the healthiest definition of office politics?
options: How influence, relationships and information shape decisions
quiz.why: The answer is "How influence, relationships and information shape decisions". Reason: Politics is a neutral reality; your methods make it ethical or toxic. The other choices, such as "Something only bad people do" and "Dirty tricks to get ahead", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: In a stakeholder map, your skip-level manager is usually…
options: High influence — manage closely or keep satisfied
quiz.why: The answer is "High influence — manage closely or keep satisfied". Reason: They influence ratings and opportunities. The other choices, such as "Someone to avoid" and "Irrelevant", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Why did Tanvi's 'work speaks for itself' approach fail?
options: Decision-makers didn't know her or her work
quiz.why: The answer is "Decision-makers didn't know her or her work". Reason: Work needs to be visible to the people deciding. The other choices, such as "She was too political" and "She talked too much", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Confirming a verbal agreement by email is…
quiz.why: The answer is "A sensible defensive habit". Reason: It prevents later 'I never agreed' disputes, when done politely. The other choices, such as "Illegal" and "Toxic", do not fit the question.

scenes.text: Vivek, a junior analyst in Gurugram, spends two weeks building a churn dashboard. His senior colleague Sameer presents it to the VP: 'I built this to track churn.'
The VP praises Sameer. Vivek sits in the meeting, stunned and silent.
Vivek wants to reply-all to the VP with 'Actually, I built it.' His friend stops him.
Instead, he uses a calmer, smarter approach — and a month later the VP is calling him directly for analysis.

steps.title: First, check: theft or omission?
steps.body:
Credit 'stealing' ranges from **careless omission** (a senior says 'we' or forgets names under time pressure) to **deliberate theft** (repeatedly presenting your work as theirs). Respond in proportion.

Ask yourself: Is this the first time? Did they say 'I' or 'we'? Is your manager aware of your work? Your response should escalate only as the pattern becomes clearer.

steps.title: Prevent it: make authorship visible
steps.body:
- Put your name and date on documents (*'Prepared by Vivek Rao, 12 Aug'*).
- Share work with your manager first, in writing: *'Sharing the churn dashboard I built — key insight: churn is 2× higher in month 3.'*
- Present your own work when possible: *'Would it help if I walk the VP through it for five minutes?'*
- Post progress in team channels — this creates a natural, timestamped record.

steps.title: Worked example: the calm private conversation
steps.body:
Vivek to Sameer, privately: *'Sameer, I noticed in the VP review the dashboard was presented as built by you. I spent two weeks on it, so it matters to me that my contribution is visible. In future reviews, could we present it together, or could you mention my part?'*

No accusations, a specific fact, why it matters, and a specific request. Many people correct course after this. If it happens again, speak to your manager with facts and dates — not emotion.

steps.title: What not to do
steps.body:
- Public confrontation in front of the VP or reply-all corrections — you'll look petty even if you're right.
- Taking revenge by withholding help or data.
- Complaining in gossip circles — it reaches the person, distorted.
- And on the other side: **never take credit yourself.** Say 'Priya built this model; I'll explain how we used it.' Generous credit makes you look like a leader.

a.text: In a meeting with the director, your team lead presents your analysis and says, 'I found that delays are mostly in vendor approvals.' Everyone nods. What do you do in the meeting?

choices.label: Stay calm; add a useful detail: 'In the data I pulled, 62% of delays were in two vendors — happy to share the breakdown.'
choices.feedback: You've shown authorship by adding value, not by fighting.

choices.label: Interrupt: 'Actually that was MY analysis!'
choices.feedback: Accurate but publicly embarrassing to your lead; this usually backfires.

choices.label: Say nothing and fume
choices.feedback: Silence is safe for now, but the pattern may continue.

b.text: The director asks you to send the breakdown. After the meeting, what next?

choices.label: Email the breakdown to the director, cc your lead, with a short summary
choices.feedback: Creates a visible, polite record of your work.

choices.label: Send it secretly to the director only
choices.feedback: Going around your lead can damage trust; cc them.

c.text: The room goes silent. Your lead looks embarrassed and angry. Later, what do you do?

choices.label: Apologise for the delivery, then calmly explain why credit matters to you
choices.feedback: Repairs the relationship while keeping your point.

choices.label: Ignore your lead for a week
choices.feedback: Cold wars hurt you more than them.

d.text: Two days later, it happens again in a client update. What now?

choices.label: Have a calm private talk with your lead: fact, impact, request
choices.feedback: Right step once you see a pattern.

choices.label: Complain about your lead in the cafeteria
choices.feedback: Gossip spreads and makes you look unprofessional.

e1.text: The director now knows your name and work, and your lead isn't humiliated. This is ethical politics at its best.

e2.text: You got visibility, but your lead may see it as going behind their back. Transparency (cc) is safer.

e3.text: Your lead agrees to mention your contributions. If it repeats, take facts and dates to your manager or skip-level.

e4.text: The relationship sours and your reputation suffers. Prefer private, factual conversations.

quiz.q: Best way to prevent credit theft?
options: Make authorship visible: names on documents, written updates, presenting your own work
quiz.why: The answer is "Make authorship visible: names on documents, written updates, presenting your own work". Reason: Visibility creates a natural record. The other choices, such as "Complain loudly" and "Hide your work", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A first-time 'we did this' from your lead is most likely…
quiz.why: The answer is "Possibly careless omission — respond proportionately". Reason: Escalate only as a pattern becomes clear. The other choices, such as "A POSH issue" and "Deliberate fraud", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A good private conversation about credit includes…
options: A specific fact, why it matters, and a specific request
quiz.why: The answer is "A specific fact, why it matters, and a specific request". Reason: Fact–impact–request is calm and effective. The other choices, such as "Accusations and threats" and "Crying", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: How do leaders build reputation through credit?
quiz.why: The answer is "Giving credit generously to others". Reason: Generous credit signals confidence and fairness. The other choices, such as "Taking all credit" and "Never mentioning names", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: If credit theft repeats after you've spoken privately, next step?
options: Take facts and dates to your manager or skip-level
quiz.why: The answer is "Take facts and dates to your manager or skip-level". Reason: Documented escalation through the right channel. The other choices, such as "Public reply-all" and "Sabotage their work", do not fit the question.

scenes.text: Kunal plays cricket with manager Deepak every weekend. He gets the best projects and the client trip to Singapore. Shalini, equally good, gets maintenance work.
Shalini tells her colleagues, 'It's all chamchagiri (sucking up).' She becomes cynical and does the minimum.
Her mentor asks two questions: 'Does Deepak know what you want? Have you shown him you can do it?' Shalini realises she has never asked.
She asks for a stretch project with a clear plan. She gets the next client migration — and later learns Kunal had volunteered for every tough assignment for a year.

steps.title: Is it favouritism or familiarity?
steps.body:
Managers give opportunities to people they **know, trust and see**. Sometimes that is unfair favouritism (based on caste, region, language, gender, personal loyalty or social life). Often it is **familiarity**: the favourite communicates more, volunteers more, or has a track record the manager has seen.

Before concluding it's unfair, check:
- Have I told my manager clearly what I want?
- Have I shown evidence I'm ready?
- Does the favourite do something visible I don't?

steps.title: Worked example: asking for opportunity
steps.body:
Shalini in her 1:1: *'Deepak, I'd like to work on a client-facing migration in the next quarter. I've handled the database maintenance for six months with zero P1 incidents, and I've completed the cloud migration course. What would you need to see from me to be considered for the next one?'*

This converts a grievance into a clear ask with evidence — and the last question makes the manager commit to criteria.

steps.title: When it really is unfair
steps.body:
If you see a real pattern — opportunities and ratings consistently going to one group regardless of performance, or decisions linked to caste, religion, region, gender or personal favours:
- Document specific instances (dates, assignments, outcomes).
- Seek a skip-level conversation or HR business partner discussion, focusing on fair process.
- Use the company's ethics or grievance channel if needed; many companies have whistle-blower policies.
- Build a network outside your manager — mentors, other teams — so one person doesn't control your whole career.

steps.title: Don't become bitter
steps.body: Cynicism ('everything is politics, why try?') hurts you most. Keep doing visible good work, keep relationships with the favourite civil (they may be your manager one day), and if the environment stays unfair, an internal transfer or a job change is a legitimate choice.

a.text: The manager's favourite gets the high-visibility project again. You feel overlooked. What's your first step?

choices.label: Ask your manager in a 1:1 what you'd need to show to be considered next time
choices.feedback: Turns frustration into a clear, fair ask.

choices.label: Tell colleagues the favourite is a chamcha
choices.feedback: Gossip spreads and labels you as negative.

choices.label: Quietly reduce your effort
choices.feedback: This confirms the manager's choice.

b.text: Manager: 'I need someone who can handle client calls confidently.' What do you do?

choices.label: Ask to shadow two client calls and present a small update yourself
choices.feedback: You've created a path to prove readiness.

choices.label: Say 'I can do it' and nothing more
choices.feedback: Without a plan, nothing changes.

c.text: A month later, your manager seems colder. What now?

choices.label: Reset: have the 1:1 conversation about opportunities and readiness
choices.feedback: It's never too late to switch to a constructive approach.

choices.label: Escalate to HR saying the manager is biased, without any examples
choices.feedback: Escalation needs evidence; vague complaints rarely help.

e1.text: After two shadowed calls and one presentation, you're on the next client project. Familiarity can be built.

e2.text: Your manager nods but nothing changes. Come back with a concrete plan.

e3.text: HR asks for specific examples you don't have. Document patterns first; real unfairness deserves a well-evidenced complaint.

quiz.q: Before concluding favouritism, you should check…
options: Whether you have clearly asked and shown readiness
quiz.why: The answer is "Whether you have clearly asked and shown readiness". Reason: Often the gap is communication and visibility. The other choices, such as "Their horoscope" and "Nothing", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Which question makes a manager commit to criteria?
options: 'What would you need to see from me to be considered next time?'
quiz.why: The answer is "'What would you need to see from me to be considered next time?'". Reason: It sets clear, checkable expectations. The other choices, such as "'Is Kunal your friend?'" and "'Why do you hate me?'", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Real unfair favouritism should be handled by…
options: Documenting instances and using skip-level, HR or ethics channels
quiz.why: The answer is "Documenting instances and using skip-level, HR or ethics channels". Reason: Evidence plus proper channels. The other choices, such as "Ignoring it forever" and "Social media posts", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Why build a network beyond your manager?
options: So one person doesn't control your whole career
quiz.why: The answer is "So one person doesn't control your whole career". Reason: Mentors and other teams open doors. The other choices, such as "To gossip" and "To avoid work", do not fit the question.

lessons.title: Office gossip: stay connected, stay clean

scenes.text: At the 4 pm chai break, colleagues whisper that Leena from finance was 'caught' and is being fired. Everyone looks at Abhishek, the new joiner, to see if he'll add anything.
By evening, the rumour is in three WhatsApp groups with new details.
The truth: Leena had taken medical leave for surgery. She returns to find people avoiding her.
Abhishek, who had said only 'I don't know anything about it', is one of the few she still trusts.

steps.title: Information vs gossip
steps.body:
Not all informal talk is bad. **Useful informal information**: 'The VP prefers one-page summaries', 'Finance closes books on the 25th.' **Gossip**: speculation about people's personal lives, health, relationships, salaries, conflicts, or who will be fired.

Test: *Would I say this if the person were standing here? Is it true, kind and necessary?*

steps.title: How to exit gossip without being 'boring'
steps.body:
- **Redirect:** *'No idea — by the way, did anyone try the new canteen thali?'*
- **Neutral fact:** *'I heard she's on leave; hope she's okay.'*
- **Gentle boundary:** *'I'd rather not guess about that.'*
- **Leave:** *'Got a call — catch you later.'*

You don't need to lecture anyone. Just don't add fuel.

steps.title: Digital gossip is permanent
steps.body: WhatsApp forwards and chat screenshots last forever and can be shown to HR. Spreading false information about a colleague can lead to disciplinary action, and posting confidential company information can breach your employment terms. Health information about colleagues is especially sensitive — never share it.

steps.title: Be the vault
steps.body: People quietly notice who keeps confidences. Over time, the person who doesn't leak becomes the one people trust with real information — which is real influence. If a colleague confides something serious (harassment, mental health crisis), listen, keep it private, and encourage them toward the right support (HR, POSH committee, EAP, Tele-MANAS 14416) — and seek help urgently if anyone's safety is at risk (112).

a.text: In a team WhatsApp group someone posts: 'Heard Rohan got a PIP, he's definitely out by March 😂'. What do you do?

choices.label: Don't react; if it continues, message the poster privately: 'Not cool to post about Rohan here.'
choices.feedback: A private nudge stops spread without public drama.

choices.label: Reply 'lol I knew it'
choices.feedback: You've added fuel and your name is now on the screenshot.

choices.label: Forward it to your friend in another team
choices.feedback: Spreading it makes you part of the problem.

b.text: The poster replies, 'Relax, just joking.' Rohan is in the group. What next?

choices.label: Check in privately with Rohan: 'Saw that message — hope you're okay. Anything I can help with?'
choices.feedback: Support without prying.

choices.label: Leave it there
choices.feedback: Acceptable, but a kind word could matter a lot to Rohan.

c.text: Rohan sees the chat and complains to HR with screenshots. HR asks you about your reply. What do you say?

choices.label: Admit it, apologise to Rohan, and commit not to repeat it
choices.feedback: Owning it is the only good option now.

choices.label: Claim your phone was hacked
choices.feedback: Lying makes it far worse.

e1.text: Rohan thanks you. Kindness during someone's hard time is remembered for years.

e2.text: You stayed clean. Next time consider a quiet word of support.

e3.text: You receive a warning but keep your credibility by owning it. Lesson learned: screenshots are forever.

e4.text: HR doesn't believe you. A small mistake has become a dishonesty issue.

quiz.q: Which is useful informal information, not gossip?
quiz.why: The answer is "'Finance closes the books on the 25th'". Reason: Work-relevant process information is helpful. The other choices, such as "Who is dating whom" and "A colleague's medical condition", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A graceful way to exit gossip is…
quiz.why: The answer is "Redirecting the conversation". Reason: Redirecting avoids fuel without confrontation. The other choices, such as "Recording it secretly" and "Adding a new rumour", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Why is digital gossip especially risky?
options: Screenshots are permanent and can reach HR
quiz.why: The answer is "Screenshots are permanent and can reach HR". Reason: Written records persist and can be used in disciplinary processes. The other choices, such as "It's always funny" and "It's legal everywhere", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A colleague confides about harassment. You should…
options: Listen, keep it private, and point them to POSH/HR support
quiz.why: The answer is "Listen, keep it private, and point them to POSH/HR support". Reason: Confidential support and correct channels protect them. The other choices, such as "Tell the team" and "Ignore it", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Office politics is best described as…
options: How influence and relationships shape decisions
questions.why: The answer is "How influence and relationships shape decisions". Reason: It's a neutral reality. The other choices, such as "Only about elections" and "Always evil", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which is toxic politics?
questions.why: The answer is "Taking credit for others' work". Reason: Credit theft is dishonest. The other choices, such as "Helping another team" and "Monthly impact updates", do not fit the question.

questions.q: A gossip test question is…
options: Is it true, kind and necessary?
questions.why: The answer is "Is it true, kind and necessary?". Reason: Simple filter for what to share. The other choices, such as "Will it trend?" and "Is the boss away?", do not fit the question.

questions.q: High-influence, high-interest stakeholders should be…
questions.why: The answer is "Managed closely". Reason: Frequent, relevant engagement. The other choices, such as "Monitored only" and "Avoided", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Best in-meeting response when your work is presented by someone else?
options: Add a value detail showing you know the data, then follow up in writing
questions.why: The answer is "Add a value detail showing you know the data, then follow up in writing". Reason: Demonstrates authorship gracefully. The other choices, such as "Shout" and "Cry", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Before calling something favouritism, check if you've…
questions.why: The answer is "Clearly asked and shown readiness". Reason: Visibility gaps often explain it. The other choices, such as "Bought the manager gifts" and "Joined their cricket team", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Putting 'Prepared by' and a date on documents helps…
questions.why: The answer is "Make authorship visible". Reason: Simple prevention of credit loss. The other choices, such as "Annoy people" and "Hide work", do not fit the question.

questions.q: When following up with a director, why cc your lead?
options: Transparency avoids looking like you went behind their back
questions.why: The answer is "Transparency avoids looking like you went behind their back". Reason: Visibility without bypassing. The other choices, such as "HR requires it" and "No reason", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Unfair favouritism based on region or caste should be…
options: Documented and raised through skip-level, HR or ethics channels
questions.why: The answer is "Documented and raised through skip-level, HR or ethics channels". Reason: Evidence and proper channels. The other choices, such as "Posted on social media" and "Accepted", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Fact–impact–request means…
options: State what happened, why it matters, what you'd like next
questions.why: The answer is "State what happened, why it matters, what you'd like next". Reason: Calm, effective structure. The other choices, such as "Threaten, accuse, demand" and "Hint indirectly", do not fit the question.

questions.q: A colleague's health information you overheard should be…
questions.why: The answer is "Kept confidential". Reason: Health info is especially sensitive. The other choices, such as "Posted in groups" and "Reported to clients", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Why is being 'the vault' a source of influence?
options: People trust those who keep confidences and share real information with them
questions.why: The answer is "People trust those who keep confidences and share real information with them". Reason: Trust is long-term power. The other choices, such as "It avoids work" and "It gets you a hike", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Your skip-level asks you directly whether your lead built the dashboard. Best answer?
options: Answer honestly and factually without attacking: 'I built it; my lead reviewed and presented it.'
questions.why: The answer is "Answer honestly and factually without attacking: 'I built it; my lead reviewed and presented it.'". Reason: Honest, neutral facts protect both your integrity and relationships. The other choices, such as "Lie to protect your lead" and "Insult your lead", do not fit the question.

courses.title: Hierarchy, respect and belonging
courses.summary: Navigate 'sir/ma'am' culture, say no to an elder colleague respectfully, handle regional and language cliques, and balance festival and family pressure with deadlines.
outcomes: Learners can show respect while still disagreeing and speaking up
Learners can decline requests from senior or elder colleagues without damaging relationships
Learners can respond to regional/language cliques inclusively
Learners can plan around festivals and family obligations professionally

scenes.text: Priyanka, a fresher in a Kolkata manufacturing firm, calls everyone 'sir' or 'ma'am'. In a review, she notices the plant head's estimate is off by a factor of ten — a unit mistake.
She stays silent. 'Who am I to correct sir?'
The wrong estimate goes into a purchase order. The error costs weeks to fix.
Her manager later tells her: 'Respect means telling me when I'm wrong — politely. Silence isn't respect.'

steps.title: Respect and hierarchy
steps.body:
Many Indian workplaces have a **high power-distance** culture: seniors are addressed formally, decisions flow top-down, and openly contradicting a senior can feel disrespectful. Global and startup teams often prefer first names and open debate.

Good rule: **follow the local norm for address, but never let formality stop you from raising important facts.** If your team uses first names, using 'sir' repeatedly may sound distant; if unsure, ask your buddy, or start formal and follow what seniors invite you to do (*'Please call me Ravi'*).

steps.title: Worked example: disagreeing respectfully
steps.body:
Phrases that keep respect and still deliver the fact:
- *'Sir, may I check one number? I think the quantity may be in kilograms rather than tonnes — could we verify before the PO goes out?'*
- *'I may be missing context, but the data I have shows something different — can I share it after the meeting?'*
- *'Could I offer a different view?'*

Notice: **question form, offer to verify, focus on data, not the person.** If the room is too formal, raise it right after the meeting, privately but quickly.

steps.title: Switching between cultures
steps.body: In a single day, an Indian engineer may talk to a formal plant head, a casual startup founder and an American client who wants direct pushback. Skilled professionals **code-switch**: formal address and indirect phrasing with traditional seniors; first names and direct 'I disagree, here's why' with global teams. Both are respectful within their context.

steps.title: When safety, money or ethics are involved
steps.body: If a mistake could hurt someone (safety), lose significant money, or break law or policy, **speak up even if it's uncomfortable** — and if ignored, escalate through the proper channel. 'I was only following sir's instructions' is not a defence for safety or ethics violations.

a.text: In a meeting, your senior VP says a project will cost ₹40 lakh. Your spreadsheet clearly shows ₹4 crore. Ten people are in the room. What do you do?

choices.label: Politely ask: 'Sir, may I check one figure? My sheet shows ₹4 crore — could we verify?'
choices.feedback: Respectful, factual and timely.

choices.label: Stay silent and send an email later
choices.feedback: Okay for small issues; for a 10× difference, raising it now or immediately after is better.

choices.label: Say 'That's wrong, you've made a mistake'
choices.feedback: The fact is right but the framing may embarrass a senior publicly.

b.text: The VP checks and says, 'You're right, good catch.' How do you follow up?

choices.label: Send the corrected sheet with the source after the meeting
choices.feedback: Closing the loop builds trust.

c.text: You email the VP right after the meeting. But the figure was already shared with the board. What now?

choices.label: Email clearly with the data and offer to help correct it quickly
choices.feedback: Still the right move; next time raise big issues in the room.

d.text: The VP looks irritated: 'Let's discuss later.' What do you do?

choices.label: Meet after, apologise for how you said it, and walk through the data
choices.feedback: Separating the delivery from the fact repairs it.

choices.label: Drop it to avoid conflict
choices.feedback: The wrong number goes forward — the worst outcome.

e1.text: You saved the project from a 10× error and earned a reputation for careful, respectful courage.

e2.text: The error is fixed. Lesson: speak early, politely, with data.

e3.text: The wrong estimate causes serious problems later. Silence was not respect.

quiz.q: High power-distance culture means…
options: Hierarchy is strongly respected and juniors may hesitate to disagree
quiz.why: The answer is "Hierarchy is strongly respected and juniors may hesitate to disagree". Reason: It shapes how disagreement is expressed. The other choices, such as "Everyone is equal and informal" and "Remote work only", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Which phrase disagrees respectfully?
options: 'May I check one number? My data shows something different.'
quiz.why: The answer is "'May I check one number? My data shows something different.'". Reason: Question form plus data keeps respect. The other choices, such as "'Obviously that's incorrect.'" and "'You're wrong.'", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: When must you speak up even if uncomfortable?
options: When safety, significant money or ethics are involved
quiz.why: The answer is "When safety, significant money or ethics are involved". Reason: Following instructions is no defence for harm. The other choices, such as "Only on email" and "Only when invited", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: 'Code-switching' at work means…
options: Adjusting formality and directness to the context
quiz.why: The answer is "Adjusting formality and directness to the context". Reason: Respect looks different in different cultures. The other choices, such as "Changing programming languages" and "Lying", do not fit the question.

lessons.title: Saying no to an elder colleague

scenes.text: Mr Sharma, 52, a respected senior accountant in a Jaipur firm, asks 25-year-old Neeraj to 'just quickly' prepare his monthly reconciliation — again.
Neeraj has done it four times. His own GST filing work is now late, and his manager has noticed.
Saying no to someone his father's age feels deeply wrong to Neeraj.
He learns to say a respectful 'no, but…' — and Sharma ji, surprisingly, takes it well.

steps.title: Respect the person, protect the priority
steps.body:
In Indian culture, elders are respected and refusing them can feel rude. But taking on unofficial work that delays your assigned priorities hurts you, your manager and eventually the elder too.

Key idea: **respect is in your tone and alternatives, not in automatic yes.** You can be warm and still decline.

steps.title: Worked example: four ways to say no respectfully
steps.body:
- **No + reason + alternative:** *'Sharma ji, I'd love to help, but the GST filing is due Friday and I'm behind. Could I show you the reconciliation template so it's quicker for you?'*
- **Not now:** *'I can't today — can I help on Monday afternoon?'*
- **Prioritise via manager:** *'Happy to, but my manager has asked me to finish the filing first. Shall I check with her whether this can take priority?'*
- **Teach instead of do:** offer a 20-minute walkthrough or a checklist.

Use respectful address (ji, sir), warm tone and a real alternative.

steps.title: When the 'favour' is a red flag
Keep the relationship warm
steps.body: After declining, keep the relationship strong: greet them, ask for their advice on something they know well, appreciate their experience. Elder colleagues often have deep institutional knowledge — a relationship worth more than a reconciliation sheet.

a.text: A senior colleague, 30 years older, asks you for the fifth time to do his weekly MIS report. Your own deadline is tomorrow. What do you say?

choices.label: 'I'd like to help, but my deadline is tomorrow. Can I show you a faster template on Thursday?'
choices.feedback: Respectful no with a real alternative.

choices.label: 'Yes sir' — and stay up till 2 am
choices.feedback: Your work suffers and the pattern continues.

choices.label: 'That's not my job.'
choices.feedback: True perhaps, but blunt; it may damage the relationship.

b.text: He frowns: 'In my days juniors helped seniors.' What now?

choices.label: Smile, stay warm: 'I really do want to help — Thursday I'll make sure it becomes a 10-minute job for you.'
choices.feedback: Calm consistency usually wins.

choices.label: Give in out of guilt
choices.feedback: Guilt-yes recreates the problem.

c.text: You miss your deadline; your manager asks why. What do you say?

choices.label: Explain honestly and ask how to handle such requests going forward
choices.feedback: Involving your manager makes future no's easier.

choices.label: Blame the senior colleague angrily
choices.feedback: Blame without having set a boundary looks unfair.

d.text: He's offended and complains you're arrogant. What do you do?

choices.label: Apologise for the tone, explain your deadline, offer the template help
choices.feedback: You can repair tone while keeping the boundary.

e1.text: He learns the template, the requests stop, and he still greets you warmly. Respect and boundaries can coexist.

e2.text: Your manager tells the senior that your priorities come first. Next time, set the boundary earlier.

e3.text: The relationship sours. A respectful no earlier would have avoided this.

quiz.q: Which is a respectful no?
options: 'I can't today because of my deadline — can I help Monday?'
quiz.why: The answer is "'I can't today because of my deadline — can I help Monday?'". Reason: Reason plus alternative keeps respect. The other choices, such as "Doing it and complaining later" and "Ignoring the request", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: An elder colleague asks for your password to 'save time'. You should…
options: Firmly decline; it violates security policy regardless of seniority
Write it on a sticky note
quiz.why: The answer is "Firmly decline; it violates security policy regardless of seniority". Reason: Credentials are never shared. The other choices, such as "Write it on a sticky note" and "Share it out of respect", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: How can your manager help with repeated favours?
options: They can set priorities, which makes declining easier
quiz.why: The answer is "They can set priorities, which makes declining easier". Reason: Manager-set priorities give you legitimate cover. The other choices, such as "They can't" and "They will do the work", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: 'Teach instead of do' means…
options: Offering a walkthrough or template so they can do it themselves
quiz.why: The answer is "Offering a walkthrough or template so they can do it themselves". Reason: It helps once and solves the pattern. The other choices, such as "Lecturing the senior" and "Refusing all help", do not fit the question.

story.title: Lunch in Tamil, meetings in Tamil

scenes.text: In a Chennai office, most of Kavya's team speaks Tamil at lunch and, increasingly, in meetings. Aakash from Lucknow and Ritika from Assam feel left out.
Decisions sometimes happen in quick Tamil side-conversations. Aakash misses context and his work suffers.
Kavya, who is Tamil herself, notices and starts gently switching meetings to English: 'Let's use English so everyone's in.'
Aakash starts learning a few Tamil phrases; the team enjoys teaching him. Lunch becomes a mix of languages and stories.

steps.title: Why cliques form
steps.body: People naturally bond over a shared language, region, food, college or previous company. It's comforting, especially for people far from home. The problem starts when cliques **exclude others from information and opportunities** — decisions in a language some can't follow, assignments going to 'our people', jokes about other regions.

steps.title: The work-language rule
steps.body:
A simple, widely used norm: **in work discussions, use the language everyone in the room understands** (often English in mixed teams). Social chats in a shared mother tongue are fine — but switch when someone joins, and never make work decisions in a language a team member can't follow.

If you're excluded: *'Sorry, could we switch to English? I want to make sure I don't miss anything.'* — said lightly, it rarely offends.

steps.title: Stereotypes are not jokes
steps.body: Jokes about someone's region, state, accent, food, skin colour, caste or religion can be deeply hurtful and may violate company policies on harassment and discrimination. Not every hurtful comment is meant to hurt, but impact matters. Simple response: *'Not cool, yaar.'* For repeated or serious cases, report to HR.

steps.title: Be a bridge
steps.body:
- If you're in the majority group, invite the newcomer to lunch and translate the context.
- If you're the outsider, show curiosity: learn greetings, try local food, share your own culture.
- Managers: rotate assignments transparently and run meetings in a common language. Diversity of backgrounds is a strength in teams that make everyone feel included.

a.text: Your team's planning call keeps drifting into Telugu. You don't speak it, and you've just realised a task deadline was moved without you knowing. What do you do?

choices.label: Lightly ask: 'Could we switch to English? I think I missed the deadline change.'
choices.feedback: Friendly and specific — this usually works immediately.

choices.label: Stay silent and complain to other non-Telugu colleagues
choices.feedback: Forming a counter-clique deepens the divide.

b.text: They apologise and switch. A week later it happens again. What next?

choices.label: Raise it with your manager as a process suggestion: 'Can we agree meetings are in English and decisions are posted in the channel?'
choices.feedback: Turns a personal frustration into a team norm.

choices.label: Accuse the team of being regionalist in the group chat
choices.feedback: Public accusation makes people defensive.

c.text: Two groups form. Collaboration drops. Your manager notices. What do you do?

choices.label: Suggest the common-language norm and written decisions to your manager
choices.feedback: Fixes the process rather than blaming people.

e1.text: The team agrees: meetings in English, decisions posted in the channel. Lunch stays multilingual and fun.

e2.text: Tension rises. Process suggestions work better than public accusations.

quiz.q: When do language cliques become a problem?
options: When they exclude people from work information or opportunities
quiz.why: The answer is "When they exclude people from work information or opportunities". Reason: Exclusion from work is the harm. The other choices, such as "Always" and "When friends chat at lunch", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A good work-language norm is…
options: Use the language everyone in the room understands for work
quiz.why: The answer is "Use the language everyone in the room understands for work". Reason: Inclusion in decisions. The other choices, such as "Use only Hindi" and "Never speak your mother tongue", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A stereotype joke about someone's state is…
options: Potentially hurtful and may violate policy
quiz.why: The answer is "Potentially hurtful and may violate policy". Reason: Impact matters more than intent. The other choices, such as "Harmless fun" and "Required for bonding", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A good way to bridge as an outsider?
options: Show curiosity: learn greetings, share your culture
quiz.why: The answer is "Show curiosity: learn greetings, share your culture". Reason: Curiosity invites inclusion. The other choices, such as "Avoid lunch" and "Complain constantly", do not fit the question.

lessons.title: Festival and family pressure vs deadlines

story.title: Diwali, a wedding, and a go-live

scenes.text: Harsh, from Indore, has booked tickets home for Diwali. His cousin's wedding is the same week. The client's go-live is suddenly moved to Diwali week.
His mother asks daily when he's coming. His manager asks who can support go-live.
Harsh plans: he finishes his handover early, agrees to be on-call for two hours on go-live day from home, and swaps with a colleague who will take Christmas off instead.
He attends the wedding, the go-live succeeds, and his manager notes his planning in the appraisal.

steps.title: Plan festivals like a project
steps.body:
India has many festivals and family events — Diwali, Eid, Pongal, Onam, Durga Puja, Christmas, Holi, weddings, and more — and teams are diverse, so someone is almost always celebrating something.
- Check the company holiday calendar and optional/restricted holidays at the start of the year.
- **Apply for leave early** and put it on the team calendar.
- Ask about release dates and peak periods before booking tickets.
- Offer swaps: colleagues who celebrate different festivals can cover for each other.

steps.title: Worked example: negotiating leave in a crunch
steps.body:
*'Rekha, my cousin's wedding is 10–14 Nov and I've had leave approved since August. I see go-live moved to 12 Nov. Here's my plan: I'll finish testing and the handover document by 8 Nov, Anil has agreed to be primary on go-live, and I can be on call 6–8 pm on the 12th. Does that work?'*

It states the facts, shows ownership, and offers a solution instead of just a problem.

steps.title: When work asks too much
steps.body:
Occasional crunch is normal; constant cancellation of approved leave is not. If it becomes a pattern:
- Document approved leaves and cancellations.
- Discuss with your manager calmly about planning and staffing.
- Know your company's leave policy and applicable law; HR can clarify.

Your family time and rest are not 'luxuries' — burnout harms both you and the work.

steps.title: Respect others' festivals
steps.body: Don't assume everyone celebrates what you do. Wish colleagues for their festivals, avoid scheduling key meetings on major festivals of team members, and be the one who volunteers to cover so others can go home — they'll return the favour.

a.text: Your Diwali leave was approved months ago. Two weeks before, your manager says, 'Client moved the release to Diwali week; can you cancel your leave?' What do you do?

choices.label: Propose a plan: early handover, a colleague as primary, limited on-call from home
choices.feedback: Solution-oriented and protects both priorities.

choices.label: Cancel immediately without discussing your family plans
choices.feedback: Sometimes needed, but you didn't explore options.

choices.label: Refuse flatly and stop replying
choices.feedback: Your leave is valid, but no discussion damages trust.

b.text: Manager: 'The client wants someone who knows the module.' What next?

choices.label: Offer a recorded walkthrough and an overlap session with the colleague
choices.feedback: Knowledge transfer makes your absence safe.

choices.label: Say 'Not my problem'
choices.feedback: Dismissive; keep collaborating.

c.text: Your family is upset. Next year the same thing happens. What now?

choices.label: Discuss with your manager how to plan releases and backups around festivals
choices.feedback: Fixing the process prevents repeats.

scenes.text: Rizwan works from home in Lucknow for a Bengaluru team. He keeps his Teams status green all day, even moving his mouse to stay 'active'.
Office-going colleagues chat with the manager at the coffee machine and get the interesting tasks.
His manager says in a review: 'I don't really know what you've delivered this quarter.'
Rizwan switches from 'looking busy' to 'showing outcomes': a Friday summary, demos and quick calls. His next review is the best of his career.

steps.title: Outcomes beat online status
steps.body:
Many hybrid teams show **proximity bias** — people who are physically present can get more attention and opportunities. Fighting it with a permanently green status or fake activity doesn't work; managers notice results, not dots.

Instead, make **outcomes visible**:
- A short **Friday update**: 3 wins, 1–2 next priorities, any blockers.
- **Demos** of finished work in team meetings.
- **Written decisions** in shared channels.

steps.title: Worked example: a Friday update
steps.body:
*'Week of 14 July — Rizwan*
- *Done: payment retry live; failed payments down from 4.1% to 2.6% (first 3 days).*
- *Done: reviewed 6 PRs for the new joiners.*
- *Next: refund API design doc (draft by Wed).*
- *Blocker: need sandbox keys from the bank — raised ticket SR-221.'*

Two minutes to read, impossible to ignore.

steps.title: Remote presence habits
steps.body:
- Cameras on for 1:1s and key meetings (when possible).
- Speak in the first 10 minutes of meetings.
- Schedule a 15-minute virtual chai with teammates every couple of weeks.
- Visit the office for important events (planning, offsites) if feasible.
- Be responsive within agreed hours; agree on 'core hours' with your team.

steps.title: Don't do this
steps.body: Mouse-jigglers and fake activity can breach company policy and destroy trust if discovered. Moonlighting (a second job) without permission can breach your employment contract and has led to terminations in Indian IT. Always check your company's policies.

story.title: March in a Pune IT office

scenes.text: It's March. Suddenly, everyone is volunteering, sending appreciation emails and attending every meeting. Jyoti calls it 'appraisal season theatre'.
Her colleague Manish gets a better rating despite, she feels, weaker work. Jyoti wants to fight her 'Meets' rating.
She instead prepares evidence: three outcomes with numbers, client appreciation, and her goals sheet.
Her rating isn't changed this year, but her manager commits to a growth plan and a mid-year check — and she gets 'Exceeds' the next cycle.

steps.title: Why the theatre happens
steps.body: Recency bias is real: managers remember the last few weeks more vividly. That's why people become hyper-visible in appraisal season. The ethical counter is **steady visibility all year** (wins log, monthly updates) plus a strong self-assessment — not last-minute performance.

steps.title: Discussing a rating you disagree with
steps.body:
- **Wait a day** before reacting.
- Ask for the **reasoning and evidence**: *'Could you help me understand which goals you felt I didn't fully meet?'*
- Present **your evidence calmly**, tied to goals.
- Ask about **process**: is there a review or appeal mechanism?
- Focus on **next cycle**: *'What specifically would 'Exceeds' look like for me next year? Can we check in at mid-year?'*

Ratings are rarely changed after calibration, but a well-handled conversation shapes the next year.

steps.title: Avoid these
steps.body:
- Comparing your rating with colleagues' by name (*'Manish got Exceeds!'*) — you don't know their goals, and it sounds petty.
- Threatening to resign unless you have an offer and truly intend to leave.
- Badmouthing the manager to the skip-level in anger.
- Lobbying peers to give you favourable 360° feedback.

steps.title: If you're a strong performer every year but stuck
steps.body: If evidence-based conversations repeatedly don't work, ask a skip-level or mentor for perspective, consider an internal move, or test the market. Staying where your work isn't valued is a choice, not an obligation.

a.text: You receive 'Meets Expectations'. You expected 'Exceeds'. Your manager asks, 'Any questions?' What do you say right now?

choices.label: 'I'd like to understand the reasoning. Could we talk tomorrow after I've reflected?'
choices.feedback: Calm and buys time to prepare.

choices.label: 'This is unfair! Manish got Exceeds!'
choices.feedback: Comparisons sound petty and derail the talk.

b.text: Next day: you bring evidence. Your manager says calibration is final. What next?

choices.label: Ask what 'Exceeds' would look like next year and request a mid-year check
choices.feedback: You've turned a loss into a clear plan.

choices.label: Say you'll resign
choices.feedback: An empty threat weakens your position.

c.text: Your manager becomes defensive. The talk ends badly. What can you do?

choices.label: Apologise for the comparison and ask to discuss evidence and next-year goals
choices.feedback: Repair and redirect.

e1.text: With clear criteria and a mid-year check, you get 'Exceeds' next cycle.

e2.text: Your manager says, 'That's your choice.' Never threaten what you don't plan to do.

scenes.text: Nitin, a peer in a Mumbai ad agency, interrupts Aditi in every meeting, mocks her ideas ('very creative, very useless') and blames her when deadlines slip.
Aditi starts dreading Mondays.
A senior advises: talk to Nitin directly once, document everything, then escalate with facts if it continues.
After a calm direct talk fails, Aditi brings a dated log to her manager. The manager intervenes; Nitin's behaviour changes.

steps.title: Difficult vs toxic
steps.body: **Difficult**: blunt, disorganised, different working style — irritating but not harmful. **Toxic**: repeated undermining, public humiliation, blame-shifting, sabotage, exclusion, threats. Harassment linked to gender, caste, religion, disability or other identity is more serious still and should go to HR (and the Internal Committee under POSH if sexual in nature).

steps.title: Step 1: a direct, private conversation
steps.body:
Use **SBI (Situation–Behaviour–Impact)**:
*'Nitin, in yesterday's client prep (situation), you interrupted me three times and called my idea useless in front of the team (behaviour). It made it hard for me to contribute and it looked bad to the client team (impact). I'd like us to let each other finish and disagree on ideas, not people. Can we agree on that?'*

Calm, specific, about behaviour — not character ('you're a bully').

steps.title: Step 2: document
steps.body: Keep a private log (not on a shared company drive others can access): date, what happened, exact words if possible, witnesses, impact on work, any messages. Save emails and chat links. Facts over feelings: *'12 Mar, 11:15 standup: said "very creative, very useless" about my proposal; Ravi and Sana present.'*

steps.title: Step 3: escalate the right way
steps.body:
Typical order: **your manager → skip-level or HR business partner → formal grievance/ethics channel**. For sexual harassment, go to the **Internal Committee** under the POSH Act. When you escalate:
- Lead with impact on work and team.
- Bring the log.
- State what you've already tried.
- Ask for a specific outcome (mediation, meeting norms, change of reporting).

An **escalation is not snitching** — it's using the system designed for this.

steps.title: Protect your wellbeing
steps.body: Limit 1:1 time with the person, keep interactions in writing when possible, and lean on supportive colleagues. If it's affecting your sleep or health, talk to someone — EAP if available, or Tele-MANAS (14416).

choices.label: Calmly state the fact in the meeting: 'I received the input on 14 March; I'll share the thread.'
choices.feedback: Neutral facts, no attack.

choices.feedback: Separate tone from facts.

choices.feedback: Facts in writing correct the record.

e.text: He laughs it off and continues. You've logged five incidents. Next?

choices.feedback: Exactly the right escalation.

choices.feedback: Following the process helps your case.

g.text: Your manager sets meeting norms and talks to the peer; behaviour improves. If not, the documented case moves to HR — and you're well prepared.

scenes.text: Amit gets a great offer and resigns by email at 11 pm with one line: 'I resign. Last day ASAP.' He mentally checks out and leaves no handover.
Swati gets an offer too. She tells her manager first in a 1:1, submits a formal letter, and builds a handover plan.
Two years later, Swati's old manager refers her for a senior role. Amit's background verification includes a lukewarm note and a delayed relieving letter.
The industry is smaller than it looks — especially in Indian tech hubs.

steps.title: Before you resign
steps.body:
- **Have a signed offer** (not just a verbal one) and ideally clear your background-verification documents.
- **Read your contract**: notice period (commonly 30–90 days in Indian corporate roles), buyout rules, leave adjustment, bond/clawback clauses (joining bonus, relocation, training costs).
- Know your **last working day** options: full notice, early release by mutual agreement, or buyout where permitted.

This is general education, not legal advice — check your own contract and HR policy.

steps.title: Worked example: telling your manager and the letter
steps.body:
**Tell your manager first, in person or on a call**, before HR or colleagues:
*'Priya, I wanted you to hear this from me first. I've accepted an offer and will be resigning. I've learned a lot here and want to make the transition smooth.'*

**Letter (short, positive, factual):**
*'Dear Priya, Please accept this as formal notice of my resignation from the role of Senior Analyst. As per my notice period of 60 days, my last working day will be 30 September. I will ensure a complete handover. Thank you for the opportunities and support. Regards, Swati'*

Submit it through the official HR system if there is one.

steps.title: Counter-offers and the notice period
steps.body:
Your company may make a **counter-offer**. Decide in advance what would make you stay — if the reasons you're leaving are not about money (growth, culture, manager), a raise often doesn't fix them. Never use a fake offer to get a raise; it can backfire badly.

During notice: keep working properly, write a **handover document** (ongoing tasks, contacts, passwords handed over through approved methods, known issues), train your replacement, don't take confidential data, and don't badmouth the company.

steps.title: Exit cleanly
steps.body:
- Collect your **relieving letter, experience letter, final settlement** details, and Form 16.
- Transfer **PF** using your UAN.
- In the exit interview, be honest but constructive.
- Send a warm goodbye note with your personal contact (LinkedIn). Thank people specifically.

Also: accepting an offer and then not joining ('ghosting') damages your reputation; if you change your mind, inform the new company promptly and politely.
